guide.common.0: Unplug the USB cable before connecting or removing any wire.
guide.common.1: After plugging in a sensor, press 'Rescan sensors' in the app.
guide.common.2: Never connect the 5V (or 3.3V) pin directly to GND (a short circuit can shut down or damage the board).
guide.common.3: Do not swap the module's VCC and GND. If a module gets hot, unplug the USB right away.
guide.common.4: Keep water and solutions away from the board, and place the board on a tray or stand.
guide.common.5: When the experiment is over, unplug the USB and put the sensors away. Rinse wet sensors and dry them before storing.
board.uno-r4-wifi.firmwareNote: Reference board. Tested on real hardware. Works over both USB and Bluetooth.
board.uno-r4-wifi.notes.0: I2C sensors are detected whether plugged into the Qwiic connector or the SDA/SCL pins.
board.uno-r4-minima.firmwareNote: Supports all sensors (compiles; not yet tested on real hardware). USB connection only.
board.nano-r4.firmwareNote: Supports all sensors (compiles; not yet tested on real hardware). USB connection only.
board.nano-r4.notes.0: Plugging it into a breadboard makes wiring easier. Pin names are printed on the side of the board.
board.mega-2560.name: Mega 2560 (incl. compatibles)
board.mega-2560.firmwareNote: Supports all sensors (compiles; not yet tested on real hardware). USB connection only.
board.mega-2560.notes.0: The I2C pins are D20/D21, not A4/A5.
board.mega-2560.notes.1: Compatible boards (CH340 chip) may need the CH340 driver on a Mac. If no port appears, install the driver from the seller.
board.uno-r3.name: UNO R3 (incl. compatibles)
board.uno-r3.notes.0: Compatible boards (CH340 chip) may need the CH340 driver on a Mac. If no port appears, install the driver from the seller.
board.nano.name: Nano (incl. compatibles)
board.nano.firmwareNote: A light version (same as UNO R3). Compiles; not yet tested on real hardware.
board.nano.notes.0: Compatible boards (CH340 chip) may need the CH340 driver on a Mac. If no port appears, install the driver from the seller.
board.nano.notes.1: If uploading to a compatible Nano fails, choose 'ATmega328P (Old Bootloader)' under Tools > Processor in the IDE.
board.leonardo.firmwareNote: The lightest version (BME280 and HX711 also left out). Compiles; not yet tested on real hardware.
board.leonardo.notes.0: D2/D3 are the I2C pins, so connect the DS18B20 to D9.
board.nano-every.firmwareNote: ChemDict firmware is in preparation. Use this only as a wiring reference.
board.nano-esp32.firmwareNote: ChemDict firmware is in preparation. Use this only as a wiring reference.
board.nano-esp32.notes.0: This is a 3.3 V board. Do not connect the signal wire of 5 V modules (MQ gas, HC-SR04, 5 V-only pH modules, etc.) directly.
board.nano-33-iot.firmwareNote: ChemDict firmware is in preparation. Use this only as a wiring reference.
board.nano-33-iot.notes.0: This is a 3.3 V board. Do not connect the signal wire of 5 V modules (MQ gas, HC-SR04, 5 V-only pH modules, etc.) directly.
board.nano-33-ble-sense.firmwareNote: ChemDict firmware is in preparation. Use this only as a wiring reference.
board.nano-33-ble-sense.notes.0: This is a 3.3 V board. Do not connect the signal wire of 5 V modules (MQ gas, HC-SR04, 5 V-only pH modules, etc.) directly.
board.nano-33-ble-sense.notes.1: The board has built-in temperature/humidity, pressure, color, sound and motion sensors (usable in the Arduino Science Journal app).
board.giga-r1.firmwareNote: ChemDict firmware is in preparation. Use this only as a wiring reference.
board.giga-r1.notes.0: This is a 3.3 V board. Do not connect the signal wire of 5 V modules (MQ gas, HC-SR04, 5 V-only pH modules, etc.) directly.
board.uno-q.firmwareNote: All sensors supported. Tested on a real board. Measures over Bluetooth only (USB-C is for power and uploading). Upload the measurement program once with the Arduino IDE.
board.uno-q.notes.0: Plug I2C sensors into the Qwiic connector or the SDA·SCL pins next to AREF. On the UNO Q, A4·A5 are not I2C.
conn.analog.name: Analog, 3 wires
conn.analog.steps.0: You can use A1–A3 instead of A0. Press the same port under 'Port' and the app sets it up automatically.
conn.analog.cautions.0: An analog input must not exceed the board voltage (5 V or 3.3 V).
conn.analog-divider.name: Analog + 10 kΩ resistor
conn.analog-divider.steps.0: From the wire joining the sensor's other leg to A0, connect a 10 kΩ resistor to GND (use a breadboard).
conn.analog-divider.bb: The sensor and the 10 kΩ resistor must meet in the same row.
conn.probe.name: Voltage, 2 wires
conn.probe.steps.0: Using alligator-clip leads, connect the cell's (+) terminal to A0 and its (−) terminal to GND.
conn.probe.cautions.0: Only 0–5 V can be measured (0–3.3 V on 3.3 V boards). Do not reverse the terminals or apply a higher voltage.
conn.probe.cautions.1: Do not measure several batteries connected in series.
conn.onewire.name: 1-Wire, 3 wires + 4.7 kΩ
conn.onewire.steps.0: Connect a 4.7 kΩ resistor between DATA and VCC. Skip this if you use a terminal adapter board, which has the resistor built in.
conn.onewire.cautions.0: Without the resistor the sensor will not be detected.
conn.onewire.bb: Use it to fit the 4.7 kΩ resistor or to plug several sensors side by side. Not needed for 1 sensor on an adapter board with a built-in resistor.
conn.dht.name: Digital, 3 wires
conn.dht.steps.0: For a bare 4-pin sensor (not a module), connect a 10 kΩ resistor between DATA and VCC. Leave pin 3 empty.
conn.dht.bb: A bare 4-pin sensor (not a module) needs a breadboard to fit the 10 kΩ resistor. 3-pin modules do not need one.
conn.qwiic.name: Qwiic cable
conn.qwiic.steps.0: If there is a Qwiic connector, push the cable in until it clicks. Either connector on the module works.
conn.qwiic.steps.1: On boards without a Qwiic connector, use a Qwiic-to-jumper cable and connect the pins as in the table above.
conn.qwiic.steps.2: With several modules, you can daisy-chain them with Qwiic cables.
conn.i2c.name: I2C, 4 wires (SDA/SCL)
conn.i2c.steps.0: If the module has a Qwiic/STEMMA QT connector, you can also use a Qwiic cable.
conn.i2c.steps.1: Several modules can share the same I2C lines (if their addresses differ).
conn.i2c.cautions.0: Connecting VCC to 3.3V is the safe choice. If the module is marked 'VIN 3–5 V', 5V is also fine.
conn.hx711.name: HX711, 4 wires + load cell
conn.hx711.steps.0: Connect the load cell wires to the HX711: red → E+, black → E−, white → A−, green → A+ (may vary by product).
conn.hx711.steps.1: Screw the base plate and pan to the load cell so the force acts in the direction of the arrow.
conn.hx711.cautions.0: On first use, in 'Calibrate', set zero (empty pan) and then a reference weight (e.g. 100 g) so the readings in g are correct.
conn.spi-tc.name: MAX6675, 5 wires
conn.spi-tc.steps.0: Connect the K-type thermocouple's (+) and (−) wires to the module's + / − screw terminals (usually red = −, yellow or blue = +; if reversed, the temperature goes down).
conn.ultrasonic.bb: If the sensor pins cannot reach the board directly, plug it into a breadboard and connect it with jumper wires.
part.ds18b20.name: Waterproof temperature sensor DS18B20
part.ds18b20.items.1: 1 × 4.7 kΩ resistor (not needed with an adapter board)
part.ds18b20.cautions.0: Wire colors vary by product. Check VCC, GND and DATA in the manual.
part.ds18b20.cautions.1: Put only the metal tip into the liquid. Keep the cable joint out of the water.
part.ds18b20.cautions.2: Range −55 to 125 °C. Boiling water is fine, but do not hold it in a flame.
part.ds18b20.cautions.3: Using 2 or more (thermal equilibrium, specific heat comparison): plug them side by side on the same VCC, GND and DATA rows. One 4.7 kΩ resistor is enough. Up to 4 on UNO R4/Mega, 2 on UNO R3/Nano.
part.lm35.name: LM35 temperature sensor
part.lm35.cautions.0: With the flat side facing you, the pins from left are VCC · signal · GND.
part.lm35.cautions.1: To put it in water, seal the legs with heat-shrink tubing.
part.tmp36.name: TMP36 temperature sensor
part.tmp36.cautions.0: With the flat side facing you, the pins from left are VCC · signal · GND.
part.max6675.name: K-type thermocouple MAX6675 (high temperature)
part.max6675.cautions.0: Measures 0 to 1024 °C, so it suits alcohol lamp and burner experiments. Keep the module board away from the flame.
part.max6675.cautions.1: Heat only the metal tip of the thermocouple.
part.dht.name: DHT11 / DHT22 temperature & humidity
part.dht.items.1: 3 jumper wires (add a 10 kΩ resistor for 4-pin types)
part.dht.cautions.0: DHT11 reads in steps of 1 °C and 1 %, DHT22 in steps of 0.1. The firmware tells them apart automatically.
part.dht.cautions.1: The sensor gives a new value once every 2 seconds. Humidity responds slowly, so wait 5–10 seconds.
part.dht.cautions.2: Pin order varies by product. Connect by the +, −, S (OUT) labels printed on the module.
part.modulino-thermo.name: Modulino Thermo (temperature & humidity)
part.modulino-thermo.cautions.0: It is not waterproof. Keep water drops off the sensor.
part.modulino-thermo.cautions.1: Holding the chip with your fingers raises the reading through body heat. Hold it by the edges.
part.modulino-thermo.cautions.2: Both the old version (0x44) and the new one (V0.5 or later, 0x45) are detected.
part.sht3x.name: SHT30 / SHT31 temperature & humidity module
part.sht3x.cautions.0: More accurate and faster than a DHT. The waterproof type (metal cap) connects the same way.
part.bme280.name: BME280 (temperature, humidity, pressure)
part.bme280.cautions.0: It looks the same as the BMP280. Only the BME280 gives humidity (its chip is nearly square).
part.bme280.cautions.1: Connecting the SDO pin to GND gives address 0x76; connecting it to 3.3V gives 0x77 (both are detected).
part.bmp280.name: BMP280 pressure sensor
part.bmp280.cautions.0: For atmospheric pressure. For syringe experiments (Boyle's law), put the whole module in a sealed container or use the gas pressure sensor.
part.modulino-pressure.name: Modulino Pressure (air pressure)
part.modulino-pressure.cautions.0: Measures atmospheric pressure and pressure differences with height.
part.mpx5700.name: Gas pressure sensor MPX5700AP (syringe)
part.mpx5700.cautions.0: Push the tubing firmly onto the sensor port and check for leaks.
part.mpx5700.cautions.1: It measures up to 700 kPa, but do not press the syringe so hard that the tubing pops off.
part.mpx5700.cautions.2: In 'Calibrate', do a 1-point calibration at atmospheric pressure (about 101.3 kPa).
part.scd4x.name: Carbon dioxide sensor SCD40 / SCD41
part.scd4x.items.1: 4 jumper wires (a cable for modules with a Qwiic connector)
part.scd4x.cautions.0: A new value comes every 5 seconds. For the first 1–2 minutes after power-on, values fluctuate.
part.scd4x.cautions.1: Great for respiration, fermentation and soda experiments. Keep water drops out of the sensor.
part.mq-gas.name: Gas sensor MQ-2 / MQ-3 / MQ-135 (relative)
part.mq-gas.cautions.0: Shows only relative change (%), not concentration (ppm).
part.mq-gas.cautions.1: Leave it on for at least 3 minutes to warm up before use. The sensor gets hot, so do not touch it.
part.mq-gas.cautions.2: MQ-2: flammable gases and smoke; MQ-3: alcohol; MQ-135: air quality (CO₂, NH₃, etc.).
part.o2.name: Oxygen sensor (analog, Gravity O₂)
part.o2.cautions.0: On first use, do a 1-point proportional calibration to 20.9 % in fresh air under 'Calibrate'.
part.o2.cautions.1: Used for combustion and respiration experiments. The sensor has a limited life, so keep it sealed when not in use.
part.ldr.name: Light sensor (CdS / phototransistor module)
part.ldr.cautions.0: For colorimeter experiments (light through a solution), fix the LED and sensor facing each other across the cuvette and block out room light.
part.tcs34725.name: Color sensor TCS34725
part.tcs34725.cautions.0: Shows R, G and B as a share (%) of total light. Used for indicator color changes and comparing solution concentrations.
part.tcs34725.cautions.1: The module's white LED turns on. Keep a constant distance (about 1 cm) from the sample.
part.uv.name: UV sensor GUVA-S12SD
part.uv.cautions.0: An approximate UV index. Used for sunscreen experiments.
part.ph.name: pH sensor (PH-4502C · Gravity pH)
part.ph.cautions.0: The glass bulb at the electrode tip breaks easily. Do not let it hit the bottom.
part.ph.cautions.1: Before the experiment, do a 2-point calibration in 'Calibrate': pH 7 first, then pH 4.
part.ph.cautions.2: For storage, fill the protective cap with storage solution (KCl) and put it on. Do not leave it soaking in distilled water.
part.ec.name: Conductivity (EC) sensor
part.ec.cautions.1: Rinse with distilled water between measurements.
part.tds.name: TDS sensor (total dissolved solids)
part.turbidity.name: Turbidity sensor
part.turbidity.cautions.0: Higher values mean clearer water (clarity %). Calibrate clean water as 100 % and compare.
part.turbidity.cautions.1: Keep the top part (circuit) of the sensor out of the water.
part.water-level.name: Water level sensor
part.water-level.cautions.0: A relative value (%). The electrodes corrode if left in water, so dip it in only while measuring.
part.soil.name: Soil moisture sensor (capacitive)
part.soil.cautions.0: A 2-point calibration with dry soil (0 %) and water (100 %) makes comparison easier.
part.soil.cautions.1: Keep the circuit part out of the soil and water.
part.hx711.name: Load cell + HX711 (electronic balance)
part.hx711.cautions.0: Used for mass change before and after a reaction (conservation of mass, gas release).
part.hx711.cautions.1: Do not exceed the load cell's rated capacity.
part.hcsr04.name: Ultrasonic distance sensor HC-SR04
part.hcsr04.cautions.0: Measures from 2 cm to 4 m. The object's surface must face the sensor squarely for accuracy.
part.fsr.name: Force sensor FSR
part.fsr.cautions.0: A relative value (%) of the pressing force.
part.pot.name: Potentiometer (knob)
part.pot.cautions.0: Shows how far it is turned as 0–100 %. Good for practicing with sensors.
part.voltage.name: Voltage (chemical cells)
part.voltage.cautions.0: Used for Daniell cell and fruit battery experiments.
part.sound.name: Sound sensor
part.sound.items.0: 1 sound sensor module (with an AO pin)
part.raw.name: Other analog sensor (calibrate yourself)
part.raw.items.0: A sensor with an analog output
part.raw.cautions.0: Records the voltage as is. In 'Calibrate' you can set units using two reference values.
trouble.no-port.title: The board does not appear in the list when connecting by USB
trouble.no-port.steps.0: Try a different USB cable. Charge-only cables do not carry data.
trouble.no-port.steps.1: Use a different USB port on the computer. Plugging directly into the computer is better than a hub.
trouble.no-port.steps.2: Compatible boards (CH340 chip) on Windows need the CH340 driver installed once.
trouble.no-port.steps.3: Check that you opened the app in Chrome or Edge. Safari and Firefox cannot connect over USB.
trouble.busy.title: It says 'Another program is using the board'
trouble.busy.steps.0: Close the Serial Monitor and Serial Plotter in the Arduino IDE.
trouble.busy.steps.1: Close any other tab or window where ChemDict Lab is open.
trouble.busy.steps.2: Unplug the USB, plug it back in and press [Connect USB].
trouble.no-fw.title: It says 'No measuring program found'
trouble.no-fw.steps.0: This board is being used for the first time. Press [Install firmware] on the step 1 screen (about 30 seconds).
trouble.no-fw.steps.1: UNO R4 and Leonardo cannot be installed from the web yet. Upload once with the Arduino IDE (step 3 → Board info → Get firmware).
trouble.no-fw.steps.2: You do not need to repeat it after installing. The program stays on the board even when unplugged.
trouble.flash-fail.title: Installing the firmware fails
trouble.flash-fail.steps.0: Unplug all sensor wires, connect only the board by USB, and press it again.
trouble.flash-fail.steps.1: For a compatible board, check that you chose the right board type (UNO, Nano, Mega) in step 1.
trouble.flash-fail.steps.2: If it still fails, press the board's RESET button once right after pressing [Install].
trouble.flash-fail.steps.3: A failed install does not damage the board. Just try again.
trouble.no-sensor.title: It says no sensor was found
trouble.no-sensor.steps.0: Unplug the USB and check the wires against the connection diagram. Make sure VCC (+) and GND (-) are not swapped.
trouble.no-sensor.steps.1: Press the jumper wires in firmly. On a breadboard, parts connect only when in the same row.
trouble.no-sensor.steps.2: Plug the USB back in and press [Rescan].
trouble.no-sensor.steps.3: The board may not support this sensor. Check whether the sensor card says 'Not supported on this board'.
trouble.odd-value.title: The value is stuck at 0 or at the maximum
trouble.odd-value.steps.0: For analog sensors, the port you plugged into (A0–A3) must match the port chosen in the app.
trouble.odd-value.steps.1: Check that you used the sensor's AO (analog output) pin. The DO pin only gives on/off.
trouble.odd-value.steps.2: For sensors that need calibration, such as pH and conductivity, run [Calibrate sensor] first.
trouble.ble.title: The board does not appear over Bluetooth
trouble.ble.steps.0: Bluetooth works only on the UNO R4 WiFi. Connect other boards by USB.
trouble.ble.steps.1: Check that the board is getting USB power (a power bank also works).
trouble.ble.steps.2: If another device is already connected, the board will not appear. Disconnect it on that device.
trouble.ble.steps.3: If two boards have the same group number (ChemDict-01–08), change one of them.
trouble.stopped.title: The graph stopped during a run
trouble.stopped.steps.0: The cable may have come loose or been jostled. Check whether 'Connection lost' appeared at the top of the screen.
trouble.stopped.steps.1: When you reconnect, all data recorded so far is kept.
trouble.stopped.steps.2: Keep the laptop from going into sleep mode.
bb.intro: A breadboard lets you build circuits by plugging in parts and wires without soldering. Use it to add a resistor, to plug several sensors side by side on the same lines, or to build circuits that measure voltage and current.
bb.structure.0: On each side of the center groove, the five holes a–e (top) and f–j (bottom) are connected in one vertical row (the green cells in the picture).
bb.structure.1: Neighboring holes across a row are not connected. The two sides of the center groove (e and f) are not connected either.
bb.structure.2: The long strips at the top and bottom edges (red +, blue −) run the full length. Plug the board's 5V into the + strip and GND into the − strip to use them as power rails.
bb.structure.3: On some long breadboards the power rails are split in the middle. To use both halves, join them with a short wire.
bb.rules.0: Unplug the USB before connecting or removing any wire.
bb.rules.1: First connect board 5V → + rail and GND → − rail. If you use only 3.3 V sensors, use 3.3V instead of 5V.
bb.rules.2: If both legs of a part are in the same vertical row, the part is bypassed. Put the legs in different rows.
bb.rules.3: Resistors have no direction. For an LED the long leg is +; for an electrolytic capacitor the leg without the stripe is +.
bb.rules.4: Never join the + and − rails directly with one wire (short circuit).
bb.rules.5: Fixed wire colors cut down on mistakes: red = 5V, black = GND, other colors = signal.
bb.rules.6: Push wires all the way into the holes. Loose wires cause jumpy values or undetected sensors.
bb.res.10 kΩ.use: Light and force sensors, thermistors, 4-pin DHT
bb.circuit.divider.name: Voltage divider (LDR light sensor · FSR force sensor · thermistor)
bb.circuit.divider.what: The sensor and a 10 kΩ resistor meet in one row, and A0 reads the voltage of that row.
bb.circuit.divider.steps.1: Red wire from the + rail → column 6.
bb.circuit.divider.steps.2: Plug the sensor legs into columns 6 and 9.
bb.circuit.divider.steps.3: Plug the 10 kΩ resistor into columns 9 and 13.
bb.circuit.divider.steps.5: Column 9 (where sensor and resistor meet) → board A0.
bb.circuit.pullup.name: Several temperature sensors + 4.7 kΩ (DS18B20)
bb.circuit.pullup.what: Plug each sensor's GND, VCC and DATA wires side by side into the same three rows, and add just one 4.7 kΩ between the VCC and DATA rows.
bb.circuit.pullup.steps.1: Run wires from column 8 → − rail and column 10 → + rail.
bb.circuit.pullup.steps.2: Plug sensor 1's black, red and yellow wires into columns 8, 10 and 12.
bb.circuit.pullup.steps.3: Plug sensor 2 into other holes of the same columns 8, 10 and 12.
bb.circuit.pullup.steps.4: Plug the 4.7 kΩ resistor into columns 10 and 12 (one is enough).
bb.circuit.series-ref.name: Measuring voltage and current (test resistor + 100 Ω reference)
bb.circuit.series-ref.what: Connect the component and the reference resistor in series. Reference resistor voltage (A1) ÷ 100 Ω = current; A0 − A1 = component voltage.
bb.circuit.series-ref.steps.0: Board GND → − rail. Plug the battery (−) into the − rail too, so it shares GND with the board.
bb.circuit.series-ref.steps.2: Plug the test resistor R into columns 4 and 9.
bb.circuit.series-ref.steps.3: Plug the 100 Ω resistor into columns 9 and 14.
bb.circuit.led.name: LED turn-on voltage (potentiometer + LED + 100 Ω)
bb.circuit.led.what: Raise the voltage little by little with the potentiometer and measure the LED voltage (A0 − A1) and current (A1 ÷ 100 Ω).
bb.circuit.led.steps.1: Plug the potentiometer's three legs into columns 4, 6 and 8; column 4 → + rail, column 8 → − rail.
bb.circuit.led.steps.2: Plug the LED's long leg into column 6 (middle-leg row) and the short leg into column 10.
bb.circuit.led.steps.3: Plug the 100 Ω resistor into columns 10 and 15; column 15 → − rail.
bb.circuit.rc.name: Capacitor charge and discharge (10 kΩ + 1000 µF)
bb.circuit.rc.what: Charge the capacitor from 5 V through the resistor and measure the capacitor voltage on A0. Moving the 5 V wire to GND discharges it.
bb.circuit.rc.steps.1: + rail → column 5 (charging wire). To discharge, move this wire to the − rail.
bb.circuit.rc.steps.2: Plug the 10 kΩ resistor into columns 5 and 10.
bb.circuit.rc.steps.3: Plug the capacitor's + leg into column 10 and its − leg (stripe side) into column 13; column 13 → − rail.
bb.circuit.rc.caution: An electrolytic capacitor can swell or burst if reversed. Put the striped leg toward the − rail.

exp.cur-b-ecosystem.title: Day and night in a pondweed-and-snail jar (cycling of matter)
exp.cur-b-ecosystem.subject: Life Science
exp.cur-b-ecosystem.summary: Track water pH through light–dark cycles to see how producers and consumers cycle matter.
exp.cur-b-ecosystem.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-b-ecosystem.steps.0: Put the pH electrode into a jar with pondweed and snails, and place the light sensor beside it.
exp.cur-b-ecosystem.steps.2: Check whether pH rises by day and falls at night. Compare with a jar holding only snails.
exp.cur-b-ecosystem.std.0: Students can understand the structure of ecosystems and explain the importance of ecosystem components by inferring the cycling of matter and the flow of energy.
exp.cur-b-exercise.title: Exercise intensity, breath and sweat (integration of organ systems)
exp.cur-b-exercise.subject: Life Science
exp.cur-b-exercise.summary: Compare exhaled CO2, humidity and recovery time at different exercise intensities.
exp.cur-b-exercise.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-b-exercise.steps.0: Breathe out once into a 5 L container and measure for 2 minutes.
exp.cur-b-exercise.steps.1: Repeat the same way after walking and after jogging on the spot ('New run').
exp.cur-b-exercise.steps.2: Compare the peak values and the time to return to baseline.
exp.cur-b-exercise.std.0: Students can infer, in connection with physiological changes in the body, that digestion, circulation, respiration and excretion result from the integrated action of organ systems.
exp.cur-b-exercise.cautions.0: CO2 values are diluted, so use them only for relative comparison.
exp.cur-b-homeostasis.title: Hand temperature recovery after cold water (homeostasis)
exp.cur-b-homeostasis.subject: Life Science
exp.cur-b-homeostasis.summary: Compare how long the skin on the back of the hand takes to cool and recover.
exp.cur-b-homeostasis.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-b-homeostasis.steps.0: Tape the temperature sensor to the back of the hand.
exp.cur-b-homeostasis.steps.1: Record for 1 minute, then dip the hand in cold water for 30 seconds and take it out.
exp.cur-b-homeostasis.steps.2: Compare between people how long it takes to return to the original temperature.
exp.cur-b-homeostasis.std.0: Students can infer how homeostasis is maintained in the body based on an understanding of how the endocrine and nervous systems work and interact.
exp.cur-b-homeostasis.cautions.0: Do not keep hands in ice water for long.
exp.cur-b-seed-heat.title: Heat and CO2 from germinating seeds
exp.cur-b-seed-heat.subject: Life Science
exp.cur-b-seed-heat.summary: Use the temperature and CO2 of germinating seeds in a vacuum flask to see energy conversion in metabolism.
exp.cur-b-seed-heat.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-b-seed-heat.steps.0: Fill a vacuum flask with soaked beans and insert the sensors.
exp.cur-b-seed-heat.steps.1: Record every 1 minute for a day.
exp.cur-b-seed-heat.steps.2: Compare with a flask of boiled beans (control).
exp.cur-b-seed-heat.std.0: Students can infer the use of energy in various life activities based on energy conversion during metabolism.
exp.cur-b-yeast-growth.title: Yeast population growth curve (turbidity)
exp.cur-b-yeast-growth.subject: Life Science
exp.cur-b-yeast-growth.summary: Draw an S-shaped growth curve from the drop in light passing through a yeast culture.
exp.cur-b-yeast-growth.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-b-yeast-growth.steps.0: Put an LED on one side of a clear bottle of sugar water with a little yeast, and the light sensor on the other side.
exp.cur-b-yeast-growth.steps.2: Make absorbance with ‘Calculated column → log10’ and find the three phases of the S-curve.
exp.cur-b-yeast-growth.std.0: Students can understand the characteristics of populations and communities, and research and present examples of their interactions.
exp.cur-c-bond-ec.title: Electrical properties of chemical bonds
exp.cur-c-bond-ec.subject: Chemistry
exp.cur-c-bond-ec.summary: Compare the conductivity of solids and solutions, ionic and molecular substances.
exp.cur-c-bond-ec.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-c-bond-ec.steps.0: Number the samples: NaCl(s), NaCl(aq), sugar(aq), ethanol(aq), KNO3(aq), etc.
exp.cur-c-bond-ec.steps.1: Dip the electrode and press ‘Record value’ once the reading is stable.
exp.cur-c-bond-ec.steps.2: Explain how the type of bond relates to conductivity.
exp.cur-c-bond-ec.std.0: Students can explain the electrical properties of chemical bonds through experiments.
exp.cur-c-chromate.title: Colors of the chromate–dichromate equilibrium
exp.cur-c-chromate.subject: Chemistry
exp.cur-c-chromate.summary: Watch the color (blue-channel absorbance) shift back and forth as you add acid and then base.
exp.cur-c-chromate.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-c-chromate.steps.0: Put K2CrO4 solution in a cuvette between a white LED and the color sensor.
exp.cur-c-chromate.steps.1: Measure while adding HCl drop by drop, then NaOH (mark them with ‘Add note’).
exp.cur-c-chromate.steps.2: Look at the absorbance change with ‘Calculated column → log10’.
exp.cur-c-chromate.std.0: Students can explain the characteristics of chemical equilibrium in reversible reactions.
exp.cur-c-chromate.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-c-cobalt.title: Change the temperature and cobalt chloride changes color (equilibrium shift)
exp.cur-c-cobalt.subject: Chemistry
exp.cur-c-cobalt.summary: Record the change to blue on heating and pink on cooling, together with temperature.
exp.cur-c-cobalt.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-c-cobalt.steps.0: Put cobalt chloride solution (ethanol + water) in a test tube with the color sensor and temperature sensor.
exp.cur-c-cobalt.steps.1: Measure while moving it back and forth between hot water and ice water.
exp.cur-c-cobalt.steps.2: Switch to ‘X axis → Temperature’ to see how temperature relates to color (R, B).
exp.cur-c-cobalt.std.0: Students can understand shifts in chemical equilibrium caused by changes in concentration, pressure and temperature, and appreciate the usefulness of chemistry by applying this to explain everyday phenomena.
exp.cur-c-cobalt.cautions.0: Do not touch cobalt chloride with bare hands.
exp.cur-c-fescn.title: Finding an equilibrium constant from absorbance (FeSCN²⁺)
exp.cur-c-fescn.subject: Chemistry
exp.cur-c-fescn.summary: Find equilibrium concentrations from a calibration curve and check whether the equilibrium constant stays the same.
exp.cur-c-fescn.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-c-fescn.steps.0: Make the first record with a cuvette of water (I₀).
exp.cur-c-fescn.steps.1: Insert the standard solutions in order of concentration, pressing ‘Record value’ for each.
exp.cur-c-fescn.steps.2: In the saved Excel file, make an A = −log(I/I₀) calibration curve and find the sample concentrations.
exp.cur-c-fescn.std.0: Students can explain the meaning of the equilibrium constant from concentration data of reactants and products in a chemical reaction.
exp.cur-c-stoich.title: Quantitative relationships in the reaction of calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid
exp.cur-c-stoich.subject: Chemistry
exp.cur-c-stoich.summary: Use the mass of CO2 that escapes to see the quantitative relationship between reactants and products.
exp.cur-c-stoich.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-c-stoich.steps.0: Place an Erlenmeyer flask of dilute hydrochloric acid on the load cell and set zero.
exp.cur-c-stoich.steps.1: Add calcium carbonate and measure until the mass stops decreasing.
exp.cur-c-stoich.steps.2: Repeat with different amounts of calcium carbonate, and check that the mass lost is about 44/100 of the CaCO3 mass.
exp.cur-c-stoich.std.0: Students can represent various reactions with chemical equations and explain the quantitative relationships of substances in chemical reactions.
exp.cur-c-stoich.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-ce-acidification.title: Acidified oceans and seashells
exp.cur-ce-acidification.subject: Climate Change and Ecology
exp.cur-ce-acidification.summary: Compare the mass loss of seashells soaked in water of different pH.
exp.cur-ce-acidification.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-ce-acidification.steps.0: Adjust water to pH 4, 5 and 6 (diluted vinegar) using the pH sensor.
exp.cur-ce-acidification.steps.1: Soak the shells; every day take them out, dry them, weigh them on the load cell and press ‘Record value’ (a new run for each pH).
exp.cur-ce-acidification.steps.2: Check whether lower pH makes the mass drop faster.
exp.cur-ce-acidification.std.0: Through examples of coral bleaching caused by coral die-off, students can examine the effects of climate change on marine ecosystems and present examples of science and technology that can prevent or restore ocean desertification.
exp.cur-ce-algae.title: Do algae grow more when it is warm and nutrient-rich? (algal bloom)
exp.cur-ce-algae.subject: Climate Change and Ecology
exp.cur-ce-algae.summary: Record the green-light absorption and temperature of pond water for 1–2 weeks.
exp.cur-ce-algae.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-ce-algae.steps.0: Of two bottles of pond water, add a little fertilizer to one.
exp.cur-ce-algae.steps.1: Put an LED behind the bottle and the color sensor in front, and record every 1 hour (a new run per bottle, or 2 boards).
exp.cur-ce-algae.steps.2: Compare how fast green transmission drops (algae increase).
exp.cur-ce-algae.std.0: Students can understand algal blooms in aquatic ecosystems and infer the effects of climate change on the biodiversity of aquatic ecosystems.
exp.cur-ce-carbon-capture.title: Catch the carbon dioxide (carbon capture)
exp.cur-ce-carbon-capture.subject: Climate Change and Ecology
exp.cur-ce-carbon-capture.summary: In sealed boxes, compare the CO2 decrease with calcium hydroxide, with plants and with nothing.
exp.cur-ce-carbon-capture.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-ce-carbon-capture.steps.0: Breathe into each box so they all start with the same CO2.
exp.cur-ce-carbon-capture.steps.1: Add an absorber (calcium hydroxide, activated carbon, a plant) and measure for 30 minutes ('New run').
exp.cur-ce-carbon-capture.steps.2: Compare the slopes of the decrease and link them to carbon capture technology.
exp.cur-ce-carbon-capture.std.0: Students can investigate the current development of carbon-reduction science and technology for achieving a carbon-neutral society and present examples of its application.
exp.cur-ce-ice-albedo.title: Once ice melts, things warm faster (feedback)
exp.cur-ce-ice-albedo.subject: Climate Change and Ecology
exp.cur-ce-ice-albedo.summary: Use the temperatures of a white board, a black board and an ice-covered board to see ice–albedo feedback.
exp.cur-ce-ice-albedo.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-ce-ice-albedo.steps.0: Place temperature sensors under a white board, a black board and an ice-covered black board.
exp.cur-ce-ice-albedo.steps.1: Measure under a lamp for 30 minutes.
exp.cur-ce-ice-albedo.steps.2: Check whether the temperature rises faster after the ice melts.
exp.cur-ce-ice-albedo.std.0: Students can understand the feedback processes that maintain the climate system and explain the interactions between the biosphere and the other spheres.
exp.cur-ce-ice-albedo.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-ce-ice-albedo.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-ce-sea-level.title: Does sea level rise when water warms? (thermal expansion)
exp.cur-ce-sea-level.subject: Climate Change and Ecology
exp.cur-ce-sea-level.summary: Enter the water level in a thin tube as the temperature rises to see the temperature–level relationship.
area.기후변화와 지구 환경: Climate change and the Earth's environment
exp.cur-ce-sea-level.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-ce-sea-level.steps.0: Insert a thin tube and the temperature sensor into a flask filled to the top with water.
exp.cur-ce-sea-level.steps.1: Warm it in a water bath; each time the level rises 2 mm, enter the value and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-ce-sea-level.steps.2: Also compare the level change when land ice and sea ice melt.
exp.cur-ce-sea-level.std.0: Students can explain sea-level rise due to melting ice sheets and thermal expansion in connection with climate change.
exp.cur-ce-station.title: School weather station (weather and climate)
exp.cur-ce-station.subject: Climate Change and Ecology
exp.cur-ce-station.summary: Record air temperature, humidity and pressure for a month and compare them with climate normals.
exp.cur-ce-station.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-ce-station.steps.0: Place the sensor in a ventilated spot out of direct sunlight.
exp.cur-ce-station.steps.1: Record every 10 minutes for a month.
exp.cur-ce-station.steps.2: Save to Excel, calculate daily means and compare them with the weather service's climate normals.
exp.cur-ce-station.std.0: Students can understand the characteristics of weather and climate and explain them by comparison.
exp.cur-cl-diffusion.title: Ions leaving dialysis tubing (membrane transport)
exp.cur-cl-diffusion.subject: Cells and Metabolism
exp.cur-cl-diffusion.summary: Watch conductivity rise as salt water in a dialysis bag diffuses outward.
exp.cur-cl-diffusion.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-cl-diffusion.steps.0: Fill a dialysis tubing bag with strong salt water and tie it off.
exp.cur-cl-diffusion.steps.1: Put it in a beaker of distilled water and measure the conductivity of the outer water.
exp.cur-cl-diffusion.steps.2: Repeat at different temperatures and compare diffusion rates.
exp.cur-cl-diffusion.std.0: Students can understand the structure and properties of the cell membrane and infer how substances are transported across it.
exp.cur-cl-enzyme.title: Factors affecting enzyme activity
exp.cur-cl-enzyme.subject: Cells and Metabolism
exp.cur-cl-enzyme.summary: Compare how fast pressure rises in the catalase reaction at different temperatures, pH and enzyme amounts.
exp.cur-cl-enzyme.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-cl-enzyme.steps.0: Prepare liver (or potato) extract and hydrogen peroxide for each condition.
exp.cur-cl-enzyme.steps.1: Mix, close immediately and measure (a new run for each condition).
exp.cur-cl-enzyme.steps.2: Plot the initial slope against temperature (or pH) to find the optimum.
exp.cur-cl-enzyme.std.0: Students can understand the types and properties of enzymes and design and carry out experiments on factors that affect enzyme activity.
exp.cur-cl-fermentation.title: Types of sugar and yeast fermentation
exp.cur-cl-fermentation.subject: Cells and Metabolism
exp.cur-cl-fermentation.summary: Compare the CO2 yeast produces from glucose, sucrose and lactose.
exp.cur-cl-fermentation.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-cl-fermentation.steps.0: Make yeast solutions with glucose, sucrose and lactose at the same concentration.
exp.cur-cl-fermentation.steps.1: Put each one in a sealed container and measure for 20 minutes ('New run').
exp.cur-cl-fermentation.steps.2: Use enzymes to explain why CO2 hardly increases with lactose.
exp.cur-cl-fermentation.std.0: Students can understand the similarities and differences between aerobic respiration and fermentation, and plan and carry out research on everyday uses of fermentation.
exp.cur-cl-light-color.title: Light color and photosynthesis
exp.cur-cl-light-color.subject: Cells and Metabolism
exp.cur-cl-light-color.summary: Compare how fast CO2 falls in a sealed container under red, green and blue light.
exp.cur-cl-light-color.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-cl-light-color.steps.0: Put a plant in a clear container with the CO2 and light sensors.
exp.cur-cl-light-color.steps.1: Switch between red, green and blue LEDs, measuring 10 minutes each ('New run').
exp.cur-cl-light-color.steps.2: Link the slow rate under green light to chlorophyll absorption.
exp.cur-cl-light-color.std.0: Students can distinguish the light reactions and carbon fixation reactions of photosynthesis step by step, understand their features, and infer how the two are related.
exp.cur-cl-metabolism-heat.title: Temperature of fermenting yeast
exp.cur-cl-metabolism-heat.subject: Cells and Metabolism
exp.cur-cl-metabolism-heat.summary: Use the heat from fermenting yeast in a vacuum flask to see energy release in catabolism.
exp.cur-cl-metabolism-heat.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-cl-metabolism-heat.steps.0: Fill two vacuum flasks, one with sugar water + yeast and one with sugar water only, and insert the sensors.
exp.cur-cl-metabolism-heat.steps.1: Record every 1 minute for at least 2 hours.
exp.cur-cl-metabolism-heat.steps.2: Check whether only the living one gets warmer.
exp.cur-cl-metabolism-heat.std.0: Students can understand that metabolism is the set of chemical reactions that sustain life in organisms, and infer that it involves the transfer of energy.
exp.cur-cl-metabolism-heat.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-cl-metabolism-heat.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-cs-data-problem.title: Classroom air and drowsiness (finding problems with data)
exp.cur-cs-data-problem.subject: Integrated Science Inquiry
exp.cur-cs-data-problem.summary: Overlay classroom CO2 records with a survey to find an inquiry question.
area.융합과학 탐구의 과정: The process of integrated science inquiry
exp.cur-cs-data-problem.markers.label: Note
exp.cur-cs-data-problem.steps.0: Record classroom CO2, temperature and humidity for a day.
exp.cur-cs-data-problem.steps.1: Run a drowsiness survey each period and mark it with ‘Note’.
exp.cur-cs-data-problem.steps.2: Distinguish correlation from causation and pose an inquiry question.
exp.cur-cs-data-problem.std.0: Students can independently discover integrated inquiry questions by processing data obtained directly through observation or experience in everyday life, or from public data.
exp.cur-cs-digital-vs-manual.title: Thermometer vs. sensor: what's the difference? (evaluating digital tools)
exp.cur-cs-digital-vs-manual.subject: Integrated Science Inquiry
exp.cur-cs-digital-vs-manual.summary: Compare hand recording and sensor recording of the same cooling experiment.
exp.cur-cs-digital-vs-manual.steps.0: Put a thermometer and a temperature sensor together into hot water.
exp.cur-cs-digital-vs-manual.steps.1: One student writes the reading by hand every 30 seconds while the sensor records every 1 second.
exp.cur-cs-digital-vs-manual.steps.2: Compare the number of data points, time resolution, human error and the sensor's limits.
exp.cur-cs-digital-vs-manual.std.0: Students can research examples of using digital inquiry tools and technologies, including artificial intelligence, and evaluate the significance of using them in the process of scientific inquiry.
exp.cur-cs-digital-vs-manual.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-cs-reliability.title: Can we trust the two sensors? (validity and reliability)
exp.cur-cs-reliability.subject: Integrated Science Inquiry
exp.cur-cs-reliability.summary: Measure the same thing with two different sensors and evaluate the difference and spread.
exp.cur-cs-reliability.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-cs-reliability.steps.0: Place the waterproof temperature sensor and the temperature & humidity sensor side by side.
exp.cur-cs-reliability.steps.1: Measure for 10 minutes, then warm them in your hand and let go to see the response speed.
exp.cur-cs-reliability.steps.2: Compare the mean difference (bias) and standard deviation (precision), then measure again after ‘Calibrate’.
exp.cur-cs-reliability.std.0: Students can collect data using various tools, including digital inquiry tools, and evaluate the validity and reliability of the collected data.
exp.cur-e-albedo.title: Albedo and temperature (factors in climate change)
exp.cur-e-albedo.subject: Earth Science
exp.cur-e-albedo.summary: Compare the temperature rise of white, black and foil surfaces.
exp.cur-e-albedo.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-e-albedo.steps.0: Put one temperature sensor under each of white paper, black paper and aluminum foil.
exp.cur-e-albedo.steps.1: Measure under the same lamp for 15 minutes.
exp.cur-e-albedo.steps.2: Check whether lower albedo means higher temperature, and link it to ice–albedo feedback.
exp.cur-e-albedo.std.0: Students can explain the causes of climate change by dividing them into natural and human factors, and explore scientific ways to solve climate change problems caused by human activity.
exp.cur-e-albedo.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-e-albedo.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-e-front.title: When a front passes (continuous weather observation)
exp.cur-e-front.subject: Earth Science
exp.cur-e-front.summary: Record pressure, air temperature and humidity for several days to find a front passing.
exp.cur-e-front.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-e-front.steps.0: Place the sensor in the shade by a window.
exp.cur-e-front.steps.2: Compare the time of lowest pressure and of a sharp temperature drop with weather maps.
exp.cur-e-front.std.0: Students can predict weather changes as mid-latitude cyclones and anticyclones pass by combining weather maps, satellite images and radar images.
exp.cur-e-salinity.title: Salinity and electrical conductivity (properties of seawater)
exp.cur-e-salinity.subject: Earth Science
exp.cur-e-salinity.summary: Estimate seawater salinity from a conductivity calibration curve of salt solutions.
exp.cur-e-salinity.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-e-salinity.steps.1: Dip the electrode in each concentration and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-e-salinity.steps.2: Use a ‘Curve fit → Linear’ calibration line to find the salinity of an unknown seawater sample.
exp.cur-e-salinity.std.0: Students can understand the physical and chemical properties of seawater and analyze and interpret the distribution of temperature, salinity, density, dissolved oxygen, etc. using measured data.
exp.cur-e-star-color.title: Hotter means bluer (star color and temperature)
exp.cur-e-star-color.subject: Earth Science
exp.cur-e-star-color.summary: Watch the R:B ratio of the light change as you raise an incandescent bulb's voltage.
exp.cur-e-star-color.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-e-star-color.steps.0: Connect a small incandescent bulb (flashlight bulb) to a variable power supply.
exp.cur-e-star-color.steps.1: Raise the voltage 1 V at a time and press ‘Record value’ with the color sensor.
exp.cur-e-star-color.steps.2: Calculate from the table whether the B/R ratio increases (gets bluer).
exp.cur-e-star-color.std.0: Students can understand how stellar spectral types are determined and how stars are classified, and infer the physical quantities of stars using the laws of blackbody radiation.
exp.cur-e-star-color.materials.2: Variable power supply (or number of batteries)
exp.cur-e-star-color.cautions.0: An LED is not a blackbody, so use an incandescent bulb.
exp.cur-e-thermocline.title: What wind does to the mixed layer (layered structure of seawater)
exp.cur-e-thermocline.subject: Earth Science
exp.cur-e-thermocline.summary: Use a lamp and a fan to create and compare temperature profiles with depth in a water tank.
exp.cur-e-thermocline.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-e-thermocline.steps.0: Shine a lamp onto the tank from above.
exp.cur-e-thermocline.steps.1: Lower the sensor 2 cm at a time, pressing ‘Record value’ each time.
exp.cur-e-thermocline.steps.2: Repeat after blowing with a fan and compare the mixed-layer thickness.
exp.cur-e-thermocline.std.0: Students can understand the physical and chemical properties of seawater and analyze and interpret the distribution of temperature, salinity, density, dissolved oxygen, etc. using measured data.
exp.cur-em-planck.title: Estimating Planck's constant from LED threshold voltages
exp.cur-em-planck.subject: Electromagnetism and Quantum
exp.cur-em-planck.summary: Estimate h from the turn-on voltages of LEDs of different colors (wavelengths).
exp.cur-em-planck.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-em-planck.steps.0: Wire 5 V → potentiometer middle → 100 Ω → LED long leg, and LED short leg → GND; plug A0 into the LED long-leg row. Swap LEDs starting from red (630 nm).
exp.cur-em-planck.steps.1: Press ‘Record value’ when light first appears (A0 = LED voltage).
exp.cur-em-planck.steps.2: In Excel, find h from the slope of the 1/λ–voltage line = hc/e.
exp.cur-em-planck.std.0: Students can know how light and matter interact in the photoelectric effect and research various technologies related to it, such as digital imaging, light sensors and solar cells.
exp.cur-em-planck.bb: Connects the potentiometer, 100 Ω resistor and LED.
exp.cur-em-polarizer.title: Polarizer angle and light intensity (Malus's law)
exp.cur-em-polarizer.subject: Electromagnetism and Quantum
exp.cur-em-polarizer.summary: Measure the light passing through two polarizers at different angles to see the cos² relationship.
exp.cur-em-polarizer.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-em-polarizer.steps.0: Arrange in order: lamp → polarizer 1 → polarizer 2 → light sensor.
exp.cur-em-polarizer.steps.1: Rotate polarizer 2 by 10° at a time, pressing ‘Record value’ each time.
exp.cur-em-polarizer.steps.2: Check for a maximum at 0° and a minimum at 90°, and link it to how LCDs work.
exp.cur-em-polarizer.std.0: Students can understand the principle of polarization and research examples of digital information technologies that use it.
exp.cur-em-rc-energy.title: Energy stored in a capacitor (RC discharge)
exp.cur-em-rc-energy.subject: Electromagnetism and Quantum
exp.cur-em-rc-energy.summary: Find the time constant from the discharge curve and calculate the stored energy.
exp.cur-em-rc-energy.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-em-rc-energy.steps.0: Charge via 5 V → 10 kΩ → capacitor (+), capacitor (−) → GND, then move the 5 V wire to GND and measure while it discharges.
exp.cur-em-rc-energy.steps.2: Compare ½CV² with how long it can light an LED.
exp.cur-em-rc-energy.std.0: Students can find devices that use resistors, capacitors and inductors and explain them qualitatively in terms of energy.
exp.cur-em-rc-energy.bb: Plug the resistor and capacitor in series.
exp.cur-em-transistor.title: Diode and transistor switch
exp.cur-em-transistor.subject: Electromagnetism and Quantum
exp.cur-em-transistor.summary: Find the point where LED current switches on as the base voltage rises.
exp.cur-em-transistor.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-em-transistor.steps.0: Connect potentiometer middle → 10 kΩ → base, 5 V → LED → collector, and emitter → 100 Ω → GND.
exp.cur-em-transistor.steps.1: Plug A0 into the potentiometer middle and A1 into the emitter row; turn a little at a time, pressing ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-em-transistor.steps.2: LED current ≈ A1 ÷ 100 Ω. Check whether current switches on once A0 exceeds about 0.7 V (switch).
exp.cur-em-transistor.std.0: Students can analyze electronic circuits that use semiconductor devices such as diodes and transistors, and recognize the importance of semiconductors in modern civilization.
exp.cur-em-transistor.bb: Plug in the transistor, LED and resistors.
exp.cur-es-cloud.title: Adiabatic expansion and clouds (atmospheric stability)
exp.cur-es-cloud.subject: Earth System Science
exp.cur-es-cloud.summary: See a cloud form as falling pressure drops the temperature below the dew point.
exp.cur-es-cloud.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-es-cloud.steps.0: Put a BME280 and incense smoke into a PET bottle with a little water, and pressurize it.
exp.cur-es-cloud.steps.1: Start the run and open the cap all at once.
exp.cur-es-cloud.steps.2: Calculate the dew point from temperature and humidity and compare it with when the cloud formed.
exp.cur-es-cloud.std.0: Students can understand the relationship between the vertical temperature profile and atmospheric stability, and analyze how fog and clouds form through adiabatic changes and how precipitation occurs.
exp.cur-es-greenhouse-gas.title: Air, CO2 or water vapor: which bottle gets warmer?
exp.cur-es-greenhouse-gas.subject: Earth System Science
exp.cur-es-greenhouse-gas.summary: Compare the selective absorption of greenhouse gases with a bottle model.
exp.cur-es-greenhouse-gas.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-es-greenhouse-gas.steps.0: Put temperature sensors into a bottle of air, a bottle of CO2 and a bottle with a wet sponge.
exp.cur-es-greenhouse-gas.steps.1: Measure under the same bulb for 15 minutes.
exp.cur-es-greenhouse-gas.steps.2: Repeat with the bottles swapped and discuss the limits of the model.
exp.cur-es-greenhouse-gas.std.0: Students can understand that the gases making up the atmosphere are selective absorbers, and infer the conditions for life on Earth from the greenhouse effect, the blocking of solar ultraviolet radiation and the presence of water.
exp.cur-es-greenhouse-gas.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-es-greenhouse-gas.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-es-ocean-co2.title: When the ocean dissolves carbon dioxide (carbon cycle)
exp.cur-es-ocean-co2.subject: Earth System Science
exp.cur-es-ocean-co2.summary: See whether blowing CO2 into water lowers the pH, and whether adding limestone brings it back.
exp.cur-es-ocean-co2.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-es-ocean-co2.steps.0: Put the pH electrode in water and start the run.
exp.cur-es-ocean-co2.steps.1: Blow exhaled breath (or CO2) in through a straw and press ‘Add note’.
exp.cur-es-ocean-co2.steps.2: Add powdered limestone and see whether the pH recovers.
exp.cur-es-ocean-co2.std.0: Students can trace how the geosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere have changed through the cycling of water, carbon and oxygen over the history of the Earth system's evolution.
exp.cur-es-pressure-height.title: Air pressure with height (hydrostatic equilibrium)
exp.cur-es-pressure-height.subject: Earth System Science
exp.cur-es-pressure-height.summary: Measure the pressure on each floor and find the air density from the slope.
exp.cur-es-pressure-height.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-es-pressure-height.steps.0: Make the first record on the 1st floor (0 m).
exp.cur-es-pressure-height.steps.1: Press ‘Record value’ each time you go up one floor (about 3 m) (tablet + Bluetooth).
exp.cur-es-pressure-height.steps.2: Find ρ in ΔP = −ρgΔz from the ‘Curve fit → Linear’ slope.
exp.cur-es-pressure-height.std.0: Students can understand hydrostatic balance from the vertical distribution of air pressure and infer the causes of vertical motion in the atmosphere.
exp.cur-es-pressure-height.materials.1: UNO R4 WiFi + tablet or laptop
exp.cur-es-surface.title: Daily temperature by surface type (heat budget)
exp.cur-es-surface.subject: Earth System Science
exp.cur-es-surface.summary: Record the daily temperature of sand, soil, grass and water together with sunlight.
exp.cur-es-surface.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-es-surface.steps.0: For each surface type, bury a temperature sensor 1 cm below the surface and place a light sensor beside it.
exp.cur-es-surface.steps.2: Compare the time lag between the sunlight peak and the temperature peak.
exp.cur-es-surface.std.0: Students can interpret the physical processes involved in heat exchange between the surface and the atmosphere, and the global mean heat budget.
exp.cur-es-surface.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-es-surface.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-h-abiotic.title: Light intensity and photosynthesis (abiotic factors)
exp.cur-h-abiotic.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-abiotic.summary: Compare photosynthesis by how fast CO2 falls in a sealed container as light intensity changes.
exp.cur-h-abiotic.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-abiotic.steps.0: Put a plant in a clear container with the CO2 and light sensors and close it.
exp.cur-h-abiotic.steps.1: Change the LED distance to 20, 40 and 60 cm, measuring 10 minutes each ('New run').
exp.cur-h-abiotic.steps.2: Find the CO2 slope of each run.
exp.cur-h-abiotic.steps.3: Check whether it speeds up with stronger light and then levels off.
exp.cur-h-abiotic.std.0: Students can understand the components of ecosystems and explain the interrelationships between organisms and their environment.
exp.cur-h-adc.title: Turning analog signals into digital
exp.cur-h-adc.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-adc.summary: Turn a potentiometer to see values change in steps (quantization) and how the recording interval matters.
exp.cur-h-adc.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-adc.steps.1: Measure while turning it very slowly, and use ‘Zoom to selection’ to find the staircase shape.
exp.cur-h-adc.steps.2: Change the interval to 1 second, turn it quickly and compare the changes you missed.
exp.cur-h-adc.steps.3: Discuss the advantages and limits of digital conversion.
exp.cur-h-adc.std.0: Students know that information is produced by measuring and analyzing the various changes that occur in nature, and recognize the impact on modern civilization of using technology that converts this information to digital form in information and communication.
exp.cur-h-bond-ec.title: Does electricity flow depending on the bond?
exp.cur-h-bond-ec.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-bond-ec.summary: Measure the conductivity of several substances to compare ionic and covalent substances.
exp.cur-h-bond-ec.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-bond-ec.steps.0: Number the samples in this order: distilled water, tap water, sugar water, aqueous ethanol, salt water.
exp.cur-h-bond-ec.steps.1: Dip the electrode into the sample and press ‘Record value’ once it is stable.
exp.cur-h-bond-ec.steps.2: Rinse the electrode with distilled water each time you change samples.
exp.cur-h-bond-ec.steps.3: Use ions to explain why only salt water gives a large value.
exp.cur-h-bond-ec.std.0: Students can understand the differences in bonding that form water, oxygen, salt and other substances essential for human survival, and explain them in relation to each substance's properties.
exp.cur-h-boyle-history.title: Redoing Boyle's experiment (testing a hypothesis)
exp.cur-h-boyle-history.subject: Science Inquiry Lab 1
exp.cur-h-boyle-history.summary: Form the hypothesis ‘if pressure doubles, volume halves (1/2)’ and test it with sensors.
area.과학 탐구의 과정과 절차: Processes and procedures of scientific inquiry
exp.cur-h-boyle-history.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-boyle-history.steps.0: First draw your hypothesis and expected graph with ‘Draw prediction’.
exp.cur-h-boyle-history.steps.1: Push the syringe in 2 mL at a time, pressing ‘Record value’ each time.
exp.cur-h-boyle-history.steps.2: Compare ‘Curve fit → Inverse’ with your prediction.
exp.cur-h-boyle-history.steps.3: Find the reasons for any deviation (leaking air, temperature) and revise the hypothesis.
exp.cur-h-boyle-history.std.0: (summary) Students carry out a historical science experiment that includes forming a hypothesis, and understand the features of deductive inquiry.
exp.cur-h-calibration.title: Do sensors give different values? (measurement standards and calibration)
exp.cur-h-calibration.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-calibration.summary: Measure the same water with several sensors, find the differences and repeat errors, and calibrate.
exp.cur-h-calibration.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-calibration.steps.0: Put the temperature sensors together into ice water.
exp.cur-h-calibration.steps.3: Compare means and standard deviations, and match them to the reference points with ‘Calibrate’.
exp.cur-h-calibration.std.0: Students can know the meaning of measurement and estimation in scientific inquiry, and argue for the usefulness and necessity of measurement standards in various everyday situations.
exp.cur-h-calibration.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-h-calibration.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-h-calibration.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-h-environment.title: Surveying water and air around the school
exp.cur-h-environment.subject: Science Inquiry Lab 2
exp.cur-h-environment.summary: Measure water pH and conductivity and air CO2 at different places and show them on a map.
exp.cur-h-environment.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-environment.steps.0: Number the sites to survey (rainwater, pond, tap water, etc.).
exp.cur-h-environment.steps.1: At each site, collect a sample, measure pH and conductivity, and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-h-environment.steps.2: For air, connect the CO2 sensor and measure the same way.
exp.cur-h-environment.steps.3: Make a bar graph by site from the saved Excel file and compare with reference values.
exp.cur-h-environment.std.0: (summary) Students find inquiry questions in social issues or everyday life, and plan and carry out an inquiry.
exp.cur-h-environment.std.1: (summary) Students devise solutions to real-life problems using science concepts, and design and build tools.
exp.cur-h-environment.cautions.0: Near water, always go in pairs.
exp.cur-h-enzyme-pressure.title: When the enzyme in potatoes breaks down hydrogen peroxide
exp.cur-h-enzyme-pressure.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-enzyme-pressure.summary: Compare the rate of an enzyme reaction by the pressure rise in a sealed flask.
exp.cur-h-enzyme-pressure.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-enzyme-pressure.steps.0: Put potato pieces in the flask and get the stopper with the pressure sensor ready.
exp.cur-h-enzyme-pressure.steps.1: Add hydrogen peroxide, close immediately and measure.
exp.cur-h-enzyme-pressure.std.0: Students can understand that various chemical reactions and the movement of substances are needed to maintain living systems, and research and present examples of chemical reactions used in everyday life.
exp.cur-h-enzyme-pressure.cautions.0: If the pressure rises too much, open the stopper (sensor range about 110 kPa).
exp.cur-h-galvanic.title: Change the metals and the cell voltage changes (chemical cells)
exp.cur-h-galvanic.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-galvanic.summary: Compare the voltage of different metal pairs in a lemon to see differences in reactivity.
exp.cur-h-galvanic.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-galvanic.steps.0: Number the pairs: 1 Zn–Cu, 2 Mg–Cu, 3 Fe–Cu, 4 Zn–Fe.
exp.cur-h-galvanic.steps.1: Insert an electrode pair into the lemon and connect the voltage leads.
exp.cur-h-galvanic.steps.2: Press ‘Record value’ once it is stable.
exp.cur-h-galvanic.steps.3: Check whether a bigger difference in reactivity gives a bigger voltage.
exp.cur-h-galvanic.std.0: Students can understand oxidation and reduction by finding what photosynthesis, fossil fuel use and iron smelting — which brought great changes to nature and human history — have in common, and analyze various changes around them using the features and patterns of oxidation and reduction.
exp.cur-h-galvanic.materials.2: Zinc, copper, magnesium and iron electrodes
exp.cur-h-greenhouse.title: Does more carbon dioxide mean warmer? (greenhouse effect model)
exp.cur-h-greenhouse.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-greenhouse.summary: Put a bottle of air and a bottle of CO2 under the same bulb and compare temperatures.
exp.cur-h-greenhouse.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-greenhouse.steps.0: Put a temperature sensor in each of two identical PET bottles.
exp.cur-h-greenhouse.steps.1: Fill one bottle with CO2 (baking soda + vinegar).
exp.cur-h-greenhouse.steps.2: Leave them under the same bulb for 15 minutes and measure.
exp.cur-h-greenhouse.steps.3: Swap the bottle positions, repeat, and discuss the limits of the model.
exp.cur-h-greenhouse.std.0: Students can understand the mechanism of global warming caused by an enhanced greenhouse effect, and analyze the effects of phenomena such as El Niño and desertification on the global environment and human life, and ways to respond.
exp.cur-h-greenhouse.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-h-greenhouse.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-h-heat-pack.title: Heat from de-icer, cold packs and hot packs (energy transfer)
exp.cur-h-heat-pack.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-heat-pack.summary: Compare substances that release or absorb heat as they dissolve or solidify.
exp.cur-h-heat-pack.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-heat-pack.steps.0: Put the sensor in 50 mL of water and start the run.
exp.cur-h-heat-pack.steps.1: Add calcium chloride, stir and record for 5 minutes.
exp.cur-h-heat-pack.steps.2: Repeat with ammonium nitrate in a new run.
exp.cur-h-heat-pack.steps.3: Link the direction and size of the temperature change to everyday uses.
exp.cur-h-heat-pack.std.0: Students can find phenomena around them that absorb or release energy and discuss how the absorption and release of energy is used in daily life.
exp.cur-h-heat-pack.cautions.0: Keep calcium chloride off your skin.
exp.cur-h-incline.title: A cart rolling down a slope (gravity and motion)
exp.cur-h-incline.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-incline.summary: Find the acceleration at different slope angles to see the action of gravity.
exp.cur-h-incline.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-incline.steps.0: Place the ultrasonic sensor at the top of the slope and set the cart in place.
exp.cur-h-incline.steps.1: Start the run and release the cart.
exp.cur-h-incline.steps.2: Look at speed–time with ‘Rate graph’ and find the slope of the line (acceleration).
exp.cur-h-incline.steps.3: Repeat at a different slope angle ('New run').
exp.cur-h-incline.std.0: Students can explain various motions on and around the Earth's surface caused by the action of gravity.
exp.cur-h-iot-room.title: Classroom air in real time (Internet of Things)
exp.cur-h-iot-room.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-iot-room.summary: Record classroom CO2, temperature and humidity during class and see the effect of ventilation.
exp.cur-h-iot-room.markers.label: Note
exp.cur-h-iot-room.steps.0: Place the sensor in the middle of the classroom (where breath does not hit it directly).
exp.cur-h-iot-room.steps.1: Record every 1 minute for the whole lesson.
exp.cur-h-iot-room.steps.2: Record a ‘Note’ when you open the windows.
exp.cur-h-iot-room.steps.3: Look at how long it stays above 1000 ppm and how fast it falls after ventilating.
exp.cur-h-iot-room.std.0: Students can find examples of using advances in science and technology, such as AI robots and the Internet of Things, to improve human life and the environment, and predict the usefulness and limits of these advances for future society.
exp.cur-h-iron-oxidation.title: Does oxygen decrease when iron rusts? (oxidation)
exp.cur-h-iron-oxidation.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-iron-oxidation.summary: Use pressure and temperature changes as iron oxidizes in a sealed flask to see oxygen being used up.
exp.cur-h-iron-oxidation.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-iron-oxidation.steps.0: Put steel wool soaked in vinegar (or the contents of a hand warmer) into the flask.
exp.cur-h-iron-oxidation.steps.1: Close it with the stopper holding the pressure/temperature sensor and measure for at least 30 minutes.
exp.cur-h-iron-oxidation.steps.2: Check whether the temperature rises first and the pressure then falls.
exp.cur-h-iron-oxidation.steps.3: Calculate whether the fractional pressure drop is about 20 % (the oxygen in air).
exp.cur-h-iron-oxidation.std.0: Students can understand oxidation and reduction by finding what photosynthesis, fossil fuel use and iron smelting — which brought great changes to nature and human history — have in common, and analyze various changes around them using the features and patterns of oxidation and reduction.
exp.cur-h-land-sea.title: Sand or water: which warms faster? (land and sea breezes)
exp.cur-h-land-sea.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-land-sea.summary: Explain sea and land breezes from the difference in heating and cooling of sand and water.
exp.cur-h-land-sea.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-land-sea.steps.0: Fill identical containers with sand and with water, and place a sensor 1 cm below each surface.
exp.cur-h-land-sea.steps.1: Turn the lamp on for 10 minutes, then off, and measure 10 more minutes.
exp.cur-h-land-sea.steps.2: Press ‘Add note’ when you turn the lamp off.
exp.cur-h-land-sea.steps.3: Compare which is warmer by 'day' (heating) and by 'night' (cooling).
exp.cur-h-land-sea.std.0: Students can know that the Earth system is a component of the solar system, and argue about phenomena that result from the cycling of matter and the flow of energy between the spheres that make up the Earth system.
exp.cur-h-land-sea.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-h-land-sea.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-h-mcu-motion.title: Collecting motion data with a microcontroller
exp.cur-h-mcu-motion.subject: Science Inquiry Lab 2
exp.cur-h-mcu-motion.summary: Collect and analyze the motion of objects with an ultrasonic distance sensor.
area.미래 사회와 첨단 과학 탐구: Future society and advanced science inquiry
exp.cur-h-mcu-motion.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-mcu-motion.steps.0: Connect the ultrasonic sensor to the board (TRIG D7, ECHO D8).
exp.cur-h-mcu-motion.steps.1: Choose a moving object such as a ball, a cart or a pendulum.
exp.cur-h-mcu-motion.steps.2: Measure and look at the speed with ‘Rate graph’.
exp.cur-h-mcu-motion.steps.3: Explain how the sensor measures distance (round-trip time of sound waves).
exp.cur-h-mcu-motion.std.0: (summary) Students find the scientific principles in advanced technologies and infer examples of their use.
exp.cur-h-neutral-heat.title: Does mixing acid and base make it warm? (heat of neutralization)
exp.cur-h-neutral-heat.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-neutral-heat.summary: Find the neutralization point from the maximum temperature against the volume of NaOH added.
exp.cur-h-neutral-heat.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-neutral-heat.steps.0: Put 20 mL of 1 M HCl in an insulated cup and insert the temperature sensor.
exp.cur-h-neutral-heat.steps.1: Record the starting temperature as 0 mL.
exp.cur-h-neutral-heat.steps.2: Add 1 M NaOH 2 mL at a time, stir, and press ‘Record value’ at the highest temperature.
exp.cur-h-neutral-heat.steps.3: The highest temperature (where the two lines meet) is the neutralization point.
exp.cur-h-neutral-heat.std.0: Students can know the characteristics of typical acids and bases and make use in everyday life of the neutralization reaction that occurs when acids and bases are mixed.
exp.cur-h-neutral-heat.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-h-neutral-ph-ec.title: pH and electrical conductivity in neutralization
exp.cur-h-neutral-ph-ec.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-neutral-ph-ec.summary: As NaOH is added, see pH rise sharply and conductivity change in a V shape.
exp.cur-h-neutral-ph-ec.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-neutral-ph-ec.steps.0: Put the pH electrode and the conductivity electrode together into 20 mL of dilute HCl.
exp.cur-h-neutral-ph-ec.steps.1: Add NaOH 1 mL at a time, stir, then press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-h-neutral-ph-ec.steps.2: Use ‘Find equivalence point’ on the pH graph and find the lowest point on the conductivity graph.
exp.cur-h-neutral-ph-ec.steps.3: Compare whether the two methods give the same neutralization point.
exp.cur-h-neutral-ph-ec.std.0: Students can know the characteristics of typical acids and bases and make use in everyday life of the neutralization reaction that occurs when acids and bases are mixed.
exp.cur-h-neutral-ph-ec.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-h-newton-cooling.title: How fast each cup cools (representing data)
exp.cur-h-newton-cooling.subject: Science Inquiry Lab 1
exp.cur-h-newton-cooling.summary: Represent the same cooling data in different ways: curves, logarithms and bars.
exp.cur-h-newton-cooling.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-newton-cooling.steps.0: Pour equal amounts of 80 °C water into a paper cup, a mug and a tumbler.
exp.cur-h-newton-cooling.steps.1: Measure each cup for 30 minutes (a new run each, or 3 sensors).
exp.cur-h-newton-cooling.steps.2: Compare the cooling rate (C) with ‘Curve fit → Exponential approach’.
exp.cur-h-newton-cooling.steps.3: Also make other graphs using the table's ‘Calculated column’ and the saved Excel file.
exp.cur-h-newton-cooling.std.0: (summary) Students analyze qualitative and quantitative data and communicate it by representing it in various ways.
exp.cur-h-newton-cooling.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-h-pendulum.title: Finding g from a pendulum's period (measuring base quantities)
exp.cur-h-pendulum.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-pendulum.summary: Record pendulum motion with an ultrasonic sensor, measure the period and find its relationship with length.
exp.cur-h-pendulum.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-pendulum.steps.0: Place the ultrasonic sensor in line with the direction the pendulum bob swings.
exp.cur-h-pendulum.steps.1: Give the bob a small swing and measure for 20 seconds.
exp.cur-h-pendulum.steps.2: Measure the time between peaks (period) with ‘Tangent’ or by reading values.
exp.cur-h-pendulum.steps.3: Repeat with different string lengths and find g from the slope of the length–period² graph.
exp.cur-h-pendulum.std.0: Students can know that nature can be described in time and space, and research modern methods of measuring length and time and examples of measurements at various scales.
exp.cur-h-pendulum.std.1: Students can know the meaning of the base quantities important in scientific inquiry, and explain the significance of units in describing natural phenomena with examples of their application.
exp.cur-h-ph-life.title: pH of everyday substances
exp.cur-h-ph-life.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-ph-life.summary: Measure the pH of vinegar, soda, soapy water and more, and sort them into acids and bases.
exp.cur-h-ph-life.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-ph-life.steps.0: Calibrate the pH sensor with pH 4 and 7 buffers.
exp.cur-h-ph-life.steps.1: Dip the electrode in each sample and press ‘Record value’ once stable.
exp.cur-h-ph-life.steps.2: Rinse the electrode with distilled water between samples.
exp.cur-h-ph-life.steps.3: Sort into acidic and basic using pH 7 as the dividing line.
exp.cur-h-ph-life.std.0: Students can know the characteristics of typical acids and bases and make use in everyday life of the neutralization reaction that occurs when acids and bases are mixed.
exp.cur-h-ph-life.materials.1: Vinegar, lemon juice, soda, milk, soapy water, baking soda solution
exp.cur-h-ph-life.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-h-plant-ph.title: Pondweed photosynthesis and water pH
exp.cur-h-plant-ph.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-plant-ph.summary: See water pH rise as hydrilla uses CO2 in photosynthesis (instead of a dissolved oxygen sensor).
exp.cur-h-plant-ph.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-plant-ph.steps.0: Put hydrilla in water with a little sodium hydrogen carbonate dissolved in it.
exp.cur-h-plant-ph.steps.1: Set up the pH electrode and light sensor and turn on the LED.
exp.cur-h-plant-ph.steps.2: After 30 minutes turn off the LED and measure 30 more minutes (‘Add note’).
exp.cur-h-plant-ph.steps.3: Check whether pH rises in light and falls in the dark.
exp.cur-h-plant-ph.std.0: Students can understand oxidation and reduction by finding what photosynthesis, fossil fuel use and iron smelting — which brought great changes to nature and human history — have in common, and analyze various changes around them using the features and patterns of oxidation and reduction.
exp.cur-h-plant-ph.cautions.0: Calibrate the pH electrode before measuring (pH 4 and 7 buffers).
exp.cur-h-semiconductor.title: A component whose resistance changes with temperature (thermistor)
exp.cur-h-semiconductor.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-semiconductor.summary: Record the thermistor divider voltage together with temperature to see the properties of a semiconductor component.
exp.cur-h-semiconductor.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-semiconductor.steps.0: Wire 5 V → thermistor → 10 kΩ → GND, and connect the row between them to A0 (voltage).
exp.cur-h-semiconductor.steps.1: Put the thermistor and the temperature sensor together into hot water.
exp.cur-h-semiconductor.steps.3: Switch to ‘X axis → Temperature’ to see the temperature–voltage relationship.
exp.cur-h-semiconductor.std.0: Students can classify the materials that make up the Earth by their electrical properties, and recognize that these properties are applied in various materials used in everyday life and advanced technology.
exp.cur-h-semiconductor.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-h-semiconductor.bb: Build a voltage divider with the thermistor and the 10 kΩ resistor.
exp.cur-h-smart-pot.title: Building a smart flowerpot or greenhouse (sensor invention)
exp.cur-h-smart-pot.subject: Science Inquiry Lab 2
exp.cur-h-smart-pot.summary: Record soil moisture, light, temperature and humidity to build a device that tells you when to water.
exp.cur-h-smart-pot.markers.label: Note
exp.cur-h-smart-pot.steps.0: Insert the soil moisture sensor into the pot and place the light and temperature & humidity sensors beside it.
exp.cur-h-smart-pot.steps.3: Predict the next watering day from the slope of the moisture decrease.
exp.cur-h-smart-pot.std.0: (summary) Students find the scientific principles in advanced technologies and infer examples of their use.
exp.cur-h-smart-pot.std.1: (summary) Students present and share inquiry products that use advanced technology.
exp.cur-h-solar.title: Solar cell angle and power (energy efficiency)
exp.cur-h-solar.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-solar.summary: See how the voltage (power) changes with the angle between the light and the solar cell.
exp.cur-h-solar.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-solar.steps.0: Connect solar cell (+) → 100 Ω → solar cell (−), then (−) to GND and (+) to A0.
exp.cur-h-solar.steps.1: Press ‘Record value’ with the light perpendicular (0°).
exp.cur-h-solar.steps.2: Tilt it 15° at a time, recording each time.
exp.cur-h-solar.steps.3: Calculate the power P = V²/R and compare it with the angle.
exp.cur-h-solar.std.0: Students can understand the meaning and importance of energy efficiency, and explore ways to use renewable energy technology for sustainable development and solving global environmental problems.
exp.cur-h-solar.materials.0: Small solar cell (5 V or less)
exp.cur-h-solar.cautions.0: First check that the solar cell output does not exceed 5 V.
exp.cur-h-solar.bb: Connect a load resistor to the solar cell.
exp.cur-h-yeast.title: Does more sugar make yeast ferment faster?
exp.cur-h-yeast.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-yeast.summary: Compare how fast CO2 rises from yeast solutions with different sugar concentrations.
exp.cur-h-yeast.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-yeast.steps.0: Prepare equal amounts of yeast solution with 0, 5 and 10 % sugar.
exp.cur-h-yeast.steps.1: Put each one in a sealed container with the CO2 sensor and measure for 20 minutes ('New run').
exp.cur-h-yeast.steps.2: Compare the slopes of the CO2 increase.
exp.cur-h-yeast.steps.3: Conclude that chemical reactions in living things are controlled by enzymes.
exp.cur-h-yeast.std.0: Students can understand that various chemical reactions and the movement of substances are needed to maintain living systems, and research and present examples of chemical reactions used in everyday life.
exp.cur-h-yeast.cautions.0: If CO2 goes above 2000 ppm, use a larger container.
exp.cur-m-boyle.title: Push the syringe and the pressure... (Boyle's law)
exp.cur-m-boyle.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-boyle.summary: See how pressure changes as the volume of a gas is reduced.
exp.cur-m-boyle.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-boyle.steps.0: Connect a syringe to a small sealed container holding the pressure sensor.
exp.cur-m-boyle.steps.1: Enter the total volume (container + tube + syringe) as the first value.
