exp.cur-m-boyle.steps.2: Each time you push the syringe in 2 mL, press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-m-boyle.steps.3: Check whether P×V stays constant with ‘Curve fit → Inverse’.
exp.cur-m-boyle.std.0: Students can find the relationship between the pressure and volume of a gas from experimental results and interpret it with a particle model.
exp.cur-m-boyle.cautions.0: Compress by no more than 10 % of the starting volume (sensor range about 110 kPa).
exp.cur-m-bp-amount.title: Is the boiling point the same for different amounts?
exp.cur-m-bp-amount.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-bp-amount.summary: Compare the plateau height of two samples of different amounts.
exp.cur-m-bp-amount.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-bp-amount.steps.0: Put 10 mL and 20 mL of ethanol into separate test tubes, each with a sensor.
exp.cur-m-bp-amount.steps.1: Put them together into the same water bath (about 90 °C).
exp.cur-m-bp-amount.steps.3: Compare whether the plateau heights (boiling points) are the same.
exp.cur-m-bp-amount.std.0: Students can know the meaning of characteristic properties of substances and explain density, solubility, melting point, boiling point, etc. through experiments.
exp.cur-m-bp-amount.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-m-bp-amount.cautions.0: Do not heat ethanol directly; use a water bath.
exp.cur-m-bp-amount.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-m-breath.title: Does exercise increase the carbon dioxide in your breath?
exp.cur-m-breath.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-breath.summary: Compare exhaled CO2 before and after exercise using the same method.
exp.cur-m-breath.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-breath.steps.0: Put the CO2 sensor in a 5 L container.
exp.cur-m-breath.steps.1: Breathe out once through a straw, close the lid and measure for 2 minutes.
exp.cur-m-breath.steps.2: Air out the container, then repeat the same way after 1 minute of jogging on the spot ('New run').
exp.cur-m-breath.steps.3: Compare the peak values of the two runs.
exp.cur-m-breath.std.0: Students can explain in an integrated way how animals obtain energy through cellular respiration, in relation to digestion, circulation, respiration and excretion.
exp.cur-m-breath.cautions.0: The SCD40 is less accurate above 2000 ppm. Dilute in a large container and use only for comparison.
exp.cur-m-buoyancy.title: Does it get lighter the deeper it sinks? (buoyancy)
exp.cur-m-buoyancy.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-buoyancy.summary: Find the buoyant force from the drop in weight with submerged depth.
exp.cur-m-buoyancy.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-buoyancy.steps.0: Hang a cylindrical weight from the load cell.
exp.cur-m-buoyancy.steps.1: Each time you lower the weight 1 cm further into the water, press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-m-buoyancy.steps.2: Record a few more times after it is fully submerged.
exp.cur-m-buoyancy.steps.3: Weight lost = buoyant force; check whether it becomes constant once fully submerged.
exp.cur-m-buoyancy.std.0: Students can understand gravity, elastic force, friction and buoyancy, and explain the features of each force by magnitude and direction.
exp.cur-m-charles.title: Warm it up and the gas volume... (Charles's law)
exp.cur-m-charles.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-charles.summary: Enter the volume reading as the temperature changes and draw a temperature–volume line.
exp.cur-m-charles.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-charles.steps.0: Put a sealed-tip syringe and the temperature sensor together into a water bath.
exp.cur-m-charles.steps.1: Warm the water; each time the syringe reading goes up 1 mL, enter that volume and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-m-charles.steps.2: To change the X axis, save the table to Excel and draw a temperature–volume graph.
exp.cur-m-charles.steps.3: Discuss whether extending the line gives a volume of 0 at about −273 °C.
exp.cur-m-charles.std.0: Students can find the relationship between the temperature and volume of a gas from experimental results and interpret it with a particle model.
exp.cur-m-charles.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-m-cloud.title: Making a cloud in a PET bottle
exp.cur-m-cloud.subject: Science 3
exp.cur-m-cloud.summary: See the temperature drop and a cloud form when the pressure is suddenly lowered.
exp.cur-m-cloud.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-cloud.steps.0: Put a little water and the BME280 sensor into a PET bottle.
exp.cur-m-cloud.steps.1: Add a little incense smoke and pump the pump cap several times.
exp.cur-m-cloud.steps.2: Start the run and open the cap all at once.
exp.cur-m-cloud.steps.3: Check whether the air temperature drops and the bottle turns cloudy as the pressure falls.
exp.cur-m-cloud.std.0: Students can understand the relationship between relative humidity, adiabatic expansion and condensation, and explain how clouds form and precipitation occurs.
exp.cur-m-cloud.cautions.0: Fit the sensor wire tightly in the bottle neck so it does not leak.
exp.cur-m-color.title: Object color and mixing light
exp.cur-m-color.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-color.summary: Measure colored paper and cellophane in RGB to see light mixing as numbers.
exp.cur-m-color.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-color.steps.0: Hold the color sensor against white paper and make the first record (reference).
exp.cur-m-color.steps.1: Hold it against red, green, blue and yellow paper in turn, pressing ‘Record value’ each time.
exp.cur-m-color.steps.2: Also record values with light passing through layered cellophane.
exp.cur-m-color.steps.3: Check whether R and G are both high for yellow.
exp.cur-m-color.std.0: Students can explain the color of objects in relation to the reflection of light, and understand how display devices use the mixing of light to show various colors.
exp.cur-m-cooling-curve.title: When melted stearic acid solidifies (cooling curve)
exp.cur-m-cooling-curve.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-cooling-curve.summary: Find why the temperature stays constant while it solidifies (heat of solidification).
exp.cur-m-cooling-curve.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-cooling-curve.steps.0: Melt stearic acid in a water bath and insert the sensor.
exp.cur-m-cooling-curve.steps.1: Take the test tube out and measure as it cools at room temperature.
exp.cur-m-cooling-curve.steps.2: Press ‘Add note’ when it starts to solidify.
exp.cur-m-cooling-curve.steps.3: Find the freezing point (about 69 °C) with ‘Find plateau’.
exp.cur-m-cooling-curve.std.0: Students can understand the relationship between changes of state and the transfer of heat energy, and recognize the usefulness of science by applying this to everyday life.
exp.cur-m-cooling-curve.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-m-cooling-curve.cautions.1: Do not pull the sensor out before it solidifies (once solid, melt it again to remove the sensor).
exp.cur-m-distillation.title: Separating a water–ethanol mixture (distillation)
exp.cur-m-distillation.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-distillation.summary: Confirm the difference in boiling points from the two stretches where the vapor temperature holds steady.
exp.cur-m-distillation.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-distillation.steps.0: Put the water–ethanol mixture and boiling chips into a side-arm flask.
exp.cur-m-distillation.steps.1: Place the sensor tip level with the side arm.
exp.cur-m-distillation.steps.2: Heat, and press ‘Add note’ when liquid starts to come out.
exp.cur-m-distillation.steps.3: Find the stretch at about 78 °C and the one at 100 °C.
exp.cur-m-distillation.std.0: Students can understand how mixtures are separated using the characteristic properties of substances, and find examples of this around them.
exp.cur-m-distillation.materials.2: Condenser (or a test tube in cold water)
exp.cur-m-distillation.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-m-distillation.cautions.1: Ventilate so ethanol vapor does not catch fire.
exp.cur-m-evaporation.title: Water vs. ethanol: how cool does evaporation make it?
exp.cur-m-evaporation.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-evaporation.summary: Compare how evaporation takes heat away and lowers the temperature.
exp.cur-m-evaporation.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-evaporation.steps.0: Wrap gauze around the sensor tip.
exp.cur-m-evaporation.steps.1: Wet one with water and the other with ethanol.
exp.cur-m-evaporation.steps.2: Hold them in the air and measure for 3–5 minutes.
exp.cur-m-evaporation.steps.3: Compare the lowest temperature and how fast it drops.
exp.cur-m-evaporation.std.0: Students can observe diffusion and evaporation and infer that the particles making up matter are in motion.
exp.cur-m-evaporation.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-m-evaporation.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-m-exo-endo.title: Reactions that get warm, reactions that get cold
exp.cur-m-exo-endo.subject: Science 3
exp.cur-m-exo-endo.summary: Compare heat transfer from the temperature changes of hand-warmer and cold-pack reactions.
exp.cur-m-exo-endo.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-exo-endo.steps.0: (Exothermic) Put the sensor in a bag of iron powder + salt water + activated carbon.
exp.cur-m-exo-endo.steps.1: (Endothermic) Add water to citric acid + baking soda and insert the sensor.
exp.cur-m-exo-endo.steps.3: Compare the highest and lowest temperatures and the changes, then design a cooling device.
exp.cur-m-exo-endo.std.0: Students can know that heat energy is transferred in chemical reactions, and research and present examples from everyday life.
exp.cur-m-exo-endo.cautions.0: Do not touch reacted substances with bare hands.
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.title: How is heat transferred? (conduction, radiation, insulation)
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.summary: Compare how fast temperature changes with different metals, can colors and insulators.
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.steps.0: (Conduction) Put one end of a metal rod in hot water and attach the sensor to the other end.
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.steps.1: (Radiation) Put sensors in a black can and a white can under a lamp.
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.steps.2: (Insulation) Measure hot water cooling in different kinds of cups.
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.steps.3: Compare the initial slopes with ‘Curve fit → Linear’.
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.std.0: Students can know that heat is transferred by conduction, convection and radiation, and represent heat transfer in various ways using models and other means.
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.attach.1: At the rod end, wrap the sensor tip with tape to attach it.
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-m-heat-transfer.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-m-heating-curve.title: When ice melts and water boils (heating curve)
exp.cur-m-heating-curve.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-heating-curve.summary: Find the stretches where the temperature stays constant during melting and boiling.
exp.cur-m-heating-curve.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-heating-curve.steps.0: Put crushed ice in a beaker and insert the sensor.
exp.cur-m-heating-curve.steps.2: Press ‘Add note’ when all the ice has melted and when boiling starts.
exp.cur-m-heating-curve.steps.3: Find the melting and boiling points with ‘Find plateau’.
exp.cur-m-heating-curve.std.0: Students can observe changes of state in various substances and explain them with a particle model.
exp.cur-m-heating-curve.std.1: Students can understand the relationship between changes of state and the transfer of heat energy, and recognize the usefulness of science by applying this to everyday life.
exp.cur-m-heating-curve.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-m-heating-curve.cautions.1: Do not leave the waterproof sensor cable in boiling water for long.
exp.cur-m-light-distance.title: Moving away from a light source (inverse square)
exp.cur-m-light-distance.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-light-distance.summary: Check whether the brightness drops to 1/4 when the distance is 2 times greater.
exp.cur-m-light-distance.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-light-distance.steps.0: Turn on a small bulb in a dark place.
exp.cur-m-light-distance.steps.1: Move the light sensor 10 cm farther each time, pressing ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-m-light-distance.steps.2: Check whether the exponent in ‘Curve fit → Power’ is about −2.
exp.cur-m-light-distance.steps.3: Link this to why distant stars look dim.
exp.cur-m-light-distance.std.0: Students can find the distance to stars using annual parallax, and explain the relationship between stellar magnitude and brightness and between surface temperature and color.
exp.cur-m-mass-conservation.title: Is mass the same before and after a reaction? (conservation of mass)
exp.cur-m-mass-conservation.subject: Science 3
exp.cur-m-mass-conservation.summary: Compare the change in mass for a reaction in a closed bottle and in an open bottle.
exp.cur-m-mass-conservation.steps.0: Pour vinegar into a PET bottle, and stand a small cup of baking soda inside the bottle.
exp.cur-m-mass-conservation.steps.1: Close the cap, put it on the load cell, set zero and start the run.
exp.cur-m-mass-conservation.steps.2: Tilt the bottle to mix. Check whether the mass stays the same.
exp.cur-m-mass-conservation.steps.3: Repeat with the cap open and find the mass lost (escaped CO2).
exp.cur-m-mass-conservation.std.0: Students can infer through experiments that mass is conserved in chemical reactions.
exp.cur-m-motion.title: Graphing how you walk (motion graphs)
exp.cur-m-motion.subject: Science 3
exp.cur-m-motion.summary: Walk in front of the ultrasonic sensor to make a time–distance graph and find your speed.
exp.cur-m-motion.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-motion.steps.0: Place the ultrasonic sensor at chest height.
exp.cur-m-motion.steps.1: In front of the sensor, walk steadily, stop, then walk faster and faster.
exp.cur-m-motion.steps.2: Look at the speed with ‘Tangent’ and ‘Rate graph’.
exp.cur-m-motion.steps.3: Repeating with a cart on a slope gives a straight speed–time line (uniform acceleration).
exp.cur-m-motion.std.0: Students can represent and interpret the motion of an object moving in a straight line with graphs.
exp.cur-m-motion.std.1: Students can analyze that in free fall the change in speed over time is constant.
exp.cur-m-motion.cautions.0: It cannot measure within 2 cm of the sensor.
exp.cur-m-ocean-temp.title: Water temperature with ocean depth (vertical temperature profile)
exp.cur-m-ocean-temp.subject: Science 3
exp.cur-m-ocean-temp.summary: Measure temperature at each depth in a lamp-heated tank to see the mixed layer and thermocline.
exp.cur-m-ocean-temp.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-ocean-temp.steps.0: Fill a tank with cold water and shine a lamp on it from above for 20 minutes.
exp.cur-m-ocean-temp.steps.1: Lower the sensor from the surface 2 cm at a time, pressing ‘Record value’ each time.
exp.cur-m-ocean-temp.steps.2: Mix it by blowing with a fan, then repeat ('New run').
exp.cur-m-ocean-temp.steps.3: Check on the depth–temperature graph whether the mixed layer gets thicker.
exp.cur-m-ohm.title: Voltage and current (Ohm's law)
exp.cur-m-ohm.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-ohm.summary: Find the current from the voltage across a reference resistor and compare it with the voltage across the resistor.
exp.cur-m-ohm.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-ohm.steps.0: On the breadboard, connect in series: battery (+) → test resistor R → 100 Ω reference resistor → battery (−); then connect battery (−) to the board's GND.
exp.cur-m-ohm.steps.1: Connect A0 to the row above R and A1 to the row between R and the reference resistor (both set to voltage in ‘Sensor setup’).
exp.cur-m-ohm.steps.2: Press ‘Record value’ each time you add a battery.
exp.cur-m-ohm.steps.3: Voltage across R = A0 − A1, current = A1 ÷ 100 Ω. Save the table and find the slope (resistance) of the current–voltage graph.
exp.cur-m-ohm.std.0: Students can explain current in an electric circuit with a model and derive the relationship between resistance, current and voltage through experiments.
exp.cur-m-ohm.cautions.0: Put only 0–5 V into the board. No more than 3 batteries of 1.5 V.
exp.cur-m-ohm.bb: Join two resistors in series and plug the measuring wire in between them.
exp.cur-m-photosynthesis.title: Does stronger light speed up photosynthesis?
exp.cur-m-photosynthesis.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-photosynthesis.summary: Compare photosynthesis by how fast carbon dioxide falls in a sealed container.
exp.cur-m-photosynthesis.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-photosynthesis.steps.0: Put a leafy plant with the CO2 sensor and light sensor into a clear container and close it.
exp.cur-m-photosynthesis.steps.1: Place the LED close and measure for 10 minutes.
exp.cur-m-photosynthesis.steps.2: In a new run, repeat with the LED farther away or off.
exp.cur-m-photosynthesis.steps.3: Compare photosynthesis rates by the ‘Curve fit → Linear’ slope (ppm/s).
exp.cur-m-photosynthesis.std.0: Students can understand the process of photosynthesis and design experiments to investigate the relationship between environmental factors and photosynthesis.
exp.cur-m-photosynthesis.cautions.0: Use an LED so lamp heat does not warm the container.
exp.cur-m-pure-mixture.title: Do water and salt water freeze differently? (pure substances and mixtures)
exp.cur-m-pure-mixture.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-pure-mixture.summary: See whether a pure substance shows a clear plateau while a mixture keeps dropping.
exp.cur-m-pure-mixture.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-pure-mixture.steps.0: Put water and salt water into separate test tubes, each with a sensor.
exp.cur-m-pure-mixture.steps.1: Put them together into an ice + salt cooling bath.
exp.cur-m-pure-mixture.steps.3: Compare the two curves with ‘Find plateau’.
exp.cur-m-pure-mixture.std.0: Students can classify substances around them into pure substances and mixtures based on their characteristic properties.
exp.cur-m-pure-mixture.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-m-pure-mixture.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-m-respiration.title: Do sprouting beans breathe too? (respiration)
exp.cur-m-respiration.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-respiration.summary: Compare the CO2 and temperature changes of germinating seeds and boiled beans.
exp.cur-m-respiration.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-respiration.steps.0: Put soaked beans (germinating seeds) and the sensors in a sealed container and close it.
exp.cur-m-respiration.steps.2: In a new run, repeat with boiled beans (control).
exp.cur-m-respiration.steps.3: Compare the slope of the CO2 increase and the temperature rise.
exp.cur-m-respiration.std.0: Students can understand the relationship between respiration and photosynthesis in plants and analyze the energy and material changes involved in each.
exp.cur-m-sound.title: How much quieter does sound get with distance?
exp.cur-m-sound.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-sound.summary: Compare loudness at different distances from a speaker (or volume settings).
exp.cur-m-sound.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-sound.steps.0: Play a steady sound from a speaker.
exp.cur-m-sound.steps.1: Move the sound sensor 10 cm farther each time, pressing ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-m-sound.steps.2: In a new run, repeat at a different volume setting.
exp.cur-m-sound.steps.3: This sensor cannot show frequency or waveform, so use it together with a smartphone app.
exp.cur-m-sound.std.0: Students can understand how waves are produced and transmitted, and describe the properties of sound with scientific terms such as amplitude, frequency and waveform.
exp.cur-m-sound.cautions.0: Sound sensor values are relative. Compare only readings from the same sensor.
exp.cur-m-specific-heat.title: Water or cooking oil: which warms faster? (specific heat)
exp.cur-m-specific-heat.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-specific-heat.summary: Use specific heat to explain why temperature rises at different rates for the same heat input.
exp.cur-m-specific-heat.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-specific-heat.steps.0: Put equal masses of water and cooking oil into identical test tubes.
exp.cur-m-specific-heat.steps.1: Insert a temperature sensor in each and put them into the same water bath at the same time.
exp.cur-m-specific-heat.steps.3: Find the ratio of specific heats from the ratio of the ‘Curve fit → Linear’ slopes (oil is about 2 times faster).
exp.cur-m-specific-heat.std.0: Students can know that specific heat and thermal expansion differ between substances, and recognize that these properties are useful in everyday life.
exp.cur-m-specific-heat.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-m-specific-heat.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-m-specific-heat.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-m-spring.title: Stretching a spring (elastic force)
exp.cur-m-spring.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-spring.summary: Check whether elastic force is proportional to the extension.
exp.cur-m-spring.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-spring.steps.0: Hang the spring from the load cell and set zero (Calibrate → Zero).
exp.cur-m-spring.steps.1: Pull the lower end down 1 cm at a time and hold it in place.
exp.cur-m-spring.steps.2: Press ‘Record value’ once the value is stable.
exp.cur-m-spring.steps.3: The slope of ‘Curve fit → Proportional’ is the spring constant (g to N: ×0.0098).
exp.cur-m-spring.std.0: Students can understand gravity, elastic force, friction and buoyancy, and explain the features of each force by magnitude and direction.
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.title: When hot water meets cold water
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.summary: Watch on a graph as two temperatures become equal (thermal equilibrium).
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.steps.0: Put hot water in a small cup and cold water in a large beaker.
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.steps.1: Put one temperature sensor in the cup and the other in the beaker water.
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.steps.2: Start the run and place the cup in the beaker.
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.steps.3: Check whether the two graphs meet at the same temperature.
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.std.0: Students can explain temperature and the process of thermal equilibrium in terms of the arrangement and motion of the particles that make up matter.
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-m-thermal-eq.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-m-weather.title: Does falling pressure mean rain? (continuous observation)
exp.cur-m-weather.subject: Science 3
exp.cur-m-weather.summary: Record pressure, air temperature and humidity for several days and compare with weather maps.
exp.cur-m-weather.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-weather.steps.0: Place the sensor by a window (out of direct sunlight).
exp.cur-m-weather.steps.1: Set the interval to 10 minutes and record for 3–7 days.
exp.cur-m-weather.steps.2: Leave an ‘Add note’ on rainy days.
exp.cur-m-weather.steps.3: Compare with the weather service's maps, matching the times.
exp.cur-m-weather.std.0: Students can understand the concepts of air pressure, air masses and fronts, and interpret weather from the distribution of low and high pressure on weather maps.
exp.cur-m-weather.cautions.0: Keep the laptop from going to sleep, or use USB power and a Bluetooth tablet.
exp.cur-mat-catalyst.title: Hydrogen peroxide decomposition with catalysts and temperature
exp.cur-mat-catalyst.subject: Matter and Energy
exp.cur-mat-catalyst.summary: Compare how fast pressure rises with different catalysts and temperatures.
exp.cur-mat-catalyst.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-mat-catalyst.steps.0: Add a catalyst (MnO2, potato, yeast) to hydrogen peroxide, close immediately and measure.
exp.cur-mat-catalyst.std.0: Students can understand that reaction rate depends on concentration, temperature and catalysts, and recognize the usefulness of chemistry by finding everyday examples of each.
exp.cur-mat-catalyst.cautions.0: If the pressure rises too much, open the stopper.
exp.cur-mat-evap-imf.title: Intermolecular forces and evaporative cooling
exp.cur-mat-evap-imf.subject: Matter and Energy
exp.cur-mat-evap-imf.summary: Link the size of evaporative cooling in several liquids to intermolecular forces.
exp.cur-mat-evap-imf.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-mat-evap-imf.steps.0: Wrap gauze around the sensor tips and wet them with water, ethanol and acetone (several sensors or a new run each).
exp.cur-mat-evap-imf.steps.1: Measure in the air for 3 minutes.
exp.cur-mat-evap-imf.steps.2: Compare the order of the lowest temperatures with the order of boiling points.
exp.cur-mat-evap-imf.std.0: Students can understand, in terms of intermolecular interactions, why substances can exist as liquids, and explain why boiling points differ between liquids.
exp.cur-mat-evap-imf.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-mat-evap-imf.cautions.0: Keep acetone and ethanol away from flames and ventilate.
exp.cur-mat-evap-imf.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-mat-half-life.title: Crystal violet fading (half-life of a first-order reaction)
exp.cur-mat-half-life.subject: Matter and Energy
exp.cur-mat-half-life.summary: Confirm first-order kinetics and the half-life from the absorbance curve as the color fades.
exp.cur-mat-half-life.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-mat-half-life.steps.0: Put crystal violet solution in a cuvette between the LED and the color sensor.
exp.cur-mat-half-life.steps.2: Find k and the half-life with ‘Calculated column → ln’ or ‘Curve fit → Exponential’.
exp.cur-mat-half-life.std.0: Students can understand that the half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on reactant concentration, and research and present examples where first-order half-lives are used.
exp.cur-mat-half-life.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-mat-hess.title: Checking Hess's law with a coffee-cup calorimeter
exp.cur-mat-hess.subject: Matter and Energy
exp.cur-mat-hess.summary: Find reaction enthalpies from the temperature changes of three reactions and add them up.
exp.cur-mat-hess.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-mat-hess.steps.0: Measure each separately ('New run'): ① NaOH(s) into water, ② NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq), ③ NaOH(s) into HCl(aq).
exp.cur-mat-hess.steps.1: Find q = mcΔT from the ΔT of each run.
exp.cur-mat-hess.std.0: Students can know the meaning of enthalpy and write thermochemical equations using enthalpy.
exp.cur-mat-hess.std.1: Students can find the enthalpy of hard-to-measure chemical reactions using Hess's law and recognize the usefulness of chemical laws.
exp.cur-mat-hess.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-mat-hess.cautions.1: Solid NaOH is dangerous on skin.
exp.cur-mat-ideal-gas.title: How much hydrogen magnesium makes (ideal gas equation)
exp.cur-mat-ideal-gas.subject: Matter and Energy
exp.cur-mat-ideal-gas.summary: Find the moles of H2 produced from the pressure rise in a sealed container and compare with the moles of Mg.
exp.cur-mat-ideal-gas.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-mat-ideal-gas.steps.0: Put dilute hydrochloric acid and the pressure sensor into a sealed flask of known volume.
exp.cur-mat-ideal-gas.steps.1: Drop in a (small) piece of Mg ribbon, close immediately and measure.
exp.cur-mat-ideal-gas.steps.2: Compare Δn = ΔP·V/RT with the moles of Mg.
exp.cur-mat-ideal-gas.std.0: Students can understand in an integrated way the relationship between the temperature, pressure, volume and moles of a gas, and recognize the usefulness of chemistry by researching cases where the ideal gas equation is used as an approximation.
exp.cur-mat-ideal-gas.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-mat-ideal-gas.cautions.1: Use only a very small amount of Mg (keep the pressure under 110 kPa).
exp.cur-mat-rate.title: Reaction rate and concentration (rate law)
exp.cur-mat-rate.subject: Matter and Energy
exp.cur-mat-rate.summary: Find the reaction order from the initial slope of the pressure rise in Mg + HCl.
exp.cur-mat-rate.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-mat-rate.steps.0: Prepare equal volumes of HCl at different concentrations.
exp.cur-mat-rate.steps.1: Add Mg ribbon of the same length, close immediately and measure (a new run for each concentration).
exp.cur-mat-rate.steps.2: From the initial slopes, find the slope (order) of log(rate)–log(concentration).
exp.cur-mat-rate.std.0: Students can know that a reaction rate can be expressed in terms of reactant concentrations, and find the rate law by interpreting data.
exp.cur-mat-rate.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-me-adiabatic.title: Squeeze it and it warms, release it and it cools (adiabatic processes)
exp.cur-me-adiabatic.subject: Mechanics and Energy
exp.cur-me-adiabatic.summary: Watch pressure and temperature together as a PET bottle is compressed and expanded.
exp.cur-me-adiabatic.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-me-adiabatic.steps.0: Pump the pump cap several times on a PET bottle holding a BMP280.
exp.cur-me-adiabatic.steps.1: Start the run and open the cap all at once.
exp.cur-me-adiabatic.steps.2: Compare how pressure and temperature change together.
exp.cur-me-adiabatic.std.0: Students can understand that heat added to a system can change its internal energy or do work on the surroundings, and find interest by finding examples in everyday life.
exp.cur-me-entropy.title: Mixed temperatures do not un-mix (irreversible processes)
exp.cur-me-entropy.subject: Mechanics and Energy
exp.cur-me-entropy.summary: Record a thermal equilibrium process and calculate the entropy change.
exp.cur-me-entropy.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-me-entropy.steps.0: Put a cup of hot water into a beaker of cold water and record both temperatures.
exp.cur-me-entropy.steps.1: Measure until the two temperatures are equal.
exp.cur-me-entropy.steps.2: Save to Excel and calculate ΔS = Σ mc·ln(T₂/T₁).
exp.cur-me-entropy.std.0: Students can explain irreversible phenomena such as heat flow and gas diffusion using entropy.
exp.cur-me-entropy.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-me-entropy.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-me-gay-lussac.title: Pressure and temperature at constant volume (absolute temperature)
exp.cur-me-gay-lussac.subject: Mechanics and Energy
exp.cur-me-gay-lussac.summary: Heat a sealed flask and extrapolate the pressure–temperature line to find −273 °C.
exp.cur-me-gay-lussac.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-me-gay-lussac.steps.0: Put a sealed flask holding the pressure sensor, and the temperature sensor, into a water bath.
exp.cur-me-gay-lussac.steps.1: Measure while slowly heating the water.
exp.cur-me-gay-lussac.steps.2: Use ‘X axis → Temperature’ and ‘Curve fit → Linear’ to find the temperature where P = 0.
exp.cur-me-gay-lussac.std.0: Students can understand changes in the state of matter caused by heat and explain the relationship between the temperature, pressure and volume of an ideal gas.
exp.cur-me-gay-lussac.cautions.0: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-me-insulation.title: How much more slowly does a model house cool with different insulation?
exp.cur-me-insulation.subject: Mechanics and Energy
exp.cur-me-insulation.summary: Compare insulation performance by how fast the inside–outside temperature difference shrinks.
exp.cur-me-insulation.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-me-insulation.steps.0: Put a cup of hot water and a temperature sensor inside the box, and one sensor outside.
exp.cur-me-insulation.steps.1: Change the insulation (Styrofoam, bubble wrap, none), measuring 30 minutes each.
exp.cur-me-insulation.steps.2: Compare the insulation by C from ‘Curve fit → Exponential approach’.
exp.cur-me-insulation.std.0: Students can recognize the value of science's usefulness by researching examples of insulation, thermal expansion and the like used in heat-energy technologies, including architecture.
exp.cur-me-insulation.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-me-insulation.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-me-resonance.title: Finding the speed of sound with a resonance tube (standing waves)
exp.cur-me-resonance.subject: Mechanics and Energy
exp.cur-me-resonance.summary: Find the wavelength from the spacing of loudness peaks as the air column length changes.
exp.cur-me-resonance.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-me-resonance.steps.0: Place a tuning fork (or speaker) and the sound sensor at the mouth of a tube whose length can be changed by adding water.
exp.cur-me-resonance.steps.1: Change the length 1 cm at a time, pressing ‘Record value’ each time.
exp.cur-me-resonance.steps.2: Peak spacing = λ/2; calculate the speed of sound = f·λ.
exp.cur-me-resonance.std.0: Students can explain how string and wind instruments produce sound using standing waves.
exp.cur-me-spring-osc.title: Simple harmonic motion of a spring pendulum
exp.cur-me-spring-osc.subject: Mechanics and Energy
exp.cur-me-spring-osc.summary: Analyze simple harmonic motion with the displacement–time curve and the rate graph.
exp.cur-me-spring-osc.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-me-spring-osc.steps.0: Hang a weight from a spring and place the ultrasonic sensor below it, facing up.
exp.cur-me-spring-osc.steps.1: Pull the weight down, let go, and measure for 20 seconds.
exp.cur-me-spring-osc.steps.2: Measure the period, change the mass, and find k from the m–T² line.
exp.cur-me-spring-osc.std.0: Students can understand simple harmonic motion through a spring pendulum and explain the relationship between acceleration and displacement.
exp.cur-p-joule.title: Does it get warmer the more you flip it? (mechanical energy → heat)
exp.cur-p-joule.subject: Physics
exp.cur-p-joule.summary: Confirm conservation of energy from the temperature rise with the number of times a tube of sand is flipped.
exp.cur-p-joule.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-p-joule.steps.0: Put lead shot or sand into an insulated tube (long tube) and insert the sensor.
exp.cur-p-joule.steps.2: Compare the ‘Curve fit → Linear’ slope with mgh·N = mcΔT.
exp.cur-p-joule.std.0: Students can explain that the total amount of energy does not change when mechanical energy is converted into heat.
exp.cur-p-joule.cautions.0: Wear gloves so heat from your hands is not transferred.
exp.cur-p-led.title: Turn-on voltage of each LED color (semiconductors)
exp.cur-p-led.subject: Physics
exp.cur-p-led.summary: Raise the voltage with a potentiometer to find the threshold voltage for each LED color.
exp.cur-p-led.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-p-led.steps.0: Connect 5 V → potentiometer middle leg → LED long leg, and LED short leg → 100 Ω → GND.
exp.cur-p-led.steps.1: Plug A0 into the LED long-leg row and A1 into the row between the LED and the 100 Ω. Turn the potentiometer a little at a time, pressing ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-p-led.steps.2: LED voltage = A0 − A1, current = A1 ÷ 100 Ω. Compare between colors the voltage where current starts to increase.
exp.cur-p-led.std.0: Students can know the difference between conductors and insulators from the energy band structure of solids and explain how semiconductor devices work.
exp.cur-p-led.bb: Connects the potentiometer, LED and reference resistor.
exp.cur-p-mech-energy.title: Mechanical energy of a bouncing ball
exp.cur-p-mech-energy.subject: Physics
exp.cur-p-mech-energy.summary: See energy conversion and loss from the maximum height dropping with each bounce.
exp.cur-p-mech-energy.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-p-mech-energy.steps.0: Place the ultrasonic sensor 1.5 m high, facing the floor.
exp.cur-p-mech-energy.steps.1: Measure while dropping a ping-pong ball.
exp.cur-p-mech-energy.steps.2: Calculate from the table whether the ratio of peak heights (next/previous) is constant.
exp.cur-p-mech-energy.std.0: Students can understand the relationship between work and kinetic energy and explain potential energy and the law of conservation of mechanical energy.
exp.cur-p-newton2.title: Change the pulling force and the acceleration... (Newton's laws of motion)
exp.cur-p-newton2.subject: Physics
exp.cur-p-newton2.summary: Find the cart's acceleration with different hanging masses to confirm F = ma.
exp.cur-p-newton2.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-p-newton2.steps.0: Place the ultrasonic sensor behind the cart and hang a weight over a pulley.
exp.cur-p-newton2.steps.1: Measure as you release the weight.
exp.cur-p-newton2.steps.2: Slope of the ‘Rate graph’ line = acceleration. Repeat with a different hanging mass ('New run').
exp.cur-p-newton2.std.0: Students can explain uniformly accelerated motion with Newton's laws of motion and apply it to preventing traffic accidents.
exp.cur-p-rc.title: Charging and discharging a capacitor (RC circuit)
exp.cur-p-rc.subject: Physics
exp.cur-p-rc.summary: Use a large capacitor to find the time constant from slowly charging and discharging voltage curves.
exp.cur-p-rc.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-p-rc.steps.0: Wire 5 V → 10 kΩ → capacitor (+), capacitor (−) → GND (τ ≈ 10 seconds).
exp.cur-p-rc.steps.1: Connect across the capacitor to A0 (voltage) and measure while charging from 5 V.
exp.cur-p-rc.steps.2: Remove the power and look at the discharge curve. In ‘Curve fit → Exponential’, B = −1/τ.
exp.cur-p-rc.std.0: Students can explain that the way capacitors store electrical energy is used in everyday products such as various sensors and electrical signal input devices.
exp.cur-p-rc.cautions.0: Match the + and − of an electrolytic capacitor correctly.
exp.cur-p-rc.bb: Plug the resistor and capacitor in series.
exp.cur-p-series-parallel.title: Series and parallel connections and power
exp.cur-p-series-parallel.subject: Physics
exp.cur-p-series-parallel.summary: Compare the voltage across and power in each resistor for different ways of connecting them.
exp.cur-p-series-parallel.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-p-series-parallel.steps.0: (Series) Connect battery (+) → R1 → R2 → GND; plug A0 above R1 and A1 between R1 and R2 (R1 voltage = A0 − A1, R2 voltage = A1).
exp.cur-p-series-parallel.steps.1: (Parallel) Plug the tops of both resistors into the same row and the bottoms into the GND row, and connect the top row to A0.
exp.cur-p-series-parallel.steps.2: Press ‘Record value’ for each circuit and compare power with P = V²/R.
exp.cur-p-series-parallel.std.0: Students can know that power consumption depends on how resistors are connected in a circuit, and find examples of this in various electrical appliances.
exp.cur-p-series-parallel.cautions.0: Put only 0–5 V into the board.
exp.cur-p-series-parallel.bb: Plug the resistors in series, then in parallel.
exp.cur-ps-extinction.title: Dust makes light redder (interstellar extinction)
exp.cur-ps-extinction.subject: Planetary and Space Science
exp.cur-ps-extinction.summary: See that blue drops the most in light passing through milky water.
exp.cur-ps-extinction.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-ps-extinction.steps.0: Put a white LED on one side of a clear container of water and the color sensor on the other.
exp.cur-ps-extinction.steps.1: Add milk 2 drops at a time, pressing ‘Record value’ each time.
exp.cur-ps-extinction.steps.2: Check whether B drops the most and link it to interstellar reddening.
exp.cur-ps-extinction.std.0: Students can infer the existence of interstellar dust from interstellar extinction data and explain its characteristics.
exp.cur-ps-standard-candle.title: Guessing distance from brightness (standard candles)
exp.cur-ps-standard-candle.subject: Planetary and Space Science
exp.cur-ps-standard-candle.summary: Estimate the distance of an unknown light source from the inverse-square distance–brightness relationship.
exp.cur-ps-standard-candle.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-ps-standard-candle.steps.0: Record the brightness of a reference bulb at different distances.
exp.cur-ps-standard-candle.steps.1: Find the equation with ‘Curve fit → Power’.
exp.cur-ps-standard-candle.steps.2: Measure only the brightness of an identical hidden bulb and use the equation to guess its distance.
exp.cur-ps-standard-candle.std.0: Students can compare and evaluate various methods of measuring distance using stellar parallax and brightness.
exp.cur-ps-transit.title: When a planet passes in front of a star (transit)
exp.cur-ps-transit.subject: Planetary and Space Science
exp.cur-ps-transit.summary: See the curve of brightness dipping briefly as a ball passes in front of a bulb.
exp.cur-ps-transit.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-ps-transit.steps.0: Place the light sensor in front of a bulb and swing a ball on a string (the planet) past the front of the bulb.
exp.cur-ps-transit.steps.1: Repeat with different ball sizes ('New run').
exp.cur-ps-transit.steps.2: Check whether the fractional dip in brightness is proportional to (planet/star radius)².
exp.cur-ps-transit.std.0: Students can understand the principles of exoplanet exploration, and argue about the conditions under which life could exist on exoplanets and the possibility of extraterrestrial life.
exp.cur-rx-buffer.title: Does a buffer solution protect pH?
exp.cur-rx-buffer.subject: World of Chemical Reactions
exp.cur-rx-buffer.summary: Compare the pH change when the same acid is added to water and to a buffer solution.
exp.cur-rx-buffer.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-rx-buffer.steps.0: Add 0.1 M HCl to 50 mL of water 2 drops at a time, pressing ‘Record value’ each time.
exp.cur-rx-buffer.steps.1: In a new run, repeat with an acetate buffer solution.
exp.cur-rx-buffer.steps.2: Overlay the two curves to find the buffer capacity.
exp.cur-rx-buffer.std.0: Students can explain buffering in living organisms with chemical equilibrium and feel the wonder of chemical principles.
exp.cur-rx-buffer.materials.3: Acetic acid + sodium acetate buffer solution
exp.cur-rx-buffer.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-rx-daniell.title: The Daniell cell and potential differences of metal pairs
exp.cur-rx-daniell.subject: World of Chemical Reactions
exp.cur-rx-daniell.summary: Compare measured voltages with values calculated from standard reduction potentials.
exp.cur-rx-daniell.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-rx-daniell.steps.0: Connect a Zn|ZnSO4 ‖ CuSO4|Cu cell with a salt bridge.
exp.cur-rx-daniell.steps.1: Press ‘Record value’ for each pair (1 Zn–Cu, 2 Mg–Cu, 3 Fe–Cu…).
exp.cur-rx-daniell.std.0: Students can explain how chemical cells work in terms of redox reactions and find potential differences using standard reduction potentials.
exp.cur-rx-electrolysis.title: Copper plating (Faraday's law)
exp.cur-rx-electrolysis.subject: World of Chemical Reactions
exp.cur-rx-electrolysis.summary: Watch the cathode mass increase over time in the electrolysis of CuSO4.
exp.cur-rx-electrolysis.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-rx-electrolysis.steps.0: Connect cathode → 10 Ω reference resistor → battery (−); connect battery (−) to the board's GND and the cathode-side leg of the resistor to A0 (current = A0 ÷ 10 Ω).
exp.cur-rx-electrolysis.steps.1: Every 5 minutes take out the cathode, dry it, weigh it on the load cell and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-rx-electrolysis.std.0: Students can explain the principle of electrolysis in terms of redox reactions, and research and present examples of electrolysis used in industry.
exp.cur-rx-electrolysis.bb: Put the 10 Ω reference resistor on the battery (−) side and connect the measuring wire.
exp.cur-rx-hydrolysis.title: pH of salt solutions (hydrolysis)
exp.cur-rx-hydrolysis.subject: World of Chemical Reactions
exp.cur-rx-hydrolysis.summary: Compare the pH of NaCl, NH4Cl, CH3COONa and Na2CO3 solutions.
exp.cur-rx-hydrolysis.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-rx-hydrolysis.steps.1: Dip the electrode and press ‘Record value’ once the reading is stable.
exp.cur-rx-hydrolysis.steps.2: Explain the pH order by the strength of the conjugate acids and bases.
exp.cur-rx-hydrolysis.std.0: Students can explain the hydrolysis of salts using ionization constants.
exp.cur-rx-hydrolysis.materials.1: NaCl, NH4Cl, CH3COONa and Na2CO3 solutions
exp.cur-rx-titration-curve.title: Interpreting titration curves (strong and weak acids)
exp.cur-rx-titration-curve.subject: World of Chemical Reactions
exp.cur-rx-titration-curve.summary: Find the equivalence point, half-equivalence point and buffer region on the pH titration curves of a strong and a weak acid.
exp.cur-rx-titration-curve.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-rx-titration-curve.steps.0: Add NaOH to 20 mL of 0.1 M HCl 1 mL at a time, pressing ‘Record value’ each time (0.5 mL at a time near the equivalence point).
exp.cur-rx-titration-curve.steps.1: In a new run, repeat with 0.1 M acetic acid.
exp.cur-rx-titration-curve.steps.2: Compare the two curves with ‘Find equivalence point’ and ‘Rate graph’, and read the pH at the half-equivalence point (pKa).
exp.cur-rx-titration-curve.std.0: Students can interpret pH changes in neutralization titration experiments based on data.
exp.cur-rx-titration-curve.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-rx-vitc.title: Does vitamin C stop browning? (antioxidants)
exp.cur-rx-vitc.subject: World of Chemical Reactions
exp.cur-rx-vitc.summary: Record the color change of a cut apple surface in RGB to see the reducing action of vitamin C.
exp.cur-rx-vitc.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-rx-vitc.steps.0: Of two apple slices, brush vitamin C solution onto one.
exp.cur-rx-vitc.steps.1: Place the color sensor close to the cut surface and measure every 1 minute for 1 hour (a new run per slice).
exp.cur-rx-vitc.steps.2: Compare whether browning (drop in B and G) is slower.
exp.cur-rx-vitc.std.0: Students can feel the wonder of chemistry by researching the various redox reactions used in life processes and chemical cells and the roles of the substances involved.
exp.cur-rx-weak-acid.title: Comparing strong and weak acids (ionization constants)
exp.cur-rx-weak-acid.subject: World of Chemical Reactions
exp.cur-rx-weak-acid.summary: Compare the pH and conductivity of HCl and acetic acid at the same concentration, and how pH changes with dilution.
exp.cur-rx-weak-acid.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-rx-weak-acid.steps.0: Prepare HCl and acetic acid diluted by factors of 10, starting from 0.1 M.
exp.cur-rx-weak-acid.steps.1: Press ‘Record value’ starting from the most concentrated (a new run for each acid).
exp.cur-rx-weak-acid.steps.2: Check whether the log concentration–pH slope is about −1 (strong acid) and −½ (weak acid).
exp.cur-rx-weak-acid.std.0: Students can infer the relative strengths of acids and bases using ionization constants and find the pH of weak acid and weak base solutions.
exp.cur-rx-weak-acid.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.free.title: Free measurement
exp.free.subject: General
exp.free.summary: Records all connected sensors right away.
exp.free.markers.label: Mark
exp.free.steps.0: Records the values of all connected sensors.
exp.free.steps.1: When needed, use the 'Mark' button to leave a note at that moment.
exp.freezing-point.title: Why does salt water freeze later?
exp.freezing-point.subject: Matter and Energy
exp.freezing-point.summary: Compare the freezing-point depression of salt water with cooling curves.
exp.freezing-point.markers.label: Add note
exp.freezing-point.steps.0: Put 5 mL of water in a test tube and insert the temperature sensor.
exp.freezing-point.steps.1: First sketch the cooling curve with 'Draw prediction'.
exp.freezing-point.steps.2: Put the test tube in an ice + salt cooling bath and start the run.
exp.freezing-point.steps.3: Press 'Add note' when ice first appears.
exp.freezing-point.steps.4: Press 'New run' and repeat the same process with salt water.
exp.freezing-point.steps.5: Compare the two freezing points with 'Find plateau'.
exp.freezing-point.std.0: Students can compare changes in vapor pressure, boiling point and freezing point with solution concentration using experimental data, and explain them in connection with everyday examples.
exp.ph-dilution.title: How much does pH change as you dilute?
exp.ph-dilution.subject: Chemistry
exp.ph-dilution.summary: See how pH changes as a strong acid or base is diluted by factors of 10.
exp.ph-dilution.markers.label: Record dilution step
exp.ph-dilution.steps.0: Rinse the pH sensor with distilled water and dip it into 0.1 M hydrochloric acid.
exp.ph-dilution.steps.1: When the value shows 'Stable', check that the dilution factor is 1 and press 'Record value'.
exp.ph-dilution.steps.2: Move to each solution diluted by a factor of 10, entering the dilution factor and recording each time.
exp.ph-dilution.steps.3: The X axis uses a log scale. Check the slope with 'Curve fit → Linear'.
exp.ph-dilution.std.0: Students can understand the autoionization of water and the ionization constant of water, and express the hydrogen ion concentration as pH.
exp.temp-humidity.title: How much water vapor is in your breath?
exp.temp-humidity.subject: Basic measurement · Temperature and humidity
exp.temp-humidity.summary: Practice measuring temperature and humidity with the water vapor in your breath.
exp.temp-humidity.markers.label: Add note
exp.temp-humidity.markers.prompt: Note (e.g. breathed 3 s, covered with cup)
exp.temp-humidity.steps.0: Follow the 'Connection guide' to connect a temperature & humidity sensor (Modulino Thermo or DHT), then press 'Rescan sensors'.
exp.temp-humidity.steps.1: First use 'Draw prediction' to sketch how humidity will change when you breathe on it.
exp.temp-humidity.steps.2: Start the run and record a baseline for 1 minute.
exp.temp-humidity.steps.3: Breathe on it for 3 seconds and press 'Add note'. Watch until the humidity returns to normal.
exp.temp-humidity.steps.4: Press 'New run', cover the sensor with a cup holding a wet tissue, and record for 3 minutes.
exp.temp-humidity.steps.5: Drag across sections of the graph to compare the mean of the baseline and of the peak.
exp.temp-humidity.attach.0: Lay the temperature & humidity sensor on the desk with its sensing side up (the chip on a Modulino, the side with holes on a DHT), at least 10 cm away from the board.
exp.temp-humidity.attach.1: Breath test: from 10 cm away, breathe slowly on the sensor for 3 seconds. Do not let saliva spray on it.
exp.temp-humidity.attach.2: Cup test: stick the wet tissue to the inside bottom of the cup, turn the cup upside down and cover the sensor so the tissue does not touch it.
exp.temp-humidity.cautions.0: Before measuring, first record a baseline for 1 minute without doing anything.
exp.temp-humidity.cautions.1: If water drops form on the sensor, humidity stays near 100 %. Do not wipe it; wait until it dries.
exp.temp-humidity.cautions.2: To compare between groups, breathe from the same distance for the same time.
exp.titration.title: What percentage of vinegar is acetic acid?
exp.titration.subject: Chemistry
exp.titration.summary: Titrate vinegar to find its acetic acid content (end point).
exp.titration.steps.0: Dip the pH sensor into 10 mL of diluted vinegar and start the run.
exp.titration.steps.1: When the value shows 'Stable', press 'Record value' with a volume of 0 mL.
exp.titration.steps.2: Add standard NaOH solution 1 mL at a time, mix, then enter the total volume added and record.
exp.titration.steps.3: Where the pH changes sharply, add 0.2 mL at a time.
exp.titration.steps.4: Use 'Find equivalence point' to check the equivalence volume and the half-equivalence pH (≈ pKa).
exp.titration.std.0: Students can understand neutralization reactions and explain the quantitative relationships in them.
exp.titration.std.1: Students can plan and carry out a neutralization titration experiment to find the concentration of an unknown sample.
exp.titration.std.2: Students can interpret pH changes in neutralization titration experiments based on data.
board.mega-2560.notes.2: Connect UART sensors (particulate matter, MH-Z19) to D19 (RX1) and D18 (TX1).
board.uno-r3.firmwareNote: Lightweight version due to limited memory (no LPS22 pressure, CO₂, color, thermocouple, ultrasonic, or extra I2C/UART sensors). All analog sensors work. Compile-checked, not yet tested on a real board.
conn.uart.name: UART, 4 wires (TX/RX crossed)
conn.uart.steps.0: Cross the wires: sensor TX to board RX, sensor RX to board TX.
conn.uart.steps.1: Connect only one UART sensor at a time (particulate matter or MH-Z19).
conn.uart.cautions.0: UNO R3, Nano and Leonardo use these pins for USB communication, so they do not support UART sensors.
conn.uart.cautions.1: After plugging in the sensor, reconnect the board or press 'Rescan sensors' (the type is detected at power-on).
conn.digital-out.name: Digital output (DO), 3 wires
conn.digital-out.steps.0: Plug the DO pin into one of A0–A3, then press the same port under 'Port'.
conn.digital-out.steps.1: A value of 1 means detected, 0 means not detected (may be reversed on some modules). Adjust sensitivity with the module's potentiometer.
conn.digital-out.cautions.0: Records only on/off. Very short events (0.1 s or less) may be missed.
part.ad8495.name: K-type thermocouple AD8495 (analog, high temperature)
part.ad8495.cautions.0: Output is 5 mV/°C. Put only the thermocouple tip on the heated spot.
part.mlx90614.name: Non-contact infrared thermometer MLX90614 (GY-906)
part.mlx90614.cautions.0: Measures an object's surface temperature without touching it. Keep only the target within the sensor's field of view (about 35°).
part.mlx90614.cautions.1: Shiny metal surfaces read lower than they really are.
part.mcp9808.name: Precision temperature sensor MCP9808
part.aht20.name: AHT20 / DHT20 temperature & humidity
part.aht20.cautions.0: Despite the similar name, the DHT20 is I2C (SDA/SCL, not D4).
part.htu21d.name: HTU21D / Si7021 / SHT21 temperature & humidity
part.htu21d.cautions.0: Same address (0x40) as the INA219. Do not use both together.
part.sht40.name: SHT40 / SHT41 temperature & humidity
part.bmp180.name: BMP180 pressure sensor (GY-68)
part.bmp180.cautions.0: An older sensor. If buying new, the BMP280 is recommended.
part.mq-2.name: MQ-2 flammable gas & smoke (relative)
part.mq-2.cautions.0: Responds to LPG, propane, hydrogen and smoke. Warm up for at least 3 minutes.
part.mq-2.cautions.1: The sensor gets hot. Do not touch it.
part.mq-3.name: MQ-3 alcohol gas (relative)
part.mq-3.cautions.0: Responds to ethanol vapor. Use it for fermentation and evaporation experiments. Warm up for at least 3 minutes.
part.mq-4.name: MQ-4 methane gas (relative)
part.mq-7.name: MQ-7 carbon monoxide (relative)
part.mq-7.cautions.0: For comparing incomplete combustion. Carbon monoxide is dangerous, so never produce it in a closed space.
part.mq-8.name: MQ-8 hydrogen gas (relative)
part.mq-8.cautions.0: Compare hydrogen from metal + acid reactions and from electrolysis of water.
part.mq-9.name: MQ-9 carbon monoxide & flammable gas (relative)
part.mq-9.cautions.0: After warm-up, look only at relative change.
part.mq-135.name: MQ-135 air quality (relative)
part.mq-135.cautions.0: Responds to many gases together, such as ammonia, benzene and CO₂ (cannot tell them apart).
part.mg811.name: MG811 carbon dioxide (analog, relative)
part.mg811.cautions.0: Long warm-up (10 minutes or more), and the value moves in reverse (more CO₂ means lower voltage). For accurate values, use the SCD40 or MH-Z19.
part.co2-ndir-analog.name: Infrared CO₂ sensor (analog, SEN0219)
part.co2-ndir-analog.cautions.0: 0.4–2.0 V equals 0–5000 ppm. Warm up for 3 minutes.
part.scd30.name: Carbon dioxide sensor SCD30
part.scd30.cautions.0: 400–10000 ppm. A new value every 2 seconds.
part.mhz19.name: Carbon dioxide sensor MH-Z19C (NDIR, UART)
part.mhz19.cautions.1: It must be connected when the board powers on to be detected.
part.sgp30.name: Air quality sensor SGP30 (TVOC/eCO₂)
part.sgp30.cautions.0: eCO₂ is estimated from volatile compounds, not real CO₂. It reads 400 ppm for the first 15 seconds.
part.ens160.name: Air quality sensor ENS160 (TVOC/eCO₂)
part.ens160.cautions.0: When first powered on, values are unstable for a few minutes.
part.o2-i2c.name: Oxygen sensor Gravity I2C (SEN0322)
part.o2-i2c.cautions.0: 0–25 %. Measures oxygen used up by combustion and respiration, and oxygen produced by hydrogen peroxide decomposition.
part.o2-i2c.cautions.1: On first use, check that it reads 20.9 % in clean air.
part.pms7003.name: Particulate matter sensor PMS7003 / PMS A003
part.pms7003.cautions.0: Sends PM1.0, PM2.5 and PM10 (µg/m³) every 1 second.
part.pms7003.cautions.1: It must be connected when the board powers on to be detected.
part.bh1750.name: Light sensor BH1750 (GY-302, lx)
part.bh1750.cautions.0: 1–65535 lx. Good for photosynthesis light intensity and distance vs. light intensity experiments.
part.tsl2591.name: High-sensitivity light sensor TSL2591
part.tsl2591.cautions.0: Measures even very dim light (e.g. luminol glow).
part.tcrt5000.name: Infrared reflection sensor TCRT5000
part.tcrt5000.cautions.0: Reflection from a nearby surface (relative). White tape on a spinning disc lets you count rotations.
part.flame.name: Flame sensor (infrared)
part.flame.cautions.0: Relative flame intensity. Keep the sensor at least 20 cm from the flame.
part.photo-gate.name: Photo interrupter (light-gate)
part.photo-gate.cautions.0: Switches 0↔1 when an object passes through the slot. Passes faster than 0.1 s may be missed.
part.vl53l0x.name: Laser distance sensor VL53L0X (ToF)
part.vl53l0x.cautions.0: About 3–200 cm. Better than ultrasonic for small objects and short distances.
part.vl53l0x.cautions.1: If you upload the firmware yourself, you need the Pololu VL53L0X library.
part.flex.name: Flex sensor
part.mpu6050.name: Accelerometer/gyro MPU6050 (GY-521) / MPU9250
part.mpu6050.cautions.0: Measures x, y, z acceleration (m/s²). At rest, the upward axis reads about 9.8.
part.adxl345.name: Accelerometer ADXL345 (GY-291)
part.adxl345.cautions.0: Use it for free fall, collision and vibration experiments.
part.lis3dh.name: Accelerometer LIS3DH
part.lsm6ds.name: Accelerometer/gyro LSM6DSOX
part.adxl335.name: Accelerometer ADXL335 (analog, 3-axis)
part.magnetometer.name: Magnetometer QMC5883L / HMC5883L (GY-271)
part.magnetometer.cautions.0: Magnetic field strength (µT). Earth's field is about 50 µT; it rises when a magnet comes close.
part.pir.name: Motion sensor HC-SR501 (PIR)
part.pir.cautions.0: Reads 1 when there is motion. Values fluctuate for about 1 minute after power-on.
part.vibration.name: Vibration sensor SW-420
part.tilt.name: Tilt sensor SW-520D
part.hall.name: Hall sensor A3144 (magnet detection)
part.hall.cautions.0: Switches when one pole of a magnet comes close. Attach a magnet to a wheel to count rotations.
part.piezo.name: Ceramic piezo vibration sensor
part.piezo.cautions.0: Relative tap strength. For short impacts, set the interval to 0.1 s.
part.ina219.name: Voltage/current sensor INA219
part.ina219.items.1: 4 jumper wires + wires for the test circuit
part.ina219.cautions.0: 0–26 V, ±3.2 A. Insert it in the middle of the circuit (+ side) as VIN+ → VIN−.
part.ina219.cautions.1: Accurately measures current in chemical cells, electrolysis and solar cells.
part.ina260.name: Voltage/current sensor INA260
part.ina260.items.1: 4 jumper wires + wires for the test circuit
part.acs712.name: Current sensor ACS712 (5 A)
part.acs712.cautions.0: Not accurate below 0.1 A (use the INA219 for small currents).
part.acs712.cautions.1: For 20 A or 30 A modules, choose I20A or I30A in 'Set ports manually'.
part.voltage-25.name: Voltage sensor module (0–25 V divider)
part.sound-level.name: Sound level meter (dBA, SEN0232)
part.mic-amp.name: Microphone amplifier MAX4466 / MAX9814
part.mic-amp.cautions.0: Relative loudness. The interval is too long to see the waveform (frequency).
part.dissolved-oxygen.name: Dissolved oxygen sensor (Gravity DO)
part.dissolved-oxygen.cautions.0: Fill the electrode with electrolyte and calibrate before use.
part.dissolved-oxygen.cautions.1: Use it for aquatic plant photosynthesis and water temperature vs. dissolved oxygen experiments.
part.orp.name: ORP (redox potential) sensor
part.orp.cautions.0: −2000 to 2000 mV. Check with a standard solution (e.g. 256 mV) before use.
part.rain.name: Rain sensor
part.rain.cautions.0: The wetter it is, the higher the value (relative). Keep the circuit part out of water.
part.soil-resistive.name: Soil moisture sensor (resistive)
part.soil-resistive.cautions.0: The electrodes corrode easily. For long-term use, use a capacitive sensor.
part.water-level-optical.name: Optical water level sensor (SEN0205)
part.pulse.name: Pulse sensor (Pulse Sensor)
part.pulse.cautions.0: Hold it on a fingertip or earlobe without moving. Use a 0.1 s interval to see the waveform.
part.max30102.name: Pulse/SpO₂ sensor MAX30102
part.max30102.cautions.0: Records the infrared pulse waveform (relative). Find the pulse rate from the spacing of the peaks.
part.ecg.name: ECG sensor AD8232
part.ecg.cautions.0: Attach the electrodes and stay still. Unplug the laptop charger while measuring (noise).
part.emg.name: EMG sensor (Grove EMG · SEN0240)
part.emg.cautions.0: Relative value that rises when the muscle tenses.
part.gsr.name: Galvanic skin response sensor (Grove GSR)
part.gsr.cautions.0: Relative value that changes with tension and stimuli.
sensor.TKA.name: High temperature (thermocouple)
sensor.CO2N.name: Carbon dioxide (analog)
sensor.CO2N.note: Infrared CO₂ sensor SEN0219 (0.4–2.0 V = 0–5000 ppm). Warm up 3 minutes.
sensor.REFL.name: Reflection (relative)
sensor.REFL.note: Infrared reflection sensor TCRT5000, AO output.
sensor.FLAM.name: Flame (relative)
sensor.FLAM.note: Flame sensor AO output. Higher means a stronger flame.
sensor.RAIN.name: Wetness (relative)
sensor.RAIN.note: Rain sensor AO output. Higher means wetter.
sensor.DOUT.name: On/off
sensor.AXA.name: Acceleration X (analog)
sensor.AYA.name: Acceleration Y (analog)
sensor.AZA.name: Acceleration Z (analog)
sensor.FLEX.name: Bending (relative)
sensor.I5A.name: Current (5 A)
sensor.I5A.note: ACS712 5 A module (185 mV/A). If it does not read 0 at 0 A, set the zero.
sensor.I20A.name: Current (20 A)
sensor.I30A.name: Current (30 A)
sensor.V25.name: Voltage (0–25 V)
sensor.VIB.name: Vibration (relative)
sensor.DBA.name: Sound level
sensor.DOX.name: Dissolved oxygen
sensor.DOX.note: Analog dissolved oxygen sensor. Calibrate with air-saturated water.
sensor.ORP.name: Redox potential
sensor.PULS.name: Pulse waveform (relative)
sensor.PULS.note: Pulse sensor. Use a 0.1 s interval to see the waveform.
sensor.ECG.name: ECG (relative)
sensor.EMG.name: EMG (relative)
sensor.GSR.name: Skin response (relative)
sensor.LUX.name: Illuminance
sensor.TIR.name: Surface temperature (non-contact)
sensor.VDC.name: Voltage
sensor.IDC.name: Current
sensor.AX.name: Acceleration X
sensor.AY.name: Acceleration Y
sensor.AZ.name: Acceleration Z
sensor.MAG.name: Magnetic field
sensor.ECO2.name: eCO₂ (estimated)
sensor.TVOC.name: Total volatile organic compounds
sensor.PPG.name: Pulse waveform (infrared)
sensor.PM1.name: Particulate matter PM1.0
sensor.PM25.name: Fine particulate matter PM2.5
sensor.PM10.name: Particulate matter PM10
sensor.O2I.name: Oxygen
guide.planned.3: RS485 soil sensor (moisture, EC, pH, N, P, K)
guide.planned.4: Ozone SEN0321 · multi-gas MiCS-4514 · heart-rate hub MAX32664
guide.planned.6: Firmware for Nano ESP32 · Nano 33 · GIGA
conn.pulse.name: Pulse, 3 wires (D3)
conn.pulse.steps.0: Always plug the signal wire into D3. The firmware counts pulses per second and converts them to units.
conn.pulse.steps.1: Connect only one pulse sensor to D3.
conn.pulse.cautions.1: For sensors powered by 12 V, check the manual that the signal does not exceed 5 V.
conn.spi-rtd.name: MAX31865, 6 wires (SPI)
conn.spi-rtd.steps.0: Connect the PT100 probe wires to the module's RTD terminals (for a 2-wire probe, use the two outer terminals).
conn.spi-rtd.steps.1: It can share CLK and SDO with a MAX6675 / MAX31855 thermocouple (only CS differs).
conn.spi-rtd.cautions.0: Check that the module's reference resistor is 430 Ω (for PT100). 4300 Ω is for PT1000, and values will be off by 10×.
part.tmp117.name: Precision temperature sensor TMP117 / TMP119 (±0.1 °C)
part.tmp117.cautions.0: ±0.1 °C, the most precise option. Good for calorimetry and heat of neutralization.
part.tmp102.name: Temperature sensor TMP102
part.mcp9600.name: Thermocouple amplifier MCP9600 (I2C, high temperature)
part.mcp9600.cautions.0: −200 to 1300 °C. Cold-junction compensation is built in.
part.mcp9600.cautions.1: Keep the module board away from the flame.
part.max31855.name: K-type thermocouple MAX31855 (high temperature, precise)
part.max31855.cautions.0: Plug it into the same pins as the MAX6675 (D10, D12, D13) and it is detected automatically. −200 to 1350 °C.
part.max31865.name: Platinum resistance thermometer PT100 + MAX31865
part.max31865.cautions.0: Measures −200 to 600 °C to ±0.5 °C. Assumes a PT100 module with a 430 Ω reference resistor.
part.max31865.cautions.1: For a 3-wire probe, change the solder jumper on the back of the module to 3-wire.
part.ntc.name: NTC thermistor 10 kΩ (B 3950)
part.ntc.cautions.0: An inexpensive temperature sensor. A 1-point calibration in ice water (0 °C) makes it accurate.
part.ntc.cautions.1: If the B value is not 3950, calibrate before use.
part.am2320.name: Temperature/humidity sensor AM2320
part.am2320.items.1: 4 jumper wires (add 10 kΩ pull-ups on SDA/SCL if missing)
part.am2320.cautions.0: A new value comes every 2 seconds.
part.hih6130.name: Temperature/humidity sensor HIH6130 / HIH6120
part.hih6130.cautions.0: ±4 % RH. It shares an address with the LCD adapter (0x27), so do not use them together.
part.bmp388.name: Pressure sensor BMP388 / BMP390
part.bmp388.cautions.0: ±0.03 kPa. You can also see pressure change with height.
part.dps310.name: Pressure sensor DPS310 (Grove)
part.ms5611.name: Pressure sensor MS5611 (GY-63)
part.ms5611.cautions.0: Precise enough to detect a 10 cm height difference.
part.mpl3115a2.name: Pressure sensor MPL3115A2
part.mpl3115a2.cautions.0: A new value comes every 0.6 seconds.
part.mpx5010dp.name: Differential pressure sensor MPX5010DP (0 to 10 kPa)
part.mpx5010dp.cautions.0: Measures the pressure difference between the two tubes. Use it for breath, lung capacity and flow experiments.
part.mpx5010dp.cautions.1: Before starting, leave both tubes open and set zero.
part.water-pressure.name: Water pressure sensor (SEN0257, 0 to 1.6 MPa)
part.water-pressure.cautions.0: Measures pressure vs. water depth (1 m of water ≈ 9.8 kPa). Its wide range suits deep tanks.
part.mq-5.name: MQ-5 LPG / town gas (relative)
part.mq-6.name: MQ-6 LPG / butane (relative)
part.mq-6.cautions.0: For butane gas diffusion experiments. Preheat for at least 3 minutes.
part.mq-131.name: MQ-131 ozone (relative)
part.mq-131.cautions.0: Responds to ozone. Needs a long preheat (24 hours recommended).
part.mq-137.name: MQ-137 ammonia (relative)
part.mq-137.cautions.0: For ammonia diffusion and generation experiments. Preheat for at least 3 minutes.
part.mq-138.name: MQ-138 volatile organic compounds (relative)
part.mq-138.cautions.0: Responds to alcohol, acetone, toluene and similar.
part.mics-5524.name: MiCS-5524 gas (CO, alcohol, VOC; relative)
part.mics-5524.cautions.0: Responds to several gases at once (cannot tell them apart).
part.mhz16.name: Carbon dioxide sensor MH-Z14A / MH-Z16 (UART, 0 to 50000 ppm)
part.mhz16.cautions.0: Works like the MH-Z19, so it is detected automatically. Also measures high CO₂ (fermentation, combustion).
part.cm1106.name: Carbon dioxide sensor CM1106 / CM1108 (UART)
part.cm1106.cautions.0: 0 to 5000 ppm. Preheat for 3 minutes after power-on.
part.cozir.name: Carbon dioxide sensor COZIR / SprintIR (UART)
part.cozir.cautions.0: SprintIR is fast, so it suits reaction-rate experiments. The scale factor is read automatically.
part.hcho.name: Formaldehyde sensor (SEN0231, UART)
part.hcho.cautions.0: 0 to 5 ppm. For comparing indoor air quality.
part.pms5003st.name: Particulate + formaldehyde sensor PMS5003ST
part.pms5003st.cautions.0: Measures particulates, formaldehyde, temperature and humidity together.
part.sgp40.name: VOC sensor SGP40 (raw value)
part.sgp40.cautions.0: The value drops as volatile compounds increase (for relative comparison).
part.as7341.name: Spectral sensor AS7341 (8 wavelengths, simple spectrophotometer)
part.as7341.items.2: LED light source and cuvette holder
part.as7341.cautions.0: Measures 8 light intensities from 415 to 680 nm. Good for solution absorbance (Beer–Lambert law) experiments.
part.as7341.cautions.1: Absorbance = log(distilled water value ÷ sample value). Compute it with a calculated column in the table.
part.apds9960.name: Color/proximity sensor APDS9960
part.apds9960.cautions.0: Measures red/green/blue ratios (%). For comparing color changes in solutions.
part.ltr390.name: UV sensor LTR390 (UV index)
part.ltr390.cautions.0: Gives the UV index (UVI). Compare UV blocking by sunscreen, glass and shade.
part.si1145.name: UV sensor SI1145 (Grove Sunlight)
part.ml8511.name: UV sensor ML8511 (analog)
part.modulino-light.name: Modulino Light (LTR381, color and illuminance)
part.modulino-light.cautions.0: Measures red/green/blue ratios and illuminance (lx) together.
part.vl53l1x.name: Laser distance sensor VL53L1X (up to 4 m)
part.vl53l1x.cautions.0: 4 cm to 4 m. Works right away with no library. Good for falling objects and cart motion.
part.modulino-distance.cautions.0: 1 to 130 cm. Plug in with a Qwiic cable and it works right away.
part.vl6180x.name: Short-range laser sensor VL6180X (0 to 20 cm)
part.vl6180x.cautions.0: Measures 0 to 20 cm in mm. For short movements such as spring oscillation.
part.gp2y0a21.name: Infrared distance sensor GP2Y0A21 (10 to 80 cm)
part.gp2y0a21.cautions.0: Readings are wrong closer than 10 cm.
part.gp2y0a21.cautions.1: Voltage → distance curve conversion works only on UNO R4 and Mega.
part.gp2y0a41.name: Infrared distance sensor GP2Y0A41 (4 to 30 cm)
part.gp2y0a41.cautions.0: Readings are wrong closer than 4 cm.
part.gp2y0a41.cautions.1: Voltage → distance curve conversion works only on UNO R4 and Mega.
part.tfmini.name: LiDAR distance sensor TFmini-S / TFmini Plus / TF-Luna
part.tfmini.cautions.0: 0.1 to 12 m. For long-distance motion. Use the default settings (115200, UART).
part.a02yyuw.name: Waterproof ultrasonic distance sensor A02YYUW (UART)
part.a02yyuw.cautions.0: 3 to 450 cm. For measuring water level from above (only the sensor head is waterproof).
part.maxbotix.name: Waterproof ultrasonic MaxBotix (analog)
part.maxbotix.cautions.0: Connect the AN pin. Assumes 5 V power.
part.nau7802.name: Load cell ADC NAU7802 (Qwiic scale)
part.nau7802.cautions.0: A scale that connects with a Qwiic cable instead of the HX711. In 'Calibrate', set zero first, then use the reference weight.
part.icm20948.name: 9-axis sensor ICM-20948 / ICM-20649
part.mma8452q.name: Accelerometer MMA8452Q
part.adxl313.name: Accelerometer ADXL313 (Qwiic)
part.bno055.name: Orientation sensor BNO055 (9-axis, computes angles)
part.bno055.cautions.0: Gives acceleration and heading (°) together. For the first few seconds, rotate it slowly to calibrate.
part.as5600.name: Magnetic rotation angle sensor AS5600
part.as5600.cautions.0: Measures 0 to 360°. For pendulum swings and rotational motion.
part.as5600.cautions.1: Place the magnet 1 to 3 mm directly above the chip.
part.hall-angle.name: 360° Hall angle sensor (SEN0221, analog)
part.hall-angle.cautions.0: The angle (°) the knob is turned. A 2-point calibration at 0° and 180° makes it accurate.
part.lis3mdl.name: Magnetic field sensor LIS3MDL
part.lis3mdl.cautions.0: ±400 µT. Measures field strength around coils and magnets.
part.mag3110.name: Magnetic field sensor MAG3110
part.bmm150.name: Magnetic field sensor BMM150 (Grove Compass v2)
part.bmm150.cautions.0: Approximate values without factory calibration. Use for comparing changes.
part.tmag5273.name: 3-axis Hall sensor TMAG5273 (strong fields)
part.tmag5273.cautions.0: Measures up to ±40 mT (about 40000 µT). Good near magnets and for electromagnet experiments.
part.water-flow.name: Water flow sensor YF-S201 (flow rate)
part.water-flow.cautions.0: Plug the yellow (signal) wire into D3. Calibrate with the water collected in 1 minute for accuracy.
part.water-flow.cautions.1: Other sizes, such as the Seeed G1/4, need calibration before use.
part.geiger.name: Geiger counter (radiation, 1-minute count)
part.geiger.cautions.0: Plug the signal (VIN/OUT) wire into D3. It is a 1-minute average, so values build up during the first minute.
part.geiger.cautions.1: To see µSv/h, change D3 to 'Radiation dose rate' in 'Set ports manually'.
part.anemometer-pulse.name: Anemometer (pulse type)
part.anemometer-pulse.cautions.0: Plug the signal wire into D3. The pulse-to-wind-speed ratio differs by product, so calibrate with the manual's value.
part.anemometer-analog.name: Anemometer (analog, SEN0170)
part.anemometer-analog.cautions.0: Power the anemometer separately with 12 to 24 V. Plug only the signal (0 to 5 V) into A0 and connect GND in common.
part.ear-clip-hr.name: Ear-clip heart rate sensor (Grove)
part.ear-clip-hr.cautions.0: Plug the signal wire into D3. Heart rate is a 10-second average. For before/after exercise comparisons.
part.pulse-counter.name: RPM / pulse counting (Hall sensor, photo interrupter)
part.pulse-counter.items.0: Hall sensor or photo interrupter module (DO pin)
part.pulse-counter.cautions.0: Plug the DO wire into D3. With 1 pulse per turn, the value is the RPM directly.
part.ads1115.name: Precision voltage ADS1115 (16-bit, electrochemical cells)
part.ads1115.cautions.0: Measures the voltage between A0(+) and A1(−) in 0.1 mV steps (±4 V). Good for electrochemical and concentration cells.
part.ads1115.cautions.1: These are the module's A0/A1 terminals (not the board's A0/A1).
part.acs723.name: Current sensor ACS723 (5 A)
part.acs723.cautions.0: Set zero at 0 A before use.
part.acs758.name: Current sensor ACS758 (50 A)
part.acs758.cautions.0: For large currents. Use only for teacher demonstrations.
sensor.IRD.name: Distance (infrared)
sensor.IRD.note: Sharp GP2Y0A21 (10 to 80 cm). Curve conversion only in UNO R4/Mega firmware.
sensor.IRDS.name: Distance (infrared, short)
sensor.IRDS.note: Sharp GP2Y0A41 (4 to 30 cm). Curve conversion only in UNO R4/Mega firmware.
sensor.TNTC.name: Temperature (thermistor)
sensor.TNTC.note: 10 kΩ NTC thermistor (B 3950) + 10 kΩ resistor. UNO R4/Mega firmware only.
sensor.UVML.name: UV intensity
sensor.WPRS.name: Water pressure
sensor.WPRS.note: Water pressure sensor SEN0257 (0.5 to 4.5 V = 0 to 1.6 MPa).
sensor.DP.name: Pressure difference
sensor.DP.note: Differential pressure sensor MPX5010DP (0 to 10 kPa).
sensor.WIND.name: Wind speed
sensor.WIND.note: Anemometer SEN0170 (0 to 5 V = 0 to 32.4 m/s, 12 to 24 V power).
sensor.ANGA.name: Angle (analog)
sensor.I5B.name: Current (ACS723)
sensor.I50A.name: Current (50 A)
sensor.DUS.name: Distance (analog ultrasonic)
sensor.DUS.note: MaxBotix waterproof ultrasonic, analog output (5 V).
sensor.FLOW.name: Flow rate
sensor.FLOW.note: Water flow sensor YF-S201 (7.5 Hz pulses = 1 L/min). Connect to D3.

sensor.WNDP.name: Wind speed (pulse)

sensor.RPM.name: Rotation speed

conn.analog-3v3.name: Analog, 3 wires (3.3 V supply)
conn.analog-3v3.steps.0: Always connect VCC to the 3.3V pin (5V will damage it).
conn.analog-3v3.steps.1: Connect the signal wire to one of A0~A3 and press the same port under 'Port'.
conn.analog-3v3.cautions.0: This is a 3.3 V-only module. Do not connect it to the 5V pin.
conn.uart-3v3.name: UART, 4 wires (3.3 V supply, TX/RX crossed)
conn.uart-3v3.steps.0: Cross the wires: sensor TX to board RX, sensor RX to board TX.
conn.uart-3v3.steps.1: Always connect VCC to the 3.3V pin.
conn.uart-3v3.cautions.0: UNO R3, Nano and Leonardo do not support UART sensors.
conn.uart-3v3.cautions.1: On a 5 V board, the board TX (5 V) goes into the sensor RX. If the datasheet says 5 V input is not allowed, add a resistor divider (1 kΩ+2 kΩ).
part.adxl335.cautions.0: Connect the X, Y and Z outputs to A0, A1 and A2 and set each port to AXA, AYA and AZA ('Set ports manually').
part.soil-resistive.cautions.1: Depending on the module, the value direction may be reversed, so do a 2-point calibration with dry soil (0 %) and water (100 %) before use.
part.ntc.cautions.2: As in the wiring diagram, put the NTC on the 5V side and the 10 kΩ resistor on the GND side (if reversed, the temperature comes out inverted).
part.ml8511.cautions.0: Measures UV intensity (mW/cm²). Connect the module's EN pin to 3.3V as well.
exp.cur-b-digestion-color.title: Do saliva and digestive aids break down starch? (color sensor)
exp.cur-b-digestion-color.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-b-digestion-color.summary: See digestive enzymes at work from how fast the blue of a starch–iodine solution fades.
exp.cur-b-digestion-color.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-b-digestion-color.steps.0: Add iodine solution to starch solution to make it blue, then pour it into a cuvette.
exp.cur-b-digestion-color.steps.1: Place the white LED behind the cuvette and the color sensor in front.
exp.cur-b-digestion-color.steps.2: Add saliva (or water with a dissolved digestive aid) and measure in a 37 °C water bath.
exp.cur-b-digestion-color.steps.3: Compare how fast the color fades with a sample that has only water added.
