exp.cur-b-digestion-color.std.0: Students can understand the structure and function of the digestive system, and infer the digestive process in relation to the action of digestive enzymes.
exp.cur-b-digestion-color.std.1: Students can infer, in connection with physiological changes in the body, that digestion, circulation, respiration and excretion result from the integrated action of organ systems.
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.title: How fast does your heart beat during exercise? (heart rate and homeostasis)
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.summary: Record heart rate before, during and after exercise and compare recovery times.
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.markers.label: Note
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.steps.0: Put the heart rate sensor on your earlobe (clip type) or fingertip (MAX30102) and record for 1 minute at rest.
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.steps.1: Run in place for 1 minute and mark it with ‘Note’.
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.steps.2: Sit down and watch your heart rate return over 3 minutes.
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.steps.3: Compare within your group how long it took to return to the resting value.
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.std.0: Students can understand the structure and function of the circulatory system, and present a synthesis of the pathways of blood circulation.
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.std.1: Students can infer how homeostasis is maintained in the body based on an understanding of how the endocrine and nervous systems work and interact.
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.std.2: Students can infer cases where scientific knowledge is applied, through inquiry activities that uncover the scientific principles in advanced science and technology.
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.materials.0: Heart rate sensor (clip type or MAX30102)
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.cautions.0: Students who feel unwell take on measuring only, not exercising.
exp.cur-b-heart-rate.cautions.1: This is not a medical measurement.
exp.cur-e-deep-circulation.title: Cold, salty water sinks (deep ocean circulation)
exp.cur-e-deep-circulation.subject: Earth Science
exp.cur-e-deep-circulation.summary: Record water temperature and conductivity at the top and bottom of a tank to confirm that cold, salty water sinks.
exp.cur-e-deep-circulation.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-e-deep-circulation.steps.0: Place temperature sensors at the top and bottom of the tank, and the conductivity sensor at the bottom.
exp.cur-e-deep-circulation.steps.1: Slowly pour icy salt water in at one end.
exp.cur-e-deep-circulation.steps.2: Note when the bottom temperature drops and the conductivity rises.
exp.cur-e-deep-circulation.steps.3: Compare with pouring in warm fresh water.
exp.cur-e-deep-circulation.std.0: Students can know how deep ocean circulation arises and how it is distributed, and infer its relationship with surface circulation and climate change.
exp.cur-e-deep-circulation.attach.0: Plug 2 temperature sensors side by side on the same D2 line and you get separate 'Temperature 1' and 'Temperature 2' graphs.
exp.cur-e-deep-circulation.bb: Plug 2 or more temperature sensors side by side in the same rows (not needed for 1 sensor).
exp.cur-em-magnetic-brake.title: A metal plate stops a magnet pendulum (magnetic braking)
exp.cur-em-magnetic-brake.subject: Electromagnetism and Quantum
exp.cur-em-magnetic-brake.summary: Compare how quickly a magnet pendulum's swing dies down over different metal plates.
exp.cur-em-magnetic-brake.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-em-magnetic-brake.steps.0: Attach the angle sensor to the pivot of the magnet pendulum.
exp.cur-em-magnetic-brake.steps.1: Do a New run each with nothing underneath, an aluminum plate, a copper plate and a slotted plate.
exp.cur-em-magnetic-brake.steps.2: Compare how fast the swing dies down with ‘Curve fit → Exponential’.
exp.cur-em-magnetic-brake.std.0: Students can understand electromagnetic induction in terms of changes in magnetic flux, and explain technologies that use electromagnetic induction, such as transformers and inductors.
exp.cur-es-ocean-wave.title: Waves made by wind (ocean waves)
exp.cur-es-ocean-wave.subject: Earth System Science
exp.cur-es-ocean-wave.summary: Use a distance sensor to measure changes in water-surface height (waves) at different fan speeds.
exp.cur-es-ocean-wave.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-es-ocean-wave.steps.0: Fix the distance sensor above one end of a long tank, facing down.
exp.cur-es-ocean-wave.steps.1: Do a New run at fan speed 1, 2 and 3.
exp.cur-es-ocean-wave.steps.2: Compare the wave height (max – min) and period.
exp.cur-es-ocean-wave.steps.3: Also see how the wave shape changes when you change the water depth.
exp.cur-es-ocean-wave.std.0: Students can understand how ocean waves form, and compare and explain the differences between shallow-water and deep-water waves.
exp.cur-h-conductor.title: Sorting conductors and insulators by current
exp.cur-h-conductor.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-conductor.summary: Measure the current through different objects at the same voltage to compare their electrical properties.
exp.cur-h-conductor.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-conductor.steps.0: Build a circuit: battery – current sensor – alligator-clip leads.
exp.cur-h-conductor.steps.1: Clip in copper wire, graphite, glass, rubber and silicon in turn and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-h-conductor.steps.2: Sort them into conductors, semiconductors and insulators in order of current.
exp.cur-h-conductor.std.0: Students can classify the materials that make up the Earth by their electrical properties, and recognize that these properties are applied in various materials used in everyday life and advanced technology.
exp.cur-h-free-fall.title: Motion of a falling object (free fall)
exp.cur-h-free-fall.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-free-fall.summary: See accelerated motion in the distance–time graph of a falling ball.
exp.cur-h-free-fall.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-free-fall.steps.0: Fix the distance sensor 1.5 m high, facing down.
exp.cur-h-free-fall.steps.1: Release a large ball (or coffee filter) 20 cm directly below the sensor.
exp.cur-h-free-fall.steps.2: In ‘Curve fit → Quadratic’, the x² coefficient × 2 is the acceleration.
exp.cur-h-free-fall.steps.3: Compare horizontal throws together with a video.
exp.cur-h-free-fall.std.0: Students can explain various motions on and around the Earth's surface caused by the action of gravity.
exp.cur-h-free-fall.cautions.0: Keep your hands out from under the sensor.
exp.cur-h-induction.title: Making electricity with a magnet and coil (electromagnetic induction)
exp.cur-h-induction.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-induction.summary: See how the induced voltage changes with how fast the magnet moves in and out and with the number of turns.
exp.cur-h-induction.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-induction.steps.0: Connect the two ends of the coil to the voltage input (A0) and GND (negative voltages are raised by a 1.65 V reference circuit).
exp.cur-h-induction.steps.1: Measure while moving the magnet in and out quickly and slowly.
exp.cur-h-induction.steps.2: Do a New run with a coil that has a different number of turns.
exp.cur-h-induction.steps.3: Compare peak heights to sum up Faraday's law.
exp.cur-h-induction.std.0: Students can understand how kinetic energy is converted into electrical energy in a generator, and investigate and present the effects on human life of power plants that use fossil fuels and nuclear energy as heat sources.
exp.cur-h-induction.std.1: Students can recognize the impact on modern civilization of applying electromagnetic induction to energy-transfer technologies such as sensors, wireless communication and wireless charging.
exp.cur-h-induction.bb: The coil voltage also goes negative (−), so make a 1.65 V reference with 2 resistors.
exp.cur-h-measure-basics.title: Measuring base quantities with digital tools
exp.cur-h-measure-basics.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-measure-basics.summary: Measure length, mass and temperature with sensors and compare with a ruler, scale and thermometer.
exp.cur-h-measure-basics.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-measure-basics.steps.0: Measure the distance to a wall with the distance sensor, an object's mass with the load cell, and water temperature with the temperature sensor.
exp.cur-h-measure-basics.steps.1: Also measure the same things with a ruler, scale and thermometer and write them in ‘Add note’.
exp.cur-h-measure-basics.steps.2: Repeat each measurement 5 times and find the mean and spread.
exp.cur-h-measure-basics.steps.3: Discuss how an analog value becomes a digital number (resolution).
exp.cur-h-measure-basics.std.0: Students can know the meaning of measurement and estimation in scientific inquiry, and argue for the usefulness and necessity of measurement standards in various everyday situations.
exp.cur-h-measure-basics.std.1: Students know that information is produced by measuring and analyzing the various changes that occur in nature, and recognize the impact on modern civilization of using technology that converts this information to digital form in information and communication.
exp.cur-h-noise.title: Classroom noise map (real-time data)
exp.cur-h-noise.subject: Integrated Science 2
exp.cur-h-noise.summary: Record classroom sound level (dBA) over a day and compare by time of day.
exp.cur-h-noise.markers.label: Note
exp.cur-h-noise.steps.0: Fix the sound level sensor near a classroom wall.
exp.cur-h-noise.steps.1: Record while marking class time, breaks and lunch with ‘Note’.
exp.cur-h-noise.steps.2: Find the mean and maximum and compare with noise standards (e.g. 55 dB for schools).
exp.cur-h-noise.std.0: Students can investigate cases where big data is used in science, technology and society, and infer the advantages and problems of using big data.
exp.cur-h-noise.std.1: Students can infer cases where scientific knowledge is applied, through inquiry activities that uncover the scientific principles in advanced science and technology.
exp.cur-h-pasteur.title: Why does meat broth spoil? (recreating Pasteur's experiment)
exp.cur-h-pasteur.subject: Science Inquiry Lab 1
exp.cur-h-pasteur.summary: Compare microbial growth from pH and turbidity changes in flasks with differently shaped necks.
exp.cur-h-pasteur.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-pasteur.steps.0: Divide boiled meat broth (or milk) between a straight-necked bottle and a bottle with an S-shaped tube.
exp.cur-h-pasteur.steps.1: Measure pH and turbidity at the same time every day and press ‘Record value’ (a New run for each bottle).
exp.cur-h-pasteur.steps.2: Compare which bottle's pH drops and becomes cloudy.
exp.cur-h-pasteur.std.0: Students can carry out representative inquiry experiments from the history of science, including forming hypotheses, and illustrate the features of the deductive inquiry method.
exp.cur-h-pasteur.cautions.0: Never drink spoiled samples; discard them right after the experiment.
exp.cur-h-pasteur.cautions.1: Wear gloves so you do not get burned by hot water or heaters, and keep sensor wires away from heat sources.
exp.cur-h-ride-accel.title: Acceleration on amusement rides (accelerometer)
exp.cur-h-ride-accel.subject: Science Inquiry Lab 2
exp.cur-h-ride-accel.summary: Record and compare the acceleration of model rides, elevators and shaking motions.
exp.cur-h-ride-accel.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-ride-accel.steps.0: Fix the accelerometer firmly in a box together with the board (connect via Bluetooth).
exp.cur-h-ride-accel.steps.1: Do a New run each on a model swing ride, a pendulum and an elevator.
exp.cur-h-ride-accel.steps.2: See how much the Z axis rises above and falls below 9.8 (how heavy you feel).
exp.cur-h-ride-accel.steps.3: Convert the maximum acceleration to g and compare with real rides.
exp.cur-h-ride-accel.std.0: Students can explore scientific principles in everyday life, such as in film, architecture, cooking, sports and media, through experiments, and experience the enjoyment and usefulness of science through play activities that use scientific principles.
exp.cur-h-ride-accel.std.1: Students can find the resultant of the various forces acting on an object and predict its motion quantitatively.
exp.cur-h-ride-accel.cautions.0: Tie the board down with string so it does not fall.
exp.cur-h-spectrum.title: Measuring light color by color (spectral sensor)
exp.cur-h-spectrum.subject: Integrated Science 1
exp.cur-h-spectrum.summary: Compare the intensity in 8 wavelength bands for each light source to see differences in their spectra.
exp.cur-h-spectrum.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-h-spectrum.steps.0: Place the spectral sensor (AS7341) inside a dark box.
exp.cur-h-spectrum.steps.1: Shine an incandescent lamp, fluorescent lamp, LED and neon (discharge tube) in turn and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-h-spectrum.steps.2: Compare the bars for each wavelength band to find the difference between continuous and line spectra.
exp.cur-h-spectrum.steps.3: Compare with the color bands seen through a spectroscope.
exp.cur-h-spectrum.std.0: Students can analyze the spectra of light emitted by celestial bodies to infer the elements formed in the early universe and the materials that make up celestial bodies.
exp.cur-h-spectrum.cautions.0: Discharge tubes use high voltage, so the teacher handles them.
exp.cur-m-coil-field.title: Magnetic field around a current-carrying wire or coil
exp.cur-m-coil-field.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-coil-field.summary: Measure how the magnetic field strength changes when you increase the current or change the distance.
exp.cur-m-coil-field.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-coil-field.steps.0: Fix the magnetic field sensor beside the coil (or a straight wire).
exp.cur-m-coil-field.steps.1: With the current off, record the first value (Earth's magnetic field).
exp.cur-m-coil-field.steps.2: Increase the current from the power supply in 100 mA steps and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-m-coil-field.steps.3: Do a New run at a different distance to see how distance relates to the field.
exp.cur-m-coil-field.std.0: Students can reason out the characteristics of the force on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field, and find examples of its use in daily life, such as electric motors.
exp.cur-m-coil-field.std.1: Students can know the principles of devices that convert energy using the magnetic effect of current, and design speakers, electric motors and similar devices.
exp.cur-m-coil-field.cautions.0: Keep the current under 1 A, and switch off at once if the wire gets hot.
exp.cur-m-density.title: Telling iron from aluminum (density)
exp.cur-m-density.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-density.summary: Record mass while entering volume, and find the slope of the mass–volume line (density).
exp.cur-m-density.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-density.steps.1: Add pieces of the same metal one at a time, enter the total volume measured with a graduated cylinder, and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-m-density.steps.2: Record the other metal in a New run.
exp.cur-m-density.steps.3: The slope from ‘Curve fit → Proportional’ is the density (iron about 7.9, aluminum about 2.7 g/cm³).
exp.cur-m-density.std.0: Students can know the meaning of characteristic properties of substances and explain density, solubility, melting point, boiling point, etc. through experiments.
exp.cur-m-evaporation-mass.title: Where does hand sanitizer go? (evaporation and mass)
exp.cur-m-evaporation-mass.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-evaporation-mass.summary: Record the mass lost through evaporation over time.
exp.cur-m-evaporation-mass.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-evaporation-mass.steps.0: Put a Petri dish on the load cell and zero it.
exp.cur-m-evaporation-mass.steps.1: Drop in about 5 g of hand sanitizer (or ethanol) and start measuring.
exp.cur-m-evaporation-mass.steps.2: Watch the mass decrease for 10 minutes (compare water in a New run too).
exp.cur-m-evaporation-mass.steps.3: Compare evaporation rates using the slope from ‘Curve fit → Linear’.
exp.cur-m-evaporation-mass.std.0: Students can observe diffusion and evaporation and infer that the particles making up matter are in motion.
exp.cur-m-evaporation-mass.cautions.0: Keep ethanol and sanitizer away from flames.
exp.cur-m-friction.title: What does friction depend on?
exp.cur-m-friction.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-friction.summary: Compare the force needed to pull a wooden block on different surfaces and with different weights.
exp.cur-m-friction.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-friction.steps.0: Tie a wooden block to the load cell hook with string.
exp.cur-m-friction.steps.1: Pull the block slowly and steadily while measuring (the first peak = maximum static friction).
exp.cur-m-friction.steps.2: Compare in New runs on sandpaper, glass and desk surfaces, and with different numbers of weights.
exp.cur-m-friction.steps.3: Multiply the graph value (g) by 0.0098 to get N.
exp.cur-m-friction.std.0: Students can understand gravity, elastic force, friction and buoyancy, and explain the features of each force by magnitude and direction.
exp.cur-m-gas-solubility.title: When does gas escape most from a fizzy drink? (solubility of gases)
exp.cur-m-gas-solubility.subject: Science 2
exp.cur-m-gas-solubility.summary: Compare the gas escaping at different temperatures and pressures from the pressure rise in a sealed bottle.
exp.cur-m-gas-solubility.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-gas-solubility.steps.0: Put the pressure sensor in a small sealed bottle, pour in 50 mL of fizzy drink and close it at once.
exp.cur-m-gas-solubility.steps.1: Record in a cold-water bath and a warm-water bath, each as a New run.
exp.cur-m-gas-solubility.steps.2: Compare how fast the pressure rises (the warmer it is, the more gas escapes).
exp.cur-m-gas-solubility.steps.3: Also mark the moment the pressure drops when you open the lid with ‘Add note’.
exp.cur-m-gas-solubility.std.0: Students can know the meaning of characteristic properties of substances and explain density, solubility, melting point, boiling point, etc. through experiments.
exp.cur-m-gas-solubility.cautions.0: If the pressure rises a lot (about 110 kPa), open the lid slightly to release it.
exp.cur-m-state-mass.title: Does mass stay the same when the state changes?
exp.cur-m-state-mass.subject: Science 1
exp.cur-m-state-mass.summary: Check that mass does not change during freezing, melting or sublimation.
exp.cur-m-state-mass.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-m-state-mass.steps.0: Put a piece of dry ice (or ice) in a zipper bag and seal it tightly.
exp.cur-m-state-mass.steps.1: Put it on the load cell and place the temperature sensor beside it.
exp.cur-m-state-mass.steps.2: Check that the mass graph stays flat while the state changes.
exp.cur-m-state-mass.steps.3: Record the volume change (the bag swelling) with ‘Add note’.
exp.cur-m-state-mass.std.0: Students can observe changes of state in various substances and explain them with a particle model.
exp.cur-m-state-mass.materials.3: Dry ice, or ice and olive oil
exp.cur-m-state-mass.cautions.0: Handle dry ice with gloves, and open the bag to let gas out if it swells too much.
exp.cur-mat-iodine-clock.title: Iodine clock reaction (concentration, temperature and reaction rate)
exp.cur-mat-iodine-clock.subject: Matter and Energy
exp.cur-mat-iodine-clock.summary: Time the sudden blue color change with a light sensor and relate it to concentration and temperature.
exp.cur-mat-iodine-clock.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-mat-iodine-clock.steps.0: Place an LED behind the beaker and the light sensor in front, and put in the temperature sensor.
exp.cur-mat-iodine-clock.steps.1: Start measuring the moment you mix the two solutions, and read the time when the light suddenly drops.
exp.cur-mat-iodine-clock.steps.2: Do a New run at a different concentration, then change the water-bath temperature.
exp.cur-mat-iodine-clock.steps.3: Take 1/time as the reaction rate and compare with concentration and temperature (the thiosulfate–hydrochloric acid turbidity reaction works the same way).
exp.cur-mat-iodine-clock.std.0: Students can understand that reaction rate depends on concentration, temperature and catalysts, and recognize the usefulness of chemistry by finding everyday examples of each.
exp.cur-mat-iodine-clock.cautions.0: Wear goggles and gloves when handling acids and bases; if any gets on your skin, wash it off with water right away.
exp.cur-me-resultant.title: Checking the resultant of two forces
exp.cur-me-resultant.subject: Mechanics and Energy
exp.cur-me-resultant.summary: Measure the force needed to hold the same weight as the angle between two strings changes, and compare with the parallelogram method.
exp.cur-me-resultant.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-me-resultant.steps.0: Hang a weight from two strings; attach one string to the load cell and the other to a spring scale.
exp.cur-me-resultant.steps.1: Widen the angle between the strings by 30° at a time and record the load cell value.
exp.cur-me-resultant.steps.2: Check whether the force needed grows with the angle and compare with parallelogram-method calculations.
exp.cur-me-resultant.std.0: Students can find the resultant of the various forces acting on an object and predict its motion quantitatively.
exp.cur-me-sound-interference.title: Interference of sound from two speakers
exp.cur-me-sound-interference.subject: Mechanics and Energy
exp.cur-me-sound-interference.summary: Move sideways in front of two speakers playing the same sound to find loud and quiet spots.
exp.cur-me-sound-interference.steps.0: Place two speakers 50 cm apart and play a sound of the same frequency (about 1 kHz).
exp.cur-me-sound-interference.steps.1: 1 m in front, move the sound sensor sideways 5 cm at a time and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-me-sound-interference.steps.2: Find the wavelength from the spacing of loud and quiet spots and compare with the calculated value.
exp.cur-me-sound-interference.std.0: Students can understand that the interference of sound waves is used in audio equipment and in noise control in indoor and outdoor spaces, and investigate examples used in real life.
exp.cur-p-action-reaction.title: Two forces pulling on each other (action and reaction)
exp.cur-p-action-reaction.subject: Physics
exp.cur-p-action-reaction.summary: Pull a load cell and a spring scale against each other to see whether the two forces are always equal.
exp.cur-p-action-reaction.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-p-action-reaction.steps.0: Connect the load cell hook and a spring scale with string.
exp.cur-p-action-reaction.steps.1: Measure while pulling hard, gently and suddenly.
exp.cur-p-action-reaction.steps.2: Compare the spring scale reading with the graph value and discuss any difference.
exp.cur-p-action-reaction.std.0: Students can know the action–reaction relationship and the law of conservation of momentum, and apply them to sports, transportation, projectiles and more.
exp.cur-p-collision.title: Conservation of momentum when carts collide
exp.cur-p-collision.subject: Physics
exp.cur-p-collision.summary: Measure cart speeds before and after a collision with a distance sensor and compare total momentum.
exp.cur-p-collision.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-p-collision.steps.0: Place the distance sensor at the end of the track and let cart A hit stationary cart B.
exp.cur-p-collision.steps.1: Find the slopes (speeds) before and after the collision with ‘Tangent’.
exp.cur-p-collision.steps.2: Weigh both carts and compare total momentum before and after the collision.
exp.cur-p-collision.steps.3: Also try a collision where the carts stick together with Velcro.
exp.cur-p-collision.std.0: Students can know the action–reaction relationship and the law of conservation of momentum, and apply them to sports, transportation, projectiles and more.
exp.cur-p-collision.std.1: Students can use conservation of mechanical energy to understand that escape velocity differs from planet to planet, and use conservation of momentum to explain how a spacecraft is launched into orbit.
exp.cur-p-speaker.title: Loudness of homemade speakers
exp.cur-p-speaker.subject: Physics
exp.cur-p-speaker.summary: Compare the loudness of the same signal with different numbers of coil turns, magnets and with or without amplification.
exp.cur-p-speaker.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-p-speaker.steps.0: Make a speaker by attaching a coil and magnet to a paper cup.
exp.cur-p-speaker.steps.1: Connect the same sound source (smartphone) and record the loudness 30 cm in front.
exp.cur-p-speaker.steps.2: Change the number of turns, number of magnets and transistor amplification, and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-p-speaker.std.0: Students can know the principles of devices that convert energy using the magnetic effect of current, and design speakers, electric motors and similar devices.
exp.cur-p-speaker.std.1: Students can analyze electronic circuits that use semiconductor devices such as diodes and transistors, and recognize the importance of semiconductors in modern civilization.
exp.cur-p-torque.title: Torque on a bar that does not rotate
exp.cur-p-torque.subject: Physics
exp.cur-p-torque.summary: Check torque equilibrium using the force measured at the support as the weight's position changes.
exp.cur-p-torque.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-p-torque.steps.0: Rest one end of the bar on a hinge and the other end on the load cell.
exp.cur-p-torque.steps.1: Move the weight 10 cm at a time and record the load cell value.
exp.cur-p-torque.steps.2: Check with ‘Curve fit → Linear’ whether force × distance is constant.
exp.cur-p-torque.std.0: Students can know that an object is in equilibrium when the net force and net torque acting on it are 0, and analyze the stability of various structures.
exp.ph-dilution.std.1: Students can understand the meaning of molar concentration and prepare a solution of a desired molar concentration.
ana.T.name: Temperature
ana.T.graph: Time–temperature line graph (auto y axis, do not lock at 0). Cooling/heating: 5–10 min at 1–2 s intervals.
ana.T.m.0.why: Reads the mean of the range where the temperature hardly changes. During a phase change the temperature stops, so that value is the freezing, melting or boiling point.
ana.T.m.0.ex: Reading the freezing point from paraffin, stearic acid or sodium thiosulfate cooling curves; checking the boiling point of water.
ana.T.m.1.why: Fit y = A·e^(−C·x) + B to get B (room temperature) and C (cooling constant). If Newton's law of cooling holds, the curve follows the data closely.
ana.T.m.1.ex: Cooling curve of hot water; comparing the insulation of a vacuum flask and a paper cup.
ana.T.m.2.why: The slope at one point (°C/s) is the rate of temperature change at that instant. It is largest right after the reaction starts.
ana.T.m.2.ex: Initial heat-release rate of neutralisation or dissolution; comparing specific heat from the initial heating slope.
ana.T.m.3.tool: Calculated column → Change from first value
ana.T.m.3.why: Plots ΔT directly for the heat calculation Q = c·m·ΔT. Easy to compare even when the starting temperatures differ.
ana.T.m.3.ex: Measuring heat of neutralisation or dissolution; comparing the temperature change before and after a reaction.
ana.T.tip.0: The sensor responds slowly (10–30 s), so sharp changes look rounded. Discard the values right after putting it into hot water.
ana.T.tip.1: If the plateau on a cooling curve is short or sloped, the cause is supercooling (a dip and recovery) or impurities.
ana.T.tip.2: If the temperature range is small, unlock the y axis from 0 to see the shape. Leaving a mark at room temperature makes comparison easier.
ana.TK.name: High temperature (thermocouple)
ana.TK.graph: Time–temperature line graph. It rises to several hundred °C, so use an auto y scale; noise is large, so smoothing is recommended.
ana.TK.m.0.why: The range where the temperature stops while melting is the melting point. High-temperature metals and salts have short plateaus, so shorten the interval to 0.5 s.
ana.TK.m.0.ex: Melting points of lead, tin and solder alloy; checking the melting point of salt.
ana.TK.m.1.why: Use the heating slope (°C/s) to compare the strength of the heat source or the specific heat of a material.
ana.TK.m.1.ex: Comparing heating rates of an alcohol lamp and a torch; comparing heating curves of different metals.
ana.TK.m.2.why: Fitting the cooling curve after heating stops with an exponential approach gives the ambient temperature and the cooling constant.
ana.TK.m.2.ex: Cooling curves of a heated steel ball or nichrome wire.
ana.TK.tip.0: A thermocouple jitters by about ±2 °C. Turn on smoothing and read plateaus as a mean.
ana.TK.tip.1: If only the junction is heated, the temperature drops quickly. Put the junction fully inside the sample.
ana.TK.tip.2: If the value suddenly jumps or goes negative, the junction is broken or has a poor contact.
ana.TA.name: Air temperature & humidity
ana.TA.graph: Time–temperature (°C) and time–humidity (%) stacked one above the other on the same time axis. For long runs, show clock time.
ana.TA.m.0.why: Reads the rate of temperature rise or fall (°C/min). The slope changes with sunlight and insulation conditions.
ana.TA.m.0.ex: Greenhouse-effect model (air temperature inside and outside a PET bottle); comparing temperature rise in a black and a white container.
ana.TA.m.1.why: Pick only a specific range, such as before/after ventilation or after people enter, and compare the mean and maximum.
ana.TA.m.1.ex: Humidity change before and after ventilating a classroom; recording the 24-hour daily temperature cycle.
ana.TA.m.2.why: Fits the curve as humidity near a wet cloth, or air temperature after heating, approaches a certain value.
ana.TA.m.2.ex: Evaporative cooling (wet-gauze thermometer); humidity saturation inside a sealed container.
ana.TA.tip.0: The humidity sensor takes tens of seconds to respond and saturates easily (100 %) from breath. Keep hands and breath away.
ana.TA.tip.1: Temperature and humidity often move in opposite directions (heating lowers relative humidity). Look at both graphs together.
ana.TA.tip.2: For long recordings, increase the interval to 10–60 s and switch the time axis to clock time for easier reading.
ana.BP.name: Air pressure
ana.BP.graph: Time–pressure (kPa or hPa) line graph. The change is small, so unlock the y axis from 0 and zoom automatically.
ana.BP.m.0.why: Read the pressure difference before and after changing floors to estimate the height difference (about 0.012 kPa/m).
ana.BP.m.0.ex: Pressure change while walking the stairs from the 1st to the 5th floor; pressure in a lift.
ana.BP.m.1.why: Read the trend (slope) of pressure over time to predict a change in the weather.
ana.BP.m.1.ex: Recording pressure over a day and confirming an approaching low.
ana.BP.m.2.why: Pick only the range where a syringe was pushed or pulled and compare the mean and the change.
ana.BP.m.2.ex: Pressure change inside a sealed bottle; pressure drop when sucking through a straw.
ana.BP.tip.0: Air pressure changes by less than 1 kPa a day. If you cannot see a change, narrow the y-axis range.
ana.BP.tip.1: The sensor value also shifts a little as temperature rises. Use the gas pressure sensor (P) for heating experiments.
ana.BP.tip.2: A sudden kink may be caused by a door opening or air-conditioner draught. Note the event with a mark.
ana.P.name: Gas pressure
ana.P.graph: Time mode: time–pressure line graph. Boyle's/Charles's law: value-entry (event) mode with volume (mL) or temperature on the x axis, scatter graph.
ana.P.m.0.why: Fit y = A/x to confirm P·V = constant (Boyle's law). A corresponds to nRT.
ana.P.m.0.ex: Recording pressure while reducing the syringe volume from 20→10 mL (value-entry mode).
ana.P.m.1.why: Putting 1/V on the x axis gives a straight line. A straight line confirms the inverse relationship.
ana.P.m.1.ex: Linearising Boyle's law as P–1/V; finding the constant from the slope.
ana.P.m.2.why: Estimate absolute zero from the x intercept (−273 °C) of the temperature–pressure line (Gay-Lussac's law). Converting with the Absolute temperature calculated column makes it proportional.
ana.P.m.2.ex: Recording pressure while moving a sealed flask from ice water→boiling water.
ana.P.m.3.why: The slope of the pressure rise (kPa/s) is the rate of gas production; when the slope reaches 0 the reaction is over.
ana.P.m.3.ex: Mg + HCl, hydrogen peroxide decomposition (catalyst) reaction rate, yeast fermentation.
ana.P.tip.0: In rate experiments the slope in the first 30 s is what matters. Place the tangent on a point right after the start.
ana.P.tip.1: If the pressure rises and then flattens, the reaction has ended or there is a leak. Check the stopper again.
ana.P.tip.2: Boyle's law needs constant temperature, so push the syringe slowly and press ‘Record value’ once the value settles.
ana.CO2.name: Carbon dioxide
ana.CO2.graph: Time–CO₂ (ppm) line graph. Photosynthesis/respiration: 10–20 min at 5–10 s intervals. Mark the light and dark periods.
ana.CO2.m.0.why: The slope (ppm/min) is the rate of CO₂ production (respiration) or consumption (photosynthesis). The sign tells which one dominates.
ana.CO2.m.0.ex: Leaves or sprouts in a sealed container: in light (slope −), in the dark (slope +).
ana.CO2.m.1.why: Fit a straight line to a steady range to compare rates as numbers. Tabulate the slope for each condition (light intensity, temperature).
ana.CO2.m.1.ex: Photosynthesis rate vs light intensity (distance); comparing yeast fermentation rates.
ana.CO2.m.2.why: Pick the lights-on and lights-off ranges separately and compare the slope and mean.
ana.CO2.m.2.ex: An experiment recorded in one run while alternating light ON/OFF.
ana.CO2.m.3.why: Shows the change in rate directly. The peak is when the reaction is most active.
ana.CO2.m.3.ex: Opening a fizzy drink; baking soda + vinegar reaction rate.
ana.CO2.tip.0: The sensor takes 1–2 min to settle. Exclude the initial range where the value falls from the analysis.
ana.CO2.tip.1: Human breath alone makes it jump by hundreds of ppm. Seal the container and keep your face away.
ana.CO2.tip.2: Indoor baseline is 400–1000 ppm. If the graph wobbles like a saw, a fan or door is the cause.
ana.O2.name: Oxygen
ana.O2.graph: Time–O₂ (%) line graph. Changes are only 0.1–1 %, so unlock the y axis from 0 and zoom in.
ana.O2.m.0.why: The slope of O₂ decrease (%/min) is the rate of respiration or combustion. With photosynthesis it increases.
ana.O2.m.0.ex: A candle, germinating seeds or insects respiring in a sealed container; water-plant photosynthesis.
ana.O2.m.1.why: Fit a straight line to a steady range to compare consumption rates, and read the concentration at the moment the candle goes out.
ana.O2.m.1.ex: Covering a candle with cups of different sizes; seed respiration rate vs temperature.
ana.O2.m.2.why: Reads the value where the concentration stops after the reaction ends. This is the oxygen left after the candle goes out.
ana.O2.m.2.ex: Confirming that ‘not all the oxygen is used up’ from the oxygen remaining after combustion (about 16–17 %).
ana.O2.tip.0: Electrochemical oxygen sensors respond slowly and are affected by temperature and humidity. First check that it starts at 20.9 % in air.
ana.O2.tip.1: Changes are small, so narrow the y axis to something like 18–22 %.
ana.O2.tip.2: Used together with the CO₂ sensor, respiration (O₂↓, CO₂↑) is seen at a glance. Stack the two graphs.
ana.L.name: Light (relative)
ana.L.graph: Time mode: time–light line graph. Distance/angle experiments: value-entry mode with distance (cm) or angle (°) on the x axis, scatter graph.
ana.L.m.0.why: Fit distance–brightness to y = A·x^B; if B ≈ −2 it is the inverse-square law.
ana.L.m.0.ex: Recording light level at 10, 20, 30 cm from a bulb (value-entry mode).
ana.L.m.1.why: To check proportionality to the reciprocal of distance², change x to 1/d² and see whether it becomes a straight line.
ana.L.m.1.ex: Linearising the inverse-square law; comparing light-source intensity.
ana.L.m.2.why: Creates absorbance A = −log(I/I₀). If concentration–absorbance is a straight line, it is the Beer–Lambert law.
ana.L.m.2.ex: Measuring CuSO₄ or food-dye concentration with a simple LED + light sensor colorimeter.
ana.L.m.3.why: Compare precipitation or reaction rates by the rate of clouding (slope of light decrease).
ana.L.m.3.ex: Sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid sulfur precipitation rate (by temperature and concentration).
ana.L.tip.0: Indoor lighting (fluorescent, LED) flickers at tens of Hz and makes a sawtooth. Use a blackout cover or turn on smoothing.
ana.L.tip.1: The sensor may not be linear, so % values are for relative comparison. Use the LUX sensor if you need absolute values.
ana.L.tip.2: For colorimeter experiments, fix the cuvette position and LED brightness, and record the distilled-water (I₀) value first.
ana.LUX.name: Illuminance (lx)
ana.LUX.graph: Time–illuminance (lx) line graph. To see sunlight (tens of thousands of lx) and indoor light (hundreds of lx) together, use a log scale.
ana.LUX.m.0.why: Fit distance–brightness to y = A·x^B; if B ≈ −2 it is the inverse-square law.
ana.LUX.m.0.ex: Recording light level at 10, 20, 30 cm from a bulb (value-entry mode).
ana.LUX.m.1.why: To check proportionality to the reciprocal of distance², change x to 1/d² and see whether it becomes a straight line.
ana.LUX.m.1.ex: Linearising the inverse-square law; comparing light-source intensity.
ana.LUX.m.2.why: Creates absorbance A = −log(I/I₀). If concentration–absorbance is a straight line, it is the Beer–Lambert law.
ana.LUX.m.2.ex: Measuring CuSO₄ or food-dye concentration with a simple LED + light sensor colorimeter.
ana.LUX.m.3.why: Compare precipitation or reaction rates by the rate of clouding (slope of light decrease).
ana.LUX.m.3.ex: Sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid sulfur precipitation rate (by temperature and concentration).
ana.LUX.tip.0: Indoor lighting (fluorescent, LED) flickers at tens of Hz and makes a sawtooth. Use a blackout cover or turn on smoothing.
ana.LUX.tip.1: The sensor may not be linear, so % values are for relative comparison. Use the LUX sensor if you need absolute values.
ana.LUX.tip.2: For colorimeter experiments, fix the cuvette position and LED brightness, and record the distilled-water (I₀) value first.
ana.COLR.name: Colour (RGB) & absorbance
ana.COLR.graph: R, G and B as three coloured lines on one graph. Concentration experiments: value-entry mode with x = concentration, y = absorbance, scatter graph.
ana.COLR.m.0.why: Converts to absorbance A = −log(I/I₀). Using the complementary channel (R for a blue solution) gives the largest change.
ana.COLR.m.0.ex: Measuring CuSO₄ or methylene blue concentration (simple colorimeter).
ana.COLR.m.1.why: Concentration–absorbance calibration line. Get the slope (ε·l), then put the absorbance of an unknown sample into the line to find its concentration.
ana.COLR.m.1.ex: Beer–Lambert law calibration line; estimating dye concentration in a drink.
ana.COLR.m.2.why: See the reaction rate from the rate of colour change (slope of a channel value).
ana.COLR.m.2.ex: Iodine clock reaction; rate of dye bleaching with bleach.
ana.COLR.m.3.why: Read the RGB values at a given time to compare colours as numbers.
ana.COLR.m.3.ex: Recording the stages of an indicator colour change; comparing how ripe fruit is.
ana.COLR.tip.0: Stray ambient light makes the value unstable. Cover the sensor and sample with a black box and switch on only the LED.
ana.COLR.tip.1: Absorbance has large errors at low transmittance (concentrated solutions). Dilute and measure in the range A < 1.0.
ana.COLR.tip.2: Rather than plotting all three channels, pick just the complementary channel for a cleaner graph.
ana.S415.name: Spectral (intensity per channel)
ana.S415.graph: R, G and B as three coloured lines on one graph. Concentration experiments: value-entry mode with x = concentration, y = absorbance, scatter graph.
ana.S415.m.0.why: Converts to absorbance A = −log(I/I₀). Using the complementary channel (R for a blue solution) gives the largest change.
ana.S415.m.0.ex: Measuring CuSO₄ or methylene blue concentration (simple colorimeter).
ana.S415.m.1.why: Concentration–absorbance calibration line. Get the slope (ε·l), then put the absorbance of an unknown sample into the line to find its concentration.
ana.S415.m.1.ex: Beer–Lambert law calibration line; estimating dye concentration in a drink.
ana.S415.m.2.why: See the reaction rate from the rate of colour change (slope of a channel value).
ana.S415.m.2.ex: Iodine clock reaction; rate of dye bleaching with bleach.
ana.S415.m.3.why: Read the RGB values at a given time to compare colours as numbers.
ana.S415.m.3.ex: Recording the stages of an indicator colour change; comparing how ripe fruit is.
ana.S415.tip.0: Stray ambient light makes the value unstable. Cover the sensor and sample with a black box and switch on only the LED.
ana.S415.tip.1: Absorbance has large errors at low transmittance (concentrated solutions). Dilute and measure in the range A < 1.0.
ana.S415.tip.2: Rather than plotting all three channels, pick just the complementary channel for a cleaner graph.
ana.pH.graph: Titration: value-entry mode with x = volume added (mL), y = pH, points + line. Time mode: time–pH line graph.
ana.pH.m.0.why: Finds the volume where pH changes most steeply automatically. Use this volume to calculate the sample's molar concentration; for a weak acid the pH at the half-equivalence point is the pKa.
ana.pH.m.0.ex: HCl–NaOH and vinegar (acetic acid)–NaOH titrations; titrating a fizzy drink.
ana.pH.m.1.why: Plotting ΔpH/ΔV shows the equivalence point as a peak. Two peaks mean a polyprotic acid.
ana.pH.m.1.ex: Distinguishing the 1st and 2nd equivalence points in phosphoric or carbonic acid titrations.
ana.pH.m.2.tool: Calculated column → Change from first value
ana.pH.m.2.why: Converting with a calculated column [H⁺] = 10^(−pH) shows the relationship between dilution factor and [H⁺] as a straight line.
ana.pH.m.2.ex: Measuring pH while diluting 10× each time → confirming pH rises by 1 each step.
ana.pH.m.3.why: Identifies the range in the buffer region where pH hardly changes. The pH at its midpoint is the pKa.
ana.pH.m.3.ex: Buffer region of a weak-acid titration; adding small amounts of acid or base to a buffer solution.
ana.pH.tip.0: Near the equivalence point a single drop shifts the pH by 3–4. In the steep part add 0.2–0.5 mL at a time, stir, and record once the value stops moving.
ana.pH.tip.1: The electrode responds slowly, so in time mode the value lags by a few seconds. Value-entry mode is more accurate for titrations.
ana.pH.tip.2: Values before calibration are for reference only. Do a two-point calibration first with pH 7 and 4 (or 10) buffer solutions.
ana.ORP.name: Redox potential
ana.ORP.graph: Value-entry mode with x = volume added (mL), y = potential (mV). Time mode is a time–mV line graph.
ana.ORP.m.0.why: The volume where the potential changes sharply is the equivalence point of a redox titration.
ana.ORP.m.0.ex: Potassium permanganate–iron(II) and iodine–sodium thiosulfate titrations.
ana.ORP.m.1.why: Confirm the equivalence point from the ΔE/ΔV peak.
ana.ORP.m.2.why: Read the potential of each solution to compare oxidising and reducing power.
ana.ORP.m.2.ex: Comparing the ORP of bleach and vitamin C solutions.
ana.ORP.tip.0: The electrode responds slowly: stir, wait 30 s, then record.
ana.ORP.tip.1: Absolute values depend on the state of the reference electrode, so compare changes instead.
ana.EC.name: Conductivity & TDS
ana.EC.graph: Titration: value-entry mode with x = volume (mL), y = conductivity (µS/cm), scatter graph. Dissolution/concentration: time-mode line graph.
ana.EC.m.0.why: In a conductometric titration the equivalence point is where two straight lines (falling, then rising) meet. Split the range in two and fit a line to each.
ana.EC.m.0.ex: Ba(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ precipitation titration (V shape); HCl + NaOH conductometric titration.
ana.EC.m.1.why: Pick the ranges before and after the equivalence point separately, fit a line to each, and calculate the intersection.
ana.EC.m.1.ex: Finding the intersection in a conductometric titration.
ana.EC.m.2.why: Check whether concentration–conductivity in dilute solutions is a straight line through the origin.
ana.EC.m.2.ex: Conductivity vs NaCl concentration; comparing strong and weak electrolytes (difference in slope).
ana.EC.m.3.why: Compare the effect of grain size, temperature and stirring by the dissolution rate (slope of conductivity rise).
ana.EC.m.3.ex: Dissolution rate of salt grains of different sizes.
ana.EC.tip.0: Always calibrate with the standard solution (1413 µS/cm) before use. Uncalibrated values allow only relative comparison.
ana.EC.tip.1: A 1 °C rise increases the value by about 2 %. Record temperature alongside or measure at room temperature.
ana.EC.tip.2: Concentrated solutions exceed the sensor range and flatten out. Dilute before measuring.
ana.TURB.name: Transparency & turbidity
ana.TURB.graph: Time–transparency (%) line graph. For precipitation/reaction rates, 1 s intervals.
ana.TURB.m.0.why: The slope of falling transparency is the rate of precipitate formation. Compare by concentration and temperature.
ana.TURB.m.0.ex: Sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid sulfur precipitation (with a sensor instead of ‘watching the X disappear’).
ana.TURB.m.1.why: Read the time when transparency reaches a reference value (e.g. 50 %) and use it as the reaction time.
ana.TURB.m.1.ex: Relationship between reaction rate and concentration (1/t graph).
ana.TURB.m.2.why: Fits the curve of transparency recovering as the precipitate settles with an exponential.
ana.TURB.m.2.ex: Settling rate of muddy water; comparing the effect of flocculants.
ana.TURB.tip.0: Ambient light entering makes the value unstable. Cover the container.
ana.TURB.tip.1: Bubbles make the turbidity jump. Wait a moment after stirring.
ana.TURB.tip.2: Start by taking the value of the initial clear water as the 100 % reference.
ana.V.name: Voltage
ana.V.graph: Time–voltage (V) line graph. Battery discharge takes a long time (minutes to hours); for capacitors use short 0.1 s intervals.
ana.V.m.0.why: Fit the capacitor charge/discharge curve to get the time constant τ = RC (compare C = 1/τ).
ana.V.m.0.ex: Charging and discharging an RC circuit; internal resistance of a lemon battery.
ana.V.m.1.why: Reads the stable voltage (emf) of a cell as a mean.
ana.V.m.1.ex: Comparing the voltage of fruit, voltaic and Daniell cells (by electrode combination).
ana.V.m.2.why: Compare battery life and internal resistance by the rate of voltage drop during discharge.
ana.V.m.2.ex: Discharge curve after connecting a resistor to a battery.
ana.V.m.3.why: Read the voltage at the moment a condition is changed and tabulate it.
ana.V.m.3.ex: Voltage vs electrolyte concentration and electrode spacing.
ana.V.tip.0: Reads 0–5 V only. Cells in series or negative (−) voltages exceed the range, so use V25 or VDC.
ana.V.tip.1: If the voltage wobbles like a sawtooth, there is a poor contact. Re-clip the crocodile clips.
ana.V.tip.2: Used together with the current sensor, a calculated column can give P = V·I.
ana.VDC.name: Voltage (INA219 etc.)
ana.VDC.graph: Time–voltage (V) line graph. Battery discharge takes a long time (minutes to hours); for capacitors use short 0.1 s intervals.
ana.VDC.m.0.why: Fit the capacitor charge/discharge curve to get the time constant τ = RC (compare C = 1/τ).
ana.VDC.m.0.ex: Charging and discharging an RC circuit; internal resistance of a lemon battery.
ana.VDC.m.1.why: Reads the stable voltage (emf) of a cell as a mean.
ana.VDC.m.1.ex: Comparing the voltage of fruit, voltaic and Daniell cells (by electrode combination).
ana.VDC.m.2.why: Compare battery life and internal resistance by the rate of voltage drop during discharge.
ana.VDC.m.2.ex: Discharge curve after connecting a resistor to a battery.
ana.VDC.m.3.why: Read the voltage at the moment a condition is changed and tabulate it.
ana.VDC.m.3.ex: Voltage vs electrolyte concentration and electrode spacing.
ana.VDC.tip.0: Reads 0–5 V only. Cells in series or negative (−) voltages exceed the range, so use V25 or VDC.
ana.VDC.tip.1: If the voltage wobbles like a sawtooth, there is a poor contact. Re-clip the crocodile clips.
ana.VDC.tip.2: Used together with the current sensor, a calculated column can give P = V·I.
ana.IDC.name: Current
ana.IDC.graph: Time–current (mA) line graph. I–V characteristics: value-entry mode with x = voltage, y = current, scatter graph.
ana.IDC.m.0.why: If V–I is a straight line it is Ohm's law and the reciprocal of the slope is the resistance. If it bends, it is a bulb (temperature change) or a diode.
ana.IDC.m.0.ex: Comparing the I–V characteristics of a resistor, a bulb and an LED.
ana.IDC.m.1.why: Current–time area = charge (C). Predict the mass deposited using Faraday's law.
ana.IDC.m.1.ex: Comparing with the mass of copper deposited after electrolysis of copper sulfate.
ana.IDC.m.2.why: See capacitor discharge or battery depletion from the rate of current decrease.
ana.IDC.m.2.ex: RC discharge current; battery discharge current.
ana.IDC.tip.0: The current sensor must be placed in series in the circuit. Connected in parallel it reads 0 or short-circuits.
ana.IDC.tip.1: Units are mA, so small currents are buried in noise. Turn on smoothing.
ana.IDC.tip.2: Record voltage alongside and get power with a calculated column (V×I) to compare efficiency.
ana.I5A.name: Current (A)
ana.I5A.graph: Time–current (mA) line graph. I–V characteristics: value-entry mode with x = voltage, y = current, scatter graph.
ana.I5A.m.0.why: If V–I is a straight line it is Ohm's law and the reciprocal of the slope is the resistance. If it bends, it is a bulb (temperature change) or a diode.
ana.I5A.m.0.ex: Comparing the I–V characteristics of a resistor, a bulb and an LED.
ana.I5A.m.1.why: Current–time area = charge (C). Predict the mass deposited using Faraday's law.
ana.I5A.m.1.ex: Comparing with the mass of copper deposited after electrolysis of copper sulfate.
ana.I5A.m.2.why: See capacitor discharge or battery depletion from the rate of current decrease.
ana.I5A.m.2.ex: RC discharge current; battery discharge current.
ana.I5A.tip.0: The current sensor must be placed in series in the circuit. Connected in parallel it reads 0 or short-circuits.
ana.I5A.tip.1: Units are mA, so small currents are buried in noise. Turn on smoothing.
ana.I5A.tip.2: Record voltage alongside and get power with a calculated column (V×I) to compare efficiency.
ana.M.name: Mass & force (load cell)
ana.M.graph: Time–mass (g) line graph. Reactions/evaporation: 5–30 min; impacts: 0.05 s intervals.
ana.M.m.0.why: Fit a straight line to the mass loss from evaporation or gas release to get the rate (g/min).
ana.M.m.0.ex: Evaporation rate of alcohol and water; mass loss of CO₂ from calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid.
ana.M.m.1.why: Instantaneous rate of mass change. Fastest at the start of the reaction, then gradually reaching 0 (reaction rate ∝ concentration).
ana.M.m.1.ex: Reaction rate vs size of marble chips.
ana.M.m.2.why: Force–time area is the impulse (N·s). Use this when the load cell is used as a force sensor.
ana.M.m.2.ex: Impact of a dropped ball; comparing airbag models.
ana.M.m.3.tool: Calculated column → Change from first value
ana.M.m.3.why: Plotting Δm lets you compare the change directly even when the starting masses differ.
ana.M.m.3.ex: Comparing mass loss under different conditions.
ana.M.tip.0: A load cell drifts slowly with temperature and time. Set zero (0 g) before measuring and keep runs short.
ana.M.tip.1: In gas-release experiments the container must stay open for the mass to fall. Plug the mouth with cotton wool to stop splashing.
ana.M.tip.2: If the value looks like stairs, you have hit the resolution limit. Use a load cell with a lighter range.
ana.DIST.name: Distance (ultrasonic/ToF)
ana.DIST.graph: Time–distance (cm) line graph. Motion experiments: 0.05–0.1 s intervals. Velocity via the rate graph.
ana.DIST.m.0.why: Differentiating distance with respect to time gives velocity; once more gives acceleration. A constant slope means uniform motion.
ana.DIST.m.0.ex: Pushing a cart; walking and running speed; acceleration on a ramp.
ana.DIST.m.1.why: Reads the velocity (cm/s) at one instant.
ana.DIST.m.1.ex: Velocity of a cart on a ramp at a given moment.
ana.DIST.m.2.why: For uniformly accelerated motion, distance–time is a quadratic with coefficient A = a/2.
ana.DIST.m.2.ex: Measuring acceleration on a ramp; free-fall model.
ana.DIST.m.3.why: Fit a straight line to the uniform-motion range to get the velocity.
ana.DIST.m.3.ex: Walking at constant speed; drawing distance–time graphs activity.
ana.DIST.tip.0: Ultrasonic readings jump within 2 cm, beyond 4 m, and on soft surfaces (cloth, clothing). Hold a board while moving.
ana.DIST.tip.1: Spikes are amplified into large peaks on the rate graph. Turn on smoothing before differentiating.
ana.DIST.tip.2: You can also measure water level changes (fix the sensor above the surface).
ana.FSR.name: Force (force-sensing resistor)
ana.FSR.graph: Time–force (%) line graph, 0.02–0.05 s intervals (impact experiments).
ana.FSR.m.0.why: Force–time area is the impulse. For the same impulse, the lower the peak height, the better the cushioning.
ana.FSR.m.0.ex: Comparing egg-protection devices, airbag and helmet models.
ana.FSR.m.1.why: Read the maximum force (peak) and compare it across conditions.
ana.FSR.m.1.ex: Drop impact vs height; comparing grip strength.
ana.FSR.m.2.why: Pick only one impact range to get the area and maximum.
ana.FSR.m.2.ex: Separating single hits from data with several taps.
ana.FSR.tip.0: An FSR gives relative values (%) and is non-linear. Use the load cell (M) if you need newtons.
ana.FSR.tip.1: An impact is over within 0.01 s, so use the shortest interval. If the peak is not sharp, you missed it.
ana.FSR.tip.2: The value depends on where you press. Stick a small pad on the centre of the sensor.
ana.SND.name: Sound (relative)
ana.SND.graph: Time–sound (%) line graph, 0.01–0.05 s intervals. View it as a loudness envelope, not a waveform.
ana.SND.m.0.why: Compare loudness by peak height, and read the period or beat from the spacing between peaks.
ana.SND.m.0.ex: Clap or metronome spacing; measuring a period from a pendulum's sound.
ana.SND.m.1.why: Fit the decaying sound curve (damping) with an exponential to compare sound absorption by material.
ana.SND.m.1.ex: Decay of a bell or tuning fork; comparing soundproofing materials.
ana.SND.m.2.why: Pick only the range where the sound occurred and compare the maximum and mean.
ana.SND.m.2.ex: Measuring classroom noise; comparing quiet time and lesson time.
ana.SND.tip.0: This sensor cannot show the sound wave itself (frequency). It shows only changes in loudness.
ana.SND.tip.1: Brief spikes are normal. Repeat and take the mean.
ana.SND.tip.2: Doubling the distance (2×) makes the intensity 1/4. Try recording distance–loudness in value-entry mode.
ana.DBA.name: Sound level (dBA)
ana.DBA.graph: Time–dBA line graph. dB is already a log value, so keep a linear scale; fixing the y axis to 30–100 dB makes comparison easy.
ana.DBA.m.0.why: Read the range mean (equivalent sound level) and maximum to compare conditions.
ana.DBA.m.0.ex: Measuring noise in the classroom, corridor and playground; comparing before and after a lesson.
ana.DBA.m.1.why: Read dB at each distance to confirm a drop of about 6 dB for every doubling (2×) of distance.
ana.DBA.m.1.ex: Noise vs distance from a speaker (value-entry mode).
ana.DBA.m.2.why: Fitting distance–dB with a logarithm shows the inverse-square law as a straight line on a log scale.
ana.DBA.m.2.ex: Relationship between sound intensity and distance.
ana.DBA.tip.0: Every 10 dB increase means 10× the intensity. A difference that looks small is a big change.
ana.DBA.tip.1: A-weighting makes low frequencies read low. For bass-speaker experiments, look at the relative sensor (SND) too.
ana.DBA.tip.2: Below 40 dB is the sensor limit, so it looks flat.
ana.MAG.name: Magnetic field
ana.MAG.graph: Value-entry mode with x = distance (cm), current (A) or number of turns, y = magnetic field (µT), scatter graph. Time mode for rotation or approach experiments.
ana.MAG.m.0.why: Fitting distance–field to y = A·x^B gives B ≈ −3 for a bar magnet and around −1 for a long wire.
ana.MAG.m.0.ex: Measuring while moving 1 cm at a time away from a magnet; field around a straight wire.
ana.MAG.m.1.why: Check whether current (or number of turns)–field is a straight line through the origin.
ana.MAG.m.1.ex: Changing the current or number of turns of an electromagnet coil; solenoid.
ana.MAG.m.2.why: Read the values at several points to compare N/S direction (sign) and strength.
ana.MAG.m.2.ex: Mapping the field around a magnet; measuring Earth's magnetic field.
ana.MAG.m.3.tool: Calculated column → Change from first value
ana.MAG.m.3.why: Subtracts Earth's field (about 50 µT) to see only the magnet's contribution.
ana.MAG.m.3.ex: Weak magnets; measurements at long distances.
ana.MAG.tip.0: The sensor axis direction matters. Look at one axis only (e.g. Z) and keep the orientation fixed.
ana.MAG.tip.1: A nearby phone, speaker or steel desk distorts the value. Measure on a wooden desk.
ana.MAG.tip.2: Beyond the sensor range (thousands of µT) it flattens out. Keep strong neodymium magnets at least 2 cm away.
ana.AX.name: Acceleration
ana.AX.graph: Time–acceleration (m/s²) line graph, X, Y, Z in different colours on one graph or three stacked graphs. 0.01–0.02 s intervals.
ana.AX.m.0.why: Compare impact size (g = value/9.8) by the peak maximum. At rest, the axis reading +9.8 is the direction of gravity.
ana.AX.m.0.ex: Drop impact and airbag models; lift acceleration when starting and stopping.
ana.AX.m.1.why: Acceleration–time area = change in velocity (Δv). Find the velocity change before and after a collision.
ana.AX.m.1.ex: Cart collisions; velocity change after a shake.
ana.AX.m.2.why: Pick just one oscillation period or one impact to analyse. Read the frequency from the period (peak spacing).
ana.AX.m.2.ex: Measuring the period of a pendulum or spring oscillation.
ana.AX.m.3.why: Fits the damping curve of decreasing oscillation peak heights.
ana.AX.tip.0: At rest Z ≈ 9.8 m/s² (gravity). Subtracting gravity with the Change from first value calculated column leaves only the net acceleration.
ana.AX.tip.1: Align the sensor axis with the direction of motion. If tilted, gravity leaks into the other axes.
ana.AX.tip.2: An impact peak passes within 0.01 s. Use the minimum interval, and select only the peak range for the area.
ana.ANG.name: Angle
ana.ANG.graph: Time–angle (°) line graph, 0.02–0.05 s intervals. A pendulum gives a sine shape.
ana.ANG.m.0.why: The spacing between peaks is the period (T). The peak height is the amplitude.
ana.ANG.m.0.ex: Measuring the period for different pendulum lengths → confirming T² ∝ L.
ana.ANG.m.1.why: Differentiating the angle gives angular velocity; the peak is the fastest moment (lowest point).
ana.ANG.m.1.ex: Confirming maximum speed at the lowest point of a pendulum.
ana.ANG.m.2.why: Fitting the damping curve of decreasing amplitude.
ana.ANG.m.2.ex: Damping due to air resistance and friction.
ana.ANG.m.3.why: Pick one period or the tilted range only and read the mean angle.
ana.ANG.m.3.ex: Relationship between ramp angle and acceleration.
ana.ANG.tip.1: Large amplitudes (>15°) lengthen the period. Start with a small amplitude.
ana.ANG.tip.2: If the sensor cable interferes with the pendulum, damping gets faster.
ana.BPM.name: Heart rate
ana.BPM.graph: Time–heart rate (beats/min) line graph, 1 s intervals, 5–10 min. Mark the start and end of exercise.
ana.BPM.m.0.why: Compare the means of the resting, exercising and recovery ranges.
ana.BPM.m.0.ex: Heart rate change before and after jumping on the spot.
ana.BPM.m.1.why: Fit the curve of heart rate returning to its resting value after exercise and compare the recovery rate (C).
ana.BPM.m.1.ex: Comparing fitness (recovery time) and exercise habits.
ana.BPM.m.2.why: Reads how fast the heart rate rises after exercise starts.
ana.BPM.m.2.ex: Heart rate rise vs exercise intensity.
ana.BPM.m.3.why: Reads the resting heart rate (mean of the flat range).
ana.BPM.m.3.ex: Measuring resting heart rate; effect of breathing control.
ana.BPM.tip.0: Moving the finger or pressing hard makes the value jump. Hold still for at least 10 s before reading.
ana.BPM.tip.1: In the first 10–20 s the calculation has not settled and gives odd values. Discard them.
ana.BPM.tip.2: This is an educational sensor for seeing trends, not a medical diagnosis.
ana.PPG.name: Pulse waveform
ana.PPG.graph: Time–waveform (relative) line graph, 0.01–0.02 s intervals, short runs of 10–30 s. Auto y axis.
ana.PPG.m.0.why: Calculate the heart rate directly from the spacing between peaks (s): 60/spacing.
ana.PPG.m.0.ex: Finding heart rate from the pulse waveform; comparing with the wrist pulse.
ana.PPG.m.1.why: Pick just 10 s of clean waveform, count the peaks and ×6 for beats per minute.
ana.PPG.m.2.why: Differentiating the waveform makes the peaks sharper, so the spacing is easier to read.
ana.PPG.tip.0: Rest your finger lightly on the sensor and keep it still.
ana.PPG.tip.1: If no waveform appears, block ambient light or warm your finger.
ana.PPG.tip.2: Long recordings make the graph dense, so zoom in with Select range.
ana.PM25.name: Fine dust
ana.PM25.graph: Time–PM2.5 (µg/m³) line graph, 10–60 s intervals, tens of minutes to a day. Show clock time for long runs. PM1, PM2.5 and PM10 in different colours on one graph.
ana.PM25.m.0.why: Compare the mean and maximum of each range, such as before/after ventilation, while cooking, or with a vacuum cleaner running.
ana.PM25.m.0.ex: Effect of ventilating a classroom; measuring fine dust from scented candles or chalk dust.
ana.PM25.m.1.why: Fit the falling concentration after removing the source with an exponential to compare air-purifier efficiency (decay constant).
ana.PM25.m.1.ex: Rate of concentration decrease after turning on an air purifier.
ana.PM25.m.2.why: Compare the peak concentration with the threshold (35 µg/m³ = unhealthy).
ana.PM25.m.2.ex: Recording fine dust over a day; comparing with external data.
ana.PM25.tip.0: The sensor averages, so changes appear tens of seconds late.
ana.PM25.tip.1: High humidity exaggerates the value. Record humidity too.
ana.PM25.tip.2: Wind blowing directly into the sensor inlet makes it jump. Do not block the inlet and keep it away from walls.
ana.UV.name: Ultraviolet
ana.UV.graph: Value-entry mode with x = condition (sunscreen SPF, type of glass, angle), y = UV index, scatter graph. Time mode for the daily variation.
ana.UV.m.0.why: Read the value for each condition and calculate blocking rate = (1 − measured/reference)×100 %.
ana.UV.m.0.ex: UV blocking rate of sunscreen by SPF, glass and sunglasses.
ana.UV.m.1.why: Compare the means of the shade and sunlight ranges.
ana.UV.m.1.ex: Recording UV on the playground at different times of day.
ana.UV.m.2.why: Fit sun elevation (time)–UV with a linear or power fit to confirm the maximum around noon.
ana.UV.m.2.ex: Recording UV change over the day.
ana.UV.tip.0: Under indoor lighting it is close to 0. Do this in sunlight by a window or outdoors.
ana.UV.tip.1: Point the sensor perpendicular to the sunlight and keep the angle fixed.
ana.UV.tip.2: Passing clouds cause sudden changes. Note them with a mark.
ana.SOIL.name: Soil moisture
ana.SOIL.graph: Time–soil moisture (%) line graph, 1–10 min intervals, over several days. Show clock time. Mark watering times.
ana.SOIL.m.0.why: Fit the drying curve after watering to compare evaporation rates by soil type.
ana.SOIL.m.0.ex: Comparing water retention of sand, clay and potting soil.
ana.SOIL.m.1.why: Read the drying rate (%/hour) to compare with/without a plant and sunlight conditions.
ana.SOIL.m.1.ex: Transpiration: pot with a plant vs empty pot.
ana.SOIL.m.2.why: Read the maximum right after watering and the value the next day to get the daily consumption.
ana.SOIL.tip.0: The sensor value depends on soil type and insertion depth. Keep the depth the same.
ana.SOIL.tip.1: Resistive sensors corrode when left in for long and the value drifts. A capacitive sensor is recommended.
ana.SOIL.tip.2: A sudden jump right after watering is normal. Analyse from 1 hour later.
ana.GAS.name: Gas (MQ series, relative)
ana.GAS.graph: Time–gas (%) line graph, 1 s intervals. Record the baseline (air) for 1–2 min first. Mark the moment of gas exposure.
ana.GAS.m.0.tool: Calculated column → Change from first value
ana.GAS.m.0.why: Subtracting the baseline and looking only at the change makes comparison between conditions easy.
ana.GAS.m.0.ex: Concentration changes of alcohol, butane and fermentation gas.
ana.GAS.m.1.why: Compare production rates by the rising slope, and ventilation rates by the falling slope.
ana.GAS.m.1.ex: Alcohol production in yeast fermentation; effect of opening a window to ventilate.
ana.GAS.m.2.why: Get the ventilation time constant from the curve of concentration returning to baseline after ventilation.
ana.GAS.m.2.ex: Comparing ventilation rates of a sealed box.
ana.GAS.m.3.why: Compare relative concentrations by the maximum value (not quantitative).
ana.GAS.m.3.ex: Comparing responses to different concentrations of rubbing alcohol.
ana.GAS.tip.0: Warm-up takes 1–3 min and the value drifts down meanwhile. Start after it settles.
ana.GAS.tip.1: Values are relative, so converting to ppm is difficult. Use only for comparing conditions.
ana.GAS.tip.2: The sensor gets hot and is sensitive to humidity and temperature. Do not breathe on it.
reagent.naoh.name: Sodium hydroxide
reagent.naoh.useIn: 0.1 M and 1 M solutions for titration, heat of neutralization, Hess's law and crystal violet experiments; Hess's law also uses the solid (NaOH(s))
reagent.naoh.storage: Sealed plastic bottle in a dry place. Store away from acids.
reagent.naoh.disposal: Neutralize with sodium bicarbonate (or sodium carbonate), check pH 5–9, then pour down the drain with at least 20 volumes of water (Flinn #24b).
reagent.naoh.studentLimit: Students: 1 M or less (middle school 0.1 M or less); teacher prepares solid and concentrated solutions
reagent.naoh.hazard.0: Corrosive: severe skin and eye burns (H314)
reagent.naoh.hazard.1: Solid is hygroscopic; dissolving in water releases a lot of heat
reagent.naoh.hazard.2: Corrosive to metals — reacts with aluminum to give hydrogen
reagent.naoh.handling.0: Teacher only handles the solid; weigh quickly with forceps or a spatula and close the lid at once.
reagent.naoh.handling.1: For 1 M or stronger, keep water nearby so splashes can be rinsed immediately.
reagent.naoh.prep.steps.0: Put about 200 mL of water in a plastic beaker.
reagent.naoh.prep.steps.1: Weigh 1.0 g of NaOH (10.0 g for 1 M), add to the water a little at a time and stir to dissolve (add NaOH to water, as heat is released).
reagent.naoh.prep.steps.2: After cooling, add water to 250 mL and transfer to a polyethylene bottle.
reagent.naoh.prep.notes.1: Glass stoppers seize, so store in a plastic bottle.
reagent.naoh.prep.notes.2: Absorbs CO₂ from the air, so for accurate titrations prepare on the day and standardize.
reagent.naoh.firstAid.skin: Remove clothing and rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes. Use water only; do not apply neutralizers.
reagent.naoh.firstAid.eye: Hold the eyelids open and rinse under running water (eyewash) for at least 15 minutes, then go to hospital.
reagent.naoh.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth several times. Do not induce vomiting; call emergency services.
reagent.hcl.name: Hydrochloric acid
reagent.hcl.useIn: 0.1 M and 1 M for titration, heat of neutralization, reaction rate and stoichiometry experiments (reaction rate uses several concentrations, 0.5–2 M)
reagent.hcl.storage: Sealed glass or PE bottle, away from bases and metals. Concentrated acid in a locked chemical cabinet.
reagent.hcl.disposal: Neutralize with sodium bicarbonate (or sodium carbonate), check pH 5–9, then pour down the drain with at least 20 volumes of water (Flinn #24b).
reagent.hcl.studentLimit: Students: 2 M or less (middle school 0.1–1 M); concentrated acid teacher only
reagent.hcl.hazard.0: Corrosive: concentrated acid causes skin and eye burns (H314)
reagent.hcl.hazard.1: Concentrated acid vapor irritates the airways (H335) — fumes when the lid is opened
reagent.hcl.hazard.2: Reacts with magnesium and calcium carbonate to give gas (H₂ is flammable)
reagent.hcl.handling.0: After diluting, label with concentration and date.
reagent.hcl.handling.1: Mg and CaCO₃ reactions raise the pressure in a closed vessel, so do not tighten the stopper fully; let it vent through the sensor hole.
reagent.hcl.prep.steps.0: Put about 150 mL of water in a beaker first.
reagent.hcl.prep.steps.1: Slowly add 21 mL of concentrated hydrochloric acid (35–37 %, about 12 M) to the water (always acid into water).
reagent.hcl.prep.steps.3: 0.1 M: dilute 25 mL of 1 M solution to 250 mL with water.
reagent.hcl.prep.notes.0: Flinn: 1 M = 83 mL/L concentrated acid, 0.1 M = 8.3 mL/L.
reagent.hcl.prep.notes.1: Teacher only handles concentrated acid, in a fume hood (or by a ventilated window).
reagent.hcl.firstAid.skin: Remove clothing and rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes. Use water only; do not apply neutralizers.
reagent.hcl.firstAid.eye: Hold the eyelids open and rinse under running water (eyewash) for at least 15 minutes, then go to hospital.
reagent.hcl.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth several times. Do not induce vomiting; call emergency services.
reagent.acetic.name: Acetic acid
reagent.acetic.useIn: 0.1 M solution for weak-acid titration curve, ionization constant and buffer experiments
reagent.acetic.storage: Sealed bottle, cool place, away from oxidizers and bases.
reagent.acetic.disposal: Neutralize with sodium bicarbonate (or sodium carbonate), check pH 5–9, then pour down the drain with at least 20 volumes of water (Flinn #24b).
reagent.acetic.studentLimit: Students: 1 M or less; glacial acetic acid teacher only
reagent.acetic.hazard.0: Glacial acetic acid (99 %) is a flammable liquid and causes skin and eye burns (H226, H314)
reagent.acetic.hazard.1: Dilute 0.1–1 M solutions only cause mild eye irritation
reagent.acetic.handling.0: Glacial acetic acid freezes below 16 °C, so thaw in a warm place before use.
reagent.acetic.handling.1: Use a pipette filler; never pipette by mouth.
reagent.acetic.prep.steps.0: Put about 200 mL of water in a beaker.
reagent.acetic.prep.steps.1: Pipette 1.45 mL of glacial acetic acid (17.4 M) into the water (14.5 mL for 1 M).
reagent.acetic.prep.notes.0: Flinn: 1 M = 58 mL/L glacial acetic acid, 0.1 M = 5.8 mL/L.
reagent.acetic.prep.notes.1: Without glacial acetic acid, vinegar (4–7 %, about 0.7–1.2 M) diluted and adjusted with a pH sensor also works.
reagent.acetic.firstAid.skin: Remove clothing and rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes. Use water only; do not apply neutralizers.
reagent.acetic.firstAid.eye: Hold the eyelids open and rinse under running water (eyewash) for at least 15 minutes, then go to hospital.
reagent.acetic.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth several times. Do not induce vomiting; call emergency services.
reagent.vinegar.name: Vinegar
reagent.vinegar.useIn: Ocean acidification, greenhouse gas, iron oxidation and conservation of mass experiments — use store-bought vinegar as is or diluted with water
reagent.vinegar.disposal: Pour down the drain with water.
reagent.vinegar.hazard.0: Stings and irritates if it gets in the eyes
reagent.vinegar.hazard.1: Strong odor — ventilate when using a lot in a closed room
reagent.vinegar.handling.0: Baking soda + vinegar foams over, so use a large container.
reagent.vinegar.prep.steps.0: Add vinegar a little at a time to 200 mL of water, using a pH sensor to reach the pH you want.
reagent.vinegar.prep.steps.1: When reacting with baking soda, about 5 g of baking soda per 50 mL of vinegar is enough.
reagent.vinegar.prep.notes.0: One cup of vinegar reacting with baking soda gives about 1 L of CO₂, so leave the stopper loose on closed containers.
reagent.vinegar.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.vinegar.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.citric.name: Citric acid
reagent.citric.useIn: Endothermic reaction (citric acid + baking soda) experiment — use the solid as is
reagent.citric.disposal: Pour down the drain with water.
reagent.citric.hazard.1: Airborne powder irritates the nose and throat
reagent.citric.handling.0: Foams a lot, so use a large cup.
reagent.citric.prep.steps.0: Put 10 g of citric acid and 10 g of baking soda in a cup.
reagent.citric.prep.steps.1: Insert the temperature sensor, pour in 30 mL of water and measure at once (about −5 to −10 °C change).
reagent.citric.prep.notes.0: Food-grade citric acid (baking or cleaning grade) is sufficient.
reagent.citric.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.citric.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.nahco3.name: Sodium bicarbonate
reagent.nahco3.useIn: Greenhouse gas, endothermic reaction, conservation of mass, photosynthesis (CO₂ supply) and everyday pH experiments
reagent.nahco3.disposal: Pour down the drain with water.
reagent.nahco3.hazard.1: Gives off CO₂ with acids — watch the pressure in closed containers
reagent.nahco3.handling.0: When mixing with vinegar, use a large container so it does not overflow.
reagent.nahco3.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 1.3–2.5 g of sodium bicarbonate (about 0.06–0.12 M) in 250 mL of water — for Elodea photosynthesis.
reagent.nahco3.prep.steps.1: pH sample: dissolving 1 spoon (about 5 g) in 100 mL of water gives pH about 8.3.
reagent.nahco3.prep.notes.0: Also sprinkle this powder to neutralize spilled acid (school lab safety manual).
reagent.nahco3.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.nahco3.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.caco3.name: Calcium carbonate
reagent.caco3.useIn: Stoichiometry (CaCO₃ + HCl), seawater CO₂ and ocean acidification (limestone powder, shells) experiments — solid as is
reagent.caco3.disposal: Leftover solid goes in the regular trash; neutralize solutions, then drain.
reagent.caco3.hazard.2: Reacts with hydrochloric acid to give CO₂ — foaming and pressure
reagent.caco3.handling.0: Add the powder slowly so the foam does not overflow.
reagent.caco3.prep.steps.0: Put 50 mL of dilute hydrochloric acid (1 M) in an Erlenmeyer flask and place it on the balance (load cell).
reagent.caco3.prep.steps.1: Add 1.0 g, 2.0 g and 3.0 g of calcium carbonate in turn and compare the mass lost as CO₂ (0.44 g/g).
reagent.caco3.prep.notes.0: Chalk, shells and eggshells are also calcium carbonate (with impurities).
reagent.caco3.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.caco3.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.caoh2.name: Calcium hydroxide
reagent.caoh2.useIn: Carbon capture (CO₂ absorbent) experiment — solid or saturated limewater
reagent.caoh2.disposal: Neutralize with dilute hydrochloric acid or vinegar to pH 5–9, then drain with water.
reagent.caoh2.studentLimit: Students: saturated limewater (≈0.02 M) only; teacher handles the powder
reagent.caoh2.hazard.0: Serious eye damage (H318); skin and respiratory irritation (H315, H335)
reagent.caoh2.handling.0: Move the powder slowly so your breath does not blow it around.
reagent.caoh2.handling.1: Rinse at once if it splashes in the eyes — alkalis cause serious eye damage.
reagent.caoh2.prep.steps.0: Add about 0.5 g of calcium hydroxide (≈2 g/L) to 250 mL of water, stir for a few minutes, let it settle and use the clear liquid on top.
reagent.caoh2.prep.steps.1: As a CO₂ absorbent, spread 5–10 g of powder thinly on a dish or coat damp filter paper with it.
reagent.caoh2.prep.notes.1: Absorbs CO₂ from the air and turns cloudy, so prepare on the day.
reagent.caoh2.firstAid.skin: Remove clothing and rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes. Use water only; do not apply neutralizers.
reagent.caoh2.firstAid.eye: Hold the eyelids open and rinse under running water (eyewash) for at least 15 minutes, then go to hospital.
reagent.caoh2.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth several times. Do not induce vomiting; call emergency services.
reagent.h2o2.name: Hydrogen peroxide
reagent.h2o2.useIn: 3 % solution for catalyst and enzyme (catalase) reaction rate experiments
reagent.h2o2.storage: Brown bottle, cool dark place, lid not fully tightened (gas release).
reagent.h2o2.disposal: Dilute at least 10× with water and pour down the drain.
reagent.h2o2.studentLimit: Students: 3 % or less; 30 % stock teacher only
reagent.h2o2.ghs: GHS03 Oxidizer · GHS05 Corrosive (30 % and above)
reagent.h2o2.hazard.0: 3 % antiseptic grade only causes mild eye and skin irritation
reagent.h2o2.hazard.1: 30 % and above is corrosive (H314) and oxidizing (H271) — teacher only
reagent.h2o2.hazard.2: Decomposes to give O₂ — pressure rises in closed containers
reagent.h2o2.handling.0: Adding MnO₂, potato or yeast foams at once, so fill the flask no more than half full.
reagent.h2o2.handling.1: Open the stopper holding the sensor before the pressure rises too far.
reagent.h2o2.prep.steps.0: Use pharmacy antiseptic hydrogen peroxide (3 %) as is.
reagent.h2o2.prep.steps.1: If you have 30 % stock, add 10 mL of stock to 90 mL of water to make 3 % (teacher; gloves and goggles).
reagent.h2o2.prep.notes.0: Decomposes in light, heat and dust, so keep in a brown bottle in a cool place.
reagent.h2o2.prep.notes.1: To change the concentration, dilute 3 % with water to 1.5 % and 0.75 %.
reagent.h2o2.firstAid.skin: Rinse under running water for 15 minutes (whitened skin soon recovers).
reagent.h2o2.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes and go to hospital.
reagent.h2o2.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. Do not induce vomiting; go to hospital.
reagent.mno2.name: Manganese dioxide
reagent.mno2.useIn: Catalyst for hydrogen peroxide decomposition — 0.2–0.5 g of solid
reagent.mno2.disposal: Collect the filtered solid for designated waste disposal (small amounts may go in the regular trash).
reagent.mno2.studentLimit: Students: small amounts of 0.5 g or less
reagent.mno2.hazard.0: Harmful if swallowed or inhaled (H302, H332)
reagent.mno2.hazard.1: Keep the powder from blowing around
reagent.mno2.hazard.2: Oxidizer — do not mix with combustibles
reagent.mno2.handling.0: The reaction is fast and foams up, so use a large flask.
reagent.mno2.prep.steps.0: Add 0.2–0.5 g of MnO₂ (tip of a spatula) to 20 mL of 3 % hydrogen peroxide and close the stopper at once.
reagent.mno2.prep.notes.0: It is a catalyst, so it can be filtered and reused after the reaction.
reagent.mno2.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.mno2.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.catalase.name: Potato or liver extract (catalase)
reagent.catalase.useIn: Enzyme reaction rate and pressure experiments — reacts with 3 % hydrogen peroxide
reagent.catalase.hazard.0: No hazard — raw liver may carry food-poisoning bacteria; wash hands after use
