reagent.catalase.handling.0: Liver is raw, so wash hands with soap when finished.
reagent.catalase.prep.steps.0: Blend 20 g of potato (or chicken liver) with 50 mL of cold water.
reagent.catalase.prep.steps.1: Filter through gauze, refrigerate and use the same day.
reagent.catalase.prep.steps.2: For temperature conditions, hold the extract in a water bath (20, 30, 40, 60 °C) for 10 minutes before use.
reagent.catalase.prep.notes.0: For pH conditions, mix the extract 1:1 with pH 4, 7 and 10 buffer solutions.
reagent.catalase.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.catalase.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.starch.name: Starch solution
reagent.starch.useIn: 1 % solution for digestion (iodine test) and iodine clock reaction
reagent.starch.hazard.0: No hazard — watch for burns when dissolving in hot water
reagent.starch.handling.0: Pour slowly so it does not spatter when boiling.
reagent.starch.prep.steps.0: Mix 1 g of soluble starch into a paste with 10 mL of cold water.
reagent.starch.prep.steps.1: Pour into 90 mL of boiling water while stirring, boil 1 more minute and cool.
reagent.starch.prep.steps.2: Let it settle and use the clear liquid on top.
reagent.starch.prep.notes.1: Spoils within days, so prepare on the day or refrigerate for up to 1 week.
reagent.starch.prep.notes.2: Even diluted to 0.1 % the iodine reaction is clearly visible.
reagent.starch.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.starch.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.iodine.name: Iodine solution
reagent.iodine.useIn: Starch detection (digestion experiment) — dilute iodine–potassium iodide solution
reagent.iodine.disposal: Decolorize small amounts of dilute solution with a few crystals of sodium thiosulfate (or vitamin C) and drain with water. Solid goes to designated waste.
reagent.iodine.studentLimit: Students: dilute solution (drops) only; solid teacher only
reagent.iodine.hazard.0: Solid iodine: sublimes and the vapor irritates eyes and airways; stains and burns skin (H312, H332, H315, H319, H335)
reagent.iodine.hazard.1: Dilute solution only stains skin and clothing
reagent.iodine.handling.0: Teacher only weighs solid iodine in a fume hood or by a window; use a plastic spatula instead of metal.
reagent.iodine.handling.1: Keep the solution in a brown bottle — decomposes in light.
reagent.iodine.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 1.5 g of potassium iodide (KI) in 12 mL of water.
reagent.iodine.prep.steps.1: Add 0.3 g of iodine (I₂), stir until dissolved and make up to 100 mL with water (teacher; ventilate).
reagent.iodine.prep.steps.2: Use one drop at a time — enough once the starch solution turns deep blue.
reagent.iodine.prep.notes.0: Flinn starch test solution = KI 15 g + I₂ 3 g per L.
reagent.iodine.prep.notes.1: Pharmacy povidone-iodine diluted 10× with water also works.
reagent.iodine.firstAid.skin: Wash with soap and water (stains fade after a few days).
reagent.iodine.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes and go to hospital.
reagent.iodine.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth, give water or starchy food, and go to hospital.
reagent.kio3.name: Potassium iodate
reagent.kio3.useIn: Solution A for the iodine clock reaction (about 0.02 M)
reagent.kio3.storage: Sealed container, away from combustibles and reducing agents.
reagent.kio3.disposal: Drain solutions with water (post-reaction solution contains little iodine and can go as is). Solid goes to designated waste.
reagent.kio3.studentLimit: Students: solutions of 0.02 M or less only; solid teacher only
reagent.kio3.hazard.0: Oxidizing solid (H272) — do not mix with combustibles
reagent.kio3.handling.0: Do not spill the powder on paper, wood or organic material.
reagent.kio3.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 1.1 g of potassium iodate in water and make up to 250 mL.
reagent.kio3.prep.steps.1: For concentration conditions, dilute this solution 2× and 4× with water.
reagent.kio3.prep.steps.2: Start timing the moment it is mixed with an equal volume of solution B (sodium bisulfite + starch + dilute acid).
reagent.kio3.prep.notes.1: Test the dilution beforehand so that a 1:1 mix at 20 °C turns blue after 10–30 seconds.
reagent.kio3.firstAid.skin: Remove clothing and rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes. Use water only; do not apply neutralizers.
reagent.kio3.firstAid.eye: Hold the eyelids open and rinse under running water (eyewash) for at least 15 minutes, then go to hospital.
reagent.kio3.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth several times. Do not induce vomiting; call emergency services.
reagent.nahso3.name: Sodium bisulfite
reagent.nahso3.useIn: Solution B for the iodine clock reaction (reducing agent, with starch and dilute acid)
reagent.nahso3.storage: Sealed plastic container, cool and dry, away from acids.
reagent.nahso3.disposal: Small amounts down the drain with plenty of water. Neutralize acidic solutions with sodium bicarbonate first.
reagent.nahso3.studentLimit: Students: prepared dilute solution B only; teacher handles the solid and mixing with acid
reagent.nahso3.hazard.0: Harmful if swallowed (H302); serious eye damage (H318)
reagent.nahso3.hazard.1: Gives off toxic SO₂ gas with acids (EUH031) — ventilate
reagent.nahso3.hazard.2: Students with sulfite allergy (asthma) should not smell it
reagent.nahso3.handling.0: Do not mix directly with concentrated acid.
reagent.nahso3.handling.1: Serious if splashed in the eyes — goggles required.
reagent.nahso3.prep.steps.0: Mix 0.5 g of starch into a paste with cold water, dissolve in 50 mL of boiling water and cool.
reagent.nahso3.prep.steps.1: Dissolve 0.3 g of sodium bisulfite (or sodium metabisulfite) in 150 mL of water.
reagent.nahso3.prep.steps.2: Add the starch solution and 5–10 mL of 1 M sulfuric acid (or 10 mL of 1 M hydrochloric acid if unavailable) and make up to 250 mL with water.
reagent.nahso3.prep.notes.0: CSUB: sodium metabisulfite 1.2 g/L + sulfuric acid 4 g/L.
reagent.nahso3.prep.notes.1: It is acidic and smells slightly of SO₂, so ventilate. Prepare on the day (oxidizes in air).
reagent.nahso3.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes and go to hospital.
reagent.nahso3.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth, give one or two cups of water to drink, then go to hospital. Do not induce vomiting.
reagent.crystalviolet.name: Crystal violet
reagent.crystalviolet.useIn: First-order reaction half-life experiment — 2×10⁻⁵ M solution mixed 1:1 with 0.02 M NaOH
reagent.crystalviolet.storage: Sealed brown bottle, locked chemical cabinet.
reagent.crystalviolet.disposal: Never drain. Collect in the organic dye waste container for designated disposal (the colorless post-reaction solution also goes in the waste container).
reagent.crystalviolet.studentLimit: Students: dilute 2×10⁻⁵ M solution only (gloves); solid and stock solution teacher only
reagent.crystalviolet.ghs: GHS06 Toxic · GHS08 Health hazard · GHS09 Environment
reagent.crystalviolet.hazard.1: Carcinogen 1B (H350) — never inhale or touch the solid powder
reagent.crystalviolet.handling.0: Teacher only weighs the solid in a fume hood; students get only the diluted solution.
reagent.crystalviolet.handling.1: Spills stain unless wiped at once — cover with paper towel to absorb, then water.
reagent.crystalviolet.prep.target: 2×10⁻⁵ M, 250 mL (prepared via a stock solution)
reagent.crystalviolet.prep.steps.0: Stock solution: dissolve 0.1 g of crystal violet in 100 mL of water (2.5×10⁻³ M; teacher only).
reagent.crystalviolet.prep.steps.1: Diluting 2 mL of stock to 250 mL with water gives about 2×10⁻⁵ M.
reagent.crystalviolet.prep.steps.2: NaOH 0.02 M: dilute 50 mL of 0.1 M NaOH to 250 mL with water (or NaOH 0.2 g/250 mL).
reagent.crystalviolet.prep.steps.3: Start measuring the moment equal volumes of CV solution and NaOH solution are mixed in the cuvette.
reagent.crystalviolet.prep.notes.0: Anoka-Ramsey and Vernier: CV 2.0×10⁻⁵ M + NaOH 0.020 M (1:1).
reagent.crystalviolet.prep.notes.1: Changing the NaOH concentration to 0.01 M doubles the half-life.
reagent.crystalviolet.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes and go to hospital.
reagent.crystalviolet.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and go to hospital or call emergency services at once. Do not induce vomiting.
reagent.cocl2.name: Cobalt chloride
reagent.cocl2.useIn: Equilibrium shift (color change with temperature) experiment — 0.1 M solution in ethanol
reagent.cocl2.storage: Sealed bottle (hygroscopic), locked chemical cabinet, away from oxidizers.
reagent.cocl2.disposal: Never drain. Collect in the heavy-metal waste container for designated disposal by a licensed contractor (Flinn #27f).
reagent.cocl2.studentLimit: Teacher preparation and teacher demonstration recommended. Students: solutions of 0.1 M or less in stoppered test tubes only
reagent.cocl2.handling.0: Teacher only weighs the solid; do not inhale the powder.
reagent.cocl2.handling.1: Do not touch your face with hands that have solution on them; wash hands when finished.
reagent.cocl2.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 2.4 g of cobalt chloride hexahydrate in 100 mL of ethanol (95 %) (blue).
reagent.cocl2.prep.steps.1: Add water drop by drop until it turns purple at room temperature.
reagent.cocl2.prep.steps.2: Divide 5 mL into each test tube and place them in hot water (blue) and ice water (pink).
reagent.cocl2.prep.notes.1: Setting the equilibrium with ethanol instead of concentrated hydrochloric acid reduces the corrosion hazard.
reagent.cocl2.prep.notes.2: Stopper the test tubes to reduce ethanol evaporation and odor.
reagent.cocl2.firstAid.skin: Wash with soap and water; see a doctor if a rash appears.
reagent.cocl2.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes and go to hospital.
reagent.cocl2.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth; go to hospital or call emergency services.
reagent.k2cro4.name: Potassium chromate
reagent.k2cro4.useIn: Chromate–dichromate equilibrium experiment — add dilute HCl and NaOH drop by drop to a 0.1 M solution
reagent.k2cro4.storage: Sealed bottle, locked chemical cabinet, away from reducing agents and organic material.
reagent.k2cro4.disposal: Never drain. Collect in the chromium waste container for designated disposal by a licensed contractor (Flinn #27f; Cr limit 5 mg/L).
reagent.k2cro4.studentLimit: Teacher preparation and teacher demonstration recommended (carcinogen). Students: 0.01–0.1 M solution in cuvette amounts only; not recommended for middle school
reagent.k2cro4.hazard.1: Toxic if swallowed (H301); corrosive to skin and eyes (H314)
reagent.k2cro4.handling.0: Never let the powder blow around; if spilled, cover with wet paper, collect and seal (school lab safety manual).
reagent.k2cro4.handling.1: Students handle the dilute solution only with cuvettes and droppers, and wash hands when finished.
reagent.k2cro4.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 1.94 g of potassium chromate in water and make up to 100 mL (fume hood or window; gloves and goggles).
reagent.k2cro4.prep.steps.1: For the cuvette, 0.01 M (10× dilution) suits the color sensor range.
reagent.k2cro4.prep.steps.2: Add 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M NaOH drop by drop with a dropper and watch the color change.
reagent.k2cro4.prep.notes.1: RSC and CLEAPSS: the solid is hazardous, so solutions are prepared by the teacher or technician; recommended for high school and above.
reagent.k2cro4.firstAid.skin: Remove clothing, rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes and go to hospital.
reagent.k2cro4.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes and go to hospital immediately.
reagent.k2cro4.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and call emergency services immediately. Do not induce vomiting.
reagent.feno33.name: Iron(III) nitrate
reagent.feno33.useIn: FeSCN²⁺ equilibrium constant experiment — 0.2 M for the standard, 0.002 M for samples
reagent.feno33.storage: Sealed bottle, away from combustibles and reducing agents.
reagent.feno33.disposal: Iron has low toxicity — neutralize with sodium bicarbonate and drain with water (small amounts). Neutralization is essential if the nitric acid concentration is high.
reagent.feno33.studentLimit: Students: solutions of 0.2 M or less only; teacher handles the solid and nitric acid preparation
reagent.feno33.hazard.0: Oxidizing solid (H272) — keep away from combustibles
reagent.feno33.hazard.2: Solution is acidic (corrosive if it contains nitric acid)
reagent.feno33.handling.0: Teacher only handles nitric acid; students pipette the diluted solution.
reagent.feno33.handling.1: Solution leaves brown stains on clothing.
reagent.feno33.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 8.1 g of iron(III) nitrate nonahydrate in 100 mL of 0.1 M nitric acid (or water with 1 mL of dilute hydrochloric acid) (prevents clouding by hydrolysis).
reagent.feno33.prep.steps.1: 0.002 M: dilute 2.5 mL of stock to 250 mL with water.
reagent.feno33.prep.steps.2: For the standard (excess Fe³⁺ converts all SCN⁻ to FeSCN²⁺), use the 0.2 M stock as is.
reagent.feno33.prep.notes.1: University labs (Bellevue) dissolve it in 1.0 M HNO₃, but at school 0.1 M nitric acid or a few drops of hydrochloric acid is enough.
reagent.feno33.firstAid.skin: Remove clothing and rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes. Use water only; do not apply neutralizers.
reagent.feno33.firstAid.eye: Hold the eyelids open and rinse under running water (eyewash) for at least 15 minutes, then go to hospital.
reagent.feno33.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth several times. Do not induce vomiting; call emergency services.
reagent.kscn.name: Potassium thiocyanate
reagent.kscn.useIn: FeSCN²⁺ equilibrium constant experiment — 0.002 M solution
reagent.kscn.storage: Sealed bottle, dry, away from acids.
reagent.kscn.disposal: Small amounts of dilute solution down the drain with plenty of water (do not mix with acidic waste).
reagent.kscn.studentLimit: Students: solutions of 0.1 M or less only
reagent.kscn.hazard.1: Affects the thyroid with repeated exposure (H372)
reagent.kscn.hazard.2: May give off toxic gases (HCN, COS) with acids — do not mix with concentrated acid
reagent.kscn.handling.0: Do not mix with concentrated acids or oxidizers.
reagent.kscn.handling.1: Keep away from food so it is not eaten.
reagent.kscn.prep.steps.0: 0.1 M stock: dissolve 2.43 g of KSCN in water to 250 mL (Flinn 0.1 M = 9.7 g/L).
reagent.kscn.prep.steps.1: Diluting 5 mL of stock to 250 mL with water gives 0.002 M.
reagent.kscn.prep.notes.0: Mixing with Fe³⁺ solution gives red FeSCN²⁺ — for the absorbance calibration curve, vary the 0.002 M solution from 1 to 5 mL.
reagent.kscn.prep.notes.1: Hygroscopic, so weigh quickly and close the lid.
reagent.kscn.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.kscn.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.cuso4.name: Copper(II) sulfate
reagent.cuso4.useIn: Electrolyte for the Daniell cell (0.1–1 M) and copper plating (Faraday's law, 0.5–1 M)
reagent.cuso4.storage: Sealed bottle (effloresces and absorbs moisture), cool place.
reagent.cuso4.disposal: Never drain. Collect in the copper waste container for designated disposal, or add zinc pieces to precipitate the copper and drain the filtered solution with water (Flinn #26b; check local regulations).
reagent.cuso4.studentLimit: Students: solutions of 1 M or less only
reagent.cuso4.hazard.2: Very toxic to aquatic life (H410) — never drain
reagent.cuso4.handling.0: Do not inhale the blue crystalline powder.
reagent.cuso4.handling.1: Avoid splashing the solution when removing electrodes.
reagent.cuso4.prep.target: 1 M, 250 mL (0.1 M also works for the cell)
reagent.cuso4.prep.steps.0: Add 62.4 g of copper sulfate pentahydrate (6.2 g for 0.1 M) to about 200 mL of water and stir to dissolve (dissolves faster in warm water).
reagent.cuso4.prep.steps.2: For plating, adding 5 mL of 1 M sulfuric acid gives an even current (optional).
reagent.cuso4.prep.notes.1: For the salt bridge, use filter paper or agar soaked in saturated KNO₃ or NaCl solution.
reagent.cuso4.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.cuso4.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.znso4.name: Zinc sulfate
reagent.znso4.useIn: Electrolyte for the Zn half-cell of the Daniell cell, 0.1–1 M
reagent.znso4.disposal: Never drain. Collect in the zinc waste container for designated disposal (Flinn #27f; local sewer regulations).
reagent.znso4.studentLimit: Students: solutions of 1 M or less only
reagent.znso4.hazard.2: Very toxic to aquatic life (H410) — never drain
reagent.znso4.handling.0: Goggles required to keep splashes out of the eyes.
reagent.znso4.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 71.9 g of zinc sulfate heptahydrate (7.2 g for 0.1 M) in water and make up to 250 mL.
reagent.znso4.prep.notes.1: Matching the copper sulfate concentration brings the voltage close to the standard potential (1.10 V).
reagent.znso4.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes and go to hospital.
reagent.znso4.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth, give water to drink, then go to hospital.
reagent.metals.name: Metal electrodes (Zn, Cu, Mg, Fe)
reagent.metals.useIn: Electrodes for chemical cells (lemon, salt water), the Daniell cell and copper plating
reagent.metals.disposal: Reuse. When worn out, metal waste (recycling).
reagent.metals.hazard.0: Metal pieces themselves are low hazard — watch for cuts on edges
reagent.metals.hazard.1: Mg is flammable — no flames nearby
reagent.metals.hazard.2: Lemon and salt-water cells have low voltage, so no shock hazard
reagent.metals.handling.0: Rinse with water and dry after use to reuse.
reagent.metals.handling.1: Mg electrodes give hydrogen bubbles in acidic solution — do not seal.
reagent.metals.prep.steps.0: Sand off the oxide layer, rinse with water and dry.
reagent.metals.prep.steps.1: Insert the electrodes at equal spacing (about 2 cm) and connect them to the voltage sensor leads with clip wires.
reagent.metals.prep.steps.2: For plating, weigh the copper plate before attaching it to the cathode.
reagent.metals.prep.notes.0: Zn–Cu 1.1 V, Mg–Cu about 1.5–2 V, Fe–Cu about 0.4–0.8 V (varies with the electrolyte).
reagent.metals.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.metals.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.mg.name: Magnesium ribbon
reagent.mg.useIn: Ideal gas equation (hydrogen from Mg + HCl) and reaction rate (concentration) experiments — 2–3 cm pieces
reagent.mg.storage: Sealed tin, dry, away from acids and oxidizers.
reagent.mg.disposal: Dissolve leftover Mg completely in dilute hydrochloric acid, neutralize and drain. Reuse ribbon.
reagent.mg.studentLimit: Students: pieces of 3 cm or less in acid of 2 M or less only; burning is a teacher demonstration
reagent.mg.hazard.0: Flammable solid — once lit it burns with an intensely bright light (eye damage) and high heat and cannot be put out with water
reagent.mg.hazard.1: Reacts with acids and hot water to give hydrogen (flammable)
reagent.mg.hazard.2: Skin, eye and respiratory irritation (H315, H319, H335)
reagent.mg.handling.0: Keep flames and heating equipment off the bench.
reagent.mg.handling.1: Keep your face away when opening the flask after the reaction (hydrogen release).
reagent.mg.handling.2: Do not keep the ribbon container near fire.
reagent.mg.prep.steps.0: Sand the ribbon to remove the oxide layer.
reagent.mg.prep.steps.1: Cut 2–3 cm (about 0.03–0.05 g) and weigh — an amount that will not raise the pressure in the closed flask too far.
reagent.mg.prep.steps.2: Add to 30 mL of 1 M hydrochloric acid and fit the stopper (sensor) at once.
reagent.mg.prep.notes.0: Mg 0.024 g (0.001 mol) → about 24 mL of H₂ (room temperature).
reagent.mg.prep.notes.1: With a 250 mL flask the pressure rise is about 0.1 atm, which is safe.
reagent.mg.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.mg.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.iron.name: Iron powder / steel wool
reagent.iron.useIn: Exothermic reaction (iron powder + salt water + activated charcoal) and iron oxidation (steel wool + vinegar) experiments
reagent.iron.disposal: Rusted iron goes in the regular trash; salt water down the drain.
reagent.iron.studentLimit: No limit (iron powder 10 g or less)
reagent.iron.hazard.0: Fine iron powder is a flammable solid (ignites from sparks)
reagent.iron.hazard.1: Steel wool fibers can prick hands or get in the eyes
reagent.iron.hazard.2: The exothermic reaction (hand warmer) reaches 50–60 °C — hold it by the bag
reagent.iron.handling.0: Keep iron powder away from flames and heaters.
reagent.iron.handling.1: Wear gloves when handling steel wool.
reagent.iron.prep.steps.0: Put 10 g of iron powder, 2 g of activated charcoal and 1 g of salt in a zip bag.
reagent.iron.prep.steps.1: Insert the temperature sensor, sprinkle in 3–5 mL of water, close with a little air inside and shake.
reagent.iron.prep.steps.2: For iron oxidation, soak steel wool in vinegar, wring it out, put it in the flask and close with the pressure sensor.
reagent.iron.prep.notes.0: Oxygen is needed for the heat, so a fully sealed bag cools quickly.
reagent.iron.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.iron.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.nacl.name: Sodium chloride (salt)
reagent.nacl.useIn: Salinity, deep-water circulation, diffusion, pure substances and mixtures, hydrolysis (NaCl solution) and hand warmer experiments
reagent.nacl.hazard.1: Salt water corrodes metals and electrodes, so rinse after use
reagent.nacl.handling.0: Rinse the conductivity electrode with distilled water after use.
reagent.nacl.prep.steps.0: 0.1 M: dissolve 1.46 g of salt in water to 250 mL (Flinn 0.1 M = 5.8 g/L).
reagent.nacl.prep.steps.1: Seawater model 3.5 %: 9 g of salt in 250 mL of water.
reagent.nacl.prep.steps.2: For conductivity, dilute 10× each time to 0.001, 0.01 and 0.1 M.
reagent.nacl.prep.notes.0: Table salt (refined) is sufficient. Sea salt has Mg and Ca impurities, so its conductivity differs slightly.
reagent.nacl.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.nacl.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.nh4cl.name: Ammonium chloride
reagent.nh4cl.useIn: pH of salt solutions (hydrolysis) experiment — 0.1 M solution (acidic, pH about 5)
reagent.nh4cl.disposal: Small amounts (100 g or less per day) down the drain with plenty of water (Flinn #26b).
reagent.nh4cl.hazard.2: Ammonia odor when mixed with bases
reagent.nh4cl.handling.0: Do not mix with NaOH waste in the same container (ammonia release).
reagent.nh4cl.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 1.34 g of ammonium chloride in water and make up to 250 mL.
reagent.nh4cl.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.nh4cl.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.na2co3.name: Sodium carbonate
reagent.na2co3.useIn: pH of salt solutions (hydrolysis) experiment — 0.1 M solution (basic); neutralizer for acid waste
reagent.na2co3.disposal: Neutralize with dilute acid to pH 5–9, then drain with water.
reagent.na2co3.hazard.1: Solution is a weak base (0.1 M, pH about 11.5) — alkali damage if it gets in the eyes
reagent.na2co3.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 2.65 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate in water and make up to 250 mL.
reagent.na2co3.prep.notes.1: Sprinkle the powder to neutralize spilled acid.
reagent.na2co3.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes and go to hospital.
reagent.na2co3.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink.
reagent.naoac.name: Sodium acetate
reagent.naoac.useIn: pH of salt solutions (hydrolysis, weakly basic), acetate buffer and hot pack (optional) experiments
reagent.naoac.hazard.1: Hot packs (supersaturated solution) exceed 50 °C when crystallizing
reagent.naoac.handling.0: Hot pack solution is hot, so wear gloves.
reagent.naoac.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 3.4 g of sodium acetate trihydrate (2.05 g anhydrous) in water and make up to 250 mL.
reagent.naoac.prep.steps.1: Hot pack: add 50 g of trihydrate to 10 mL of water, dissolve completely in a hot water bath and cool without shaking. Adding a seed crystal or striking it hard crystallizes it with heat release.
reagent.naoac.prep.notes.1: Mixing 1:1 with 0.1 M acetic acid gives a pH 4.76 buffer.
reagent.naoac.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.naoac.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.acetatebuffer.name: Acetate buffer solution
reagent.acetatebuffer.useIn: Experiment on whether a buffer holds its pH — add 0.1 M HCl drop by drop and compare with water
reagent.acetatebuffer.disposal: Neutralize with sodium bicarbonate and drain.
reagent.acetatebuffer.hazard.0: Dilute acid level (0.1 M) — mild eye irritation only
reagent.acetatebuffer.handling.0: Add the same volume with the same dropper as for the water control.
reagent.acetatebuffer.prep.steps.0: Mix 50 mL of 0.1 M acetic acid with 50 mL of 0.1 M sodium acetate (equal moles → pH = pKa = 4.76).
reagent.acetatebuffer.prep.steps.1: Check with the pH sensor; for a different pH, change the ratio of salt (more raises pH) to acid (more lowers pH).
reagent.acetatebuffer.prep.notes.0: Buffer capacity is proportional to concentration — 0.1 M for a comparison experiment, 1 M for more resistance.
reagent.acetatebuffer.prep.notes.1: 50 mL of buffer barely changes pH with up to 2–3 mL (about 50 drops) of 0.1 M HCl.
reagent.acetatebuffer.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.acetatebuffer.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.phbuffer.name: pH standard buffers / electrode storage solution
reagent.phbuffer.useIn: pH sensor calibration (pH 7 → 4 order, 2-point) and storage; pH conditions for enzyme experiments
reagent.phbuffer.storage: Sealed bottle, room temperature, away from light.
reagent.phbuffer.hazard.0: Low hazard — commercial buffers contain preservatives and dyes, so do not drink
reagent.phbuffer.hazard.1: pH 10 buffer is a weak base; rinse if it gets in the eyes
reagent.phbuffer.handling.0: Pour out fresh buffer every 2–3 weeks and check the expiry date.
reagent.phbuffer.prep.target: Calibration buffers 30 mL each · storage solution 100 mL
reagent.phbuffer.prep.steps.0: Pour commercial pH 4.00, 7.00 (and 10.00) standard buffers into small cups for use (do not dip the electrode into the bottle).
reagent.phbuffer.prep.steps.1: Storage solution: dissolve 10 g of KCl in 100 mL of pH 4 buffer (Vernier recommendation). Or use commercial 3 M KCl storage solution.
reagent.phbuffer.prep.steps.2: Before and after calibration and between samples, rinse the electrode with distilled water and dab off the water with a tissue.
reagent.phbuffer.prep.notes.0: Leaving the electrode in distilled water for long damages it — fill the storage cap with storage solution and fit it.
reagent.phbuffer.prep.notes.1: Do not pour used buffer back into the bottle; discard it.
reagent.phbuffer.prep.notes.2: Make the pH 4, 7 and 10 conditions for enzyme experiments from the same standards.
reagent.phbuffer.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.phbuffer.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.cacl2.name: Calcium chloride
reagent.cacl2.useIn: Heat of de-icers and hot packs (exothermic dissolution) experiment — solid as is
reagent.cacl2.disposal: Small amounts (100 g or less per day) down the drain with plenty of water (Flinn #26b).
reagent.cacl2.hazard.1: Releases a lot of heat when dissolving in water (10 g anhydrous/50 mL → about +20 °C)
reagent.cacl2.hazard.2: Hygroscopic — absorbs moisture from the air and turns runny
reagent.cacl2.handling.0: Weigh the solid and close the lid at once (hygroscopic).
reagent.cacl2.handling.1: The cup gets hot, so use a styrofoam cup.
reagent.cacl2.prep.steps.0: Put the temperature sensor in 50 mL of water and start measuring.
reagent.cacl2.prep.steps.1: Add 10 g of anhydrous calcium chloride all at once and record for 5 minutes while stirring.
reagent.cacl2.prep.notes.1: De-icer and moisture absorber (new) are mostly calcium chloride, so use as is. A used moisture absorber has already taken up water and releases little heat.
reagent.cacl2.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.cacl2.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.nh4no3.name: Ammonium nitrate
reagent.nh4no3.useIn: Heat of cold packs (endothermic dissolution) experiment — solid as is (or a commercial cold pack)
reagent.nh4no3.storage: Sealed container, locked chemical cabinet away from combustibles, dry.
reagent.nh4no3.disposal: Dilute solutions down the drain with plenty of water (dissolve the solid in water first).
reagent.nh4no3.studentLimit: Students: 10 g or less, or a commercial cold pack
reagent.nh4no3.hazard.0: Oxidizing solid (H272) — do not mix with combustibles (sugar, activated charcoal, paper) or heat
reagent.nh4no3.hazard.2: Large amounts risk explosion — keep 100 g or less at school
reagent.nh4no3.handling.0: Handle away from benches with iron powder, activated charcoal or sugar.
reagent.nh4no3.handling.1: Do not heat; keep purchased and stored quantities to a minimum.
reagent.nh4no3.prep.steps.0: Put the temperature sensor in 50 mL of water and start measuring.
reagent.nh4no3.prep.steps.1: Add 10 g of ammonium nitrate and record for 5 minutes while stirring (about −10 °C).
reagent.nh4no3.prep.notes.0: A commercial instant cold pack (ammonium nitrate or urea) squeezed to burst also works.
reagent.nh4no3.prep.notes.1: Replacing it with urea (fertilizer) is lower risk (about −5 °C).
reagent.nh4no3.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.nh4no3.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.ethanol.name: Ethanol
reagent.ethanol.useIn: Evaporative cooling, intermolecular forces, boiling point, cobalt chloride solvent and hand sanitizer evaporation experiments
reagent.ethanol.storage: Sealed bottle, flammables cabinet (double lock), away from heat sources.
reagent.ethanol.disposal: A few mL: evaporate in a ventilated place or dilute 10× with water and drain. Large amounts: organic waste container.
reagent.ethanol.studentLimit: Students: 50 mL or less, only where there are no flames
reagent.ethanol.hazard.0: Flammable liquid (H225) — keep away from flames, heaters and sparks
reagent.ethanol.hazard.2: Breathing vapor for long causes dizziness — ventilate
reagent.ethanol.handling.0: No flames within 1 m of the bench; close the lid right after use.
reagent.ethanol.handling.1: Give out no more than 50 mL per group.
reagent.ethanol.prep.steps.0: Use antiseptic ethanol (70–83 %) or reagent ethanol (95 %) as is.
reagent.ethanol.prep.steps.1: For evaporation comparisons, use the same volume (5 mL) on the same dish or gauze.
reagent.ethanol.prep.steps.2: Boiling-point experiments must use a water bath (no alcohol lamp or direct heating).
reagent.ethanol.prep.notes.0: Hand sanitizer is 60–80 % ethanol mixed with moisturizer, so it evaporates a little slower.
reagent.ethanol.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes.
reagent.ethanol.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and go to hospital (reagent and denatured alcohol may contain methanol).
reagent.acetone.name: Acetone
reagent.acetone.useIn: Intermolecular forces and evaporative cooling experiment — enough to wet gauze (2–3 mL)
reagent.acetone.storage: Sealed glass bottle, flammables cabinet, away from heat sources.
reagent.acetone.disposal: A few mL: evaporate in a ventilated place. Large amounts: organic waste container (never drain).
reagent.acetone.studentLimit: Students: 10 mL or less, dispensed by the teacher, where there are no flames
reagent.acetone.hazard.0: Flammable liquid (H225, flash point −17 °C) — never near flames
reagent.acetone.hazard.1: Eye irritation (H319); vapor causes drowsiness and dizziness (H336)
reagent.acetone.handling.0: Open the windows and switch off all heaters and heating equipment before use.
reagent.acetone.handling.1: Dries the skin on contact, so wash it off.
reagent.acetone.prep.steps.0: Dispense only 10 mL into a small glass bottle and close the lid.
reagent.acetone.prep.steps.1: Wet the sensor gauze with 2–3 mL using a dropper and close the lid at once.
reagent.acetone.prep.notes.0: Glass or metal containers only (melts plastic cups).
reagent.acetone.prep.notes.1: Evaporates fastest, so the temperature drops the most (boiling point 56 °C).
reagent.acetone.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes.
reagent.acetone.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and go to hospital. Do not induce vomiting.
reagent.stearic.name: Stearic acid (palmitic acid)
reagent.stearic.useIn: Cooling curve (freezing point) experiment — 5–10 g of solid in a test tube
reagent.stearic.disposal: Scrape out the solidified wax into the regular trash. Never pour down the drain.
reagent.stearic.hazard.1: Splashes of the molten liquid (70 °C) cause burns — melt only in a water bath
reagent.stearic.hazard.2: Blocks drains when it solidifies — never drain
reagent.stearic.handling.0: Do not heat directly (smoke and fire).
reagent.stearic.handling.1: Hold the test tube with tongs.
reagent.stearic.prep.steps.0: Put 5–10 g of stearic acid (4–5 cm deep) in a test tube and melt completely in an 80 °C water bath.
reagent.stearic.prep.steps.1: Insert the temperature sensor in the center, take out the test tube and stand it in air (or room-temperature water) to cool.
reagent.stearic.prep.steps.2: The flat section where it starts to solidify is the freezing point (stearic acid about 69 °C, palmitic acid about 63 °C, lauric acid about 44 °C).
reagent.stearic.prep.notes.0: Lauric acid has a lower freezing point, so it finishes sooner.
reagent.stearic.prep.notes.1: Remove the sensor before it solidifies, or melt it again next time to remove it.
reagent.stearic.firstAid.skin: For burns, cool in cold water for at least 10 minutes; do not force off solidified wax.
reagent.dryice.name: Dry ice
reagent.dryice.useIn: State change and mass (sublimation) experiment — small pieces in a zip bag
reagent.dryice.storage: Styrofoam box (lid not tightly closed); use the same day.
reagent.dryice.disposal: Leave in a ventilated place to sublime. Do not put in a sink or toilet.
reagent.dryice.studentLimit: Students: small pieces with tongs and gloves only; the teacher breaks it up
reagent.dryice.hazard.0: −78.5 °C — frostbite if touched with bare hands
reagent.dryice.hazard.1: Bursts from pressure in a sealed container (never do this)
reagent.dryice.hazard.2: Lots subliming in a small room can cause CO₂ asphyxiation — ventilate
reagent.dryice.handling.1: Students handle it only with tongs and gloves and never put it in the mouth.
reagent.dryice.handling.2: Do not put it in a stoppered glass or PET bottle.
reagent.dryice.prep.steps.0: Wrap the dry ice in a towel and break off small pieces (2–3 cm) with a hammer (teacher).
reagent.dryice.prep.steps.1: Put it in a zip bag with tongs, squeeze out the air and close — open the bag if it inflates.
reagent.dryice.prep.steps.2: Place it on the load cell and watch the mass change.
reagent.dryice.prep.notes.0: A 10 g piece gives about 5 L of CO₂ when it sublimes — the zip bag inflates quickly.
reagent.dryice.prep.notes.1: Without dry ice, do the same experiment with ice + olive oil (melting).
reagent.dryice.firstAid.skin: Soak the frostbitten area in lukewarm water (40 °C or less). Do not rub.
reagent.dryice.firstAid.eye: Rinse with lukewarm running water and go to hospital.
reagent.dryice.firstAid.swallow: Go to hospital or call emergency services immediately (stomach distension).
reagent.sugar.name: Sugar, glucose, lactose
reagent.sugar.useIn: Yeast fermentation, metabolic heat and respiration (CO₂) experiments — 5–10 % solution
reagent.sugar.hazard.1: Watch for burns from hot sugar solution
reagent.sugar.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 10 g of sugar (or glucose or lactose) in 100 mL of lukewarm water (30–35 °C).
reagent.sugar.prep.steps.1: To compare sugar types, use the same mass (10 g).
reagent.sugar.prep.notes.0: Yeast can barely use lactose, so it serves as the control.
reagent.sugar.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.sugar.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.yeast.name: Yeast
reagent.yeast.useIn: Fermentation, metabolic heat and hydrogen peroxide catalyst (catalase) experiments
reagent.yeast.storage: Keep dry yeast sealed and refrigerated.
reagent.yeast.hazard.1: Fermentation CO₂ raises the pressure in closed containers — leave the stopper loose
reagent.yeast.handling.0: In closed-container experiments, check that gas escapes through the sensor hole.
reagent.yeast.prep.steps.0: Add 3 g of dry yeast (1 teaspoon) and 5 g of sugar to 100 mL of lukewarm water (30–35 °C), stir and leave for 10 minutes.
reagent.yeast.prep.steps.1: Use in the experiment as soon as it starts to foam.
reagent.yeast.prep.notes.1: As a hydrogen peroxide catalyst, add 5 mL of yeast suspension to 20 mL of 3 % H₂O₂.
reagent.yeast.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.yeast.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.charcoal.name: Activated charcoal
reagent.charcoal.useIn: Carbon capture (CO₂ adsorption) and hand warmer (iron powder catalyst) experiments
reagent.charcoal.hazard.1: Airborne powder irritates the airways — handle damp
reagent.charcoal.hazard.2: Dry powder can catch fire from sparks
reagent.charcoal.handling.0: Pour slowly so the powder does not blow around.
reagent.charcoal.prep.steps.0: Spread 20–30 g of activated charcoal (aquarium or water-filter grade) on a dish and put it in a sealed box.
reagent.charcoal.prep.steps.1: For the hand warmer, mix 2 g with the iron powder.
reagent.charcoal.prep.notes.0: Charcoal that has absorbed moisture regains its adsorption after drying in a 100 °C oven.
reagent.charcoal.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.charcoal.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.fertilizer.name: Plant fertilizer (liquid fertilizer)
reagent.fertilizer.useIn: Algal bloom (eutrophication) experiment — add different fertilizer concentrations to pond water
reagent.fertilizer.disposal: After the experiment, give the water to flower beds or pots (not to streams).
reagent.fertilizer.hazard.0: May irritate eyes and skin; do not swallow (check the product label)
reagent.fertilizer.hazard.1: Nitrates and phosphates cause eutrophication — do not pour large amounts into streams or drains
reagent.fertilizer.handling.0: Pond water contains microbes, so wash hands when finished.
reagent.fertilizer.prep.steps.0: Put 500 mL of pond water in each of 3 clear bottles.
reagent.fertilizer.prep.steps.1: Add 0 mL, 1 mL and 5 mL of liquid fertilizer (commercial houseplant grade) and leave under light for 1–2 weeks.
reagent.fertilizer.prep.steps.2: Record the turbidity daily with the color sensor and light sensor.
reagent.fertilizer.prep.notes.0: For solid fertilizer, 0.5 g and 2.5 g per 1 L.
reagent.fertilizer.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.fertilizer.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.vitc.name: Vitamin C solution (ascorbic acid)
reagent.vitc.hazard.1: Solution is weakly acidic — rinse if it gets in the eyes
reagent.vitc.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 1 g of ascorbic acid (or one crushed 1000 mg vitamin C tablet) in 100 mL of water.
reagent.vitc.prep.steps.1: Brush onto a cut apple surface; brush only water on another piece.
reagent.vitc.prep.notes.0: Oxidizes in air, so prepare on the day.
reagent.vitc.prep.notes.1: Lemon juice (vitamin C + citric acid) can also be compared.
reagent.vitc.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.vitc.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.lead.name: Lead shot
reagent.lead.useIn: Joule's mechanical equivalent of heat experiment (dropped in an insulated tube) — replacing with sand recommended
reagent.lead.storage: Sealed, labeled container out of students' reach.
reagent.lead.disposal: Not in the regular trash — metal recycling or designated waste (Flinn #27f).
reagent.lead.studentLimit: Students: with gloves and inside a closed tube only; replace with sand if possible
reagent.lead.hazard.0: Reproductive toxicity 1A (H360); nerve, blood and kidney damage with repeated exposure (H372); suspected carcinogen (H351)
reagent.lead.hazard.1: Surface dust (lead oxide) gets on hands and into the mouth — the main route
reagent.lead.hazard.2: Pregnant people should not handle it
reagent.lead.handling.0: Wear gloves and wash hands with soap when finished.
reagent.lead.handling.1: Do not put it in the mouth or keep it near food.
reagent.lead.handling.2: If dust forms, wipe with a damp tissue and seal it.
reagent.lead.prep.steps.0: Replace with dry sand or steel balls (steel BBs) if possible (the temperature will not rise as much as with lead, which has a low specific heat, but the principle is the same).
reagent.lead.prep.steps.1: When using lead, keep it inside a capped tube and do not spill it.
reagent.lead.prep.notes.0: Dropping 1 kg of lead 20 times from a height of 1 m raises it about 1.5 °C.
reagent.lead.firstAid.swallow: If swallowed, go to hospital or call emergency services (lead poisoning).
reagent.phenolphthalein.name: Phenolphthalein solution
reagent.phenolphthalein.useIn: Color indicator for acid–base titration (pink at pH 8.2–10) — for comparison with sensor titration
reagent.phenolphthalein.disposal: Neutralize titration waste and drain (indicator is a tiny amount). Indicator stock goes to the organic waste container.
reagent.phenolphthalein.studentLimit: Students: prepared indicator in drops only; solid teacher only
reagent.phenolphthalein.hazard.0: Reproductive toxicity 1B (H360), suspected carcinogen (H351), suspected mutagen (H341) — solid and concentrated solution
reagent.phenolphthalein.hazard.2: The dilute solution used in 1–2 drops is low hazard
reagent.phenolphthalein.handling.0: Teacher only handles the solid; do not inhale the powder.
reagent.phenolphthalein.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 1 g of phenolphthalein in 50 mL of ethanol (95 %), then add 50 mL of water.
reagent.phenolphthalein.prep.steps.1: Keep in a dropper bottle and use only 1–2 drops at a time.
reagent.phenolphthalein.prep.notes.1: Buying a commercial indicator is the safest option.
reagent.phenolphthalein.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.phenolphthalein.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
reagent.btb.name: BTB solution (bromothymol blue)
reagent.btb.useIn: Color indicator for CO₂, photosynthesis and neutralization experiments (yellow at pH 6.0 to blue at 7.6) — for comparison with the pH sensor
reagent.btb.hazard.0: Dilute indicator is low hazard — stains clothing
reagent.btb.handling.0: Commercial BTB solution can be used as is.
reagent.btb.prep.steps.0: Dissolve 0.1 g of BTB in 16 mL of 0.01 M NaOH (or 8 mL of ethanol).
reagent.btb.prep.steps.1: Add water to 250 mL and it turns green (neutral) — if yellow, add 0.01 M NaOH drop by drop.
reagent.btb.prep.notes.1: Blowing exhaled breath in turns it yellow; Elodea photosynthesis turns it blue again.
reagent.btb.firstAid.eye: Rinse under running water for at least 15 minutes; see a doctor if discomfort persists.
reagent.btb.firstAid.swallow: Rinse the mouth and give water to drink. See a doctor if a large amount was swallowed or symptoms appear.
guide.common.6: High-current sensors (100–180 mA) such as gas (MQ), particulate matter and CO₂ (MH-Z19) can share USB power (500 mA) only two at a time. If you need more, or the values jump and the board restarts, plug a 7–12 V adapter into the DC jack or VIN.
board.uno-r4-wifi.notes.1: On USB power the 5V pin gives about 4.7 V. Sensors that output an absolute voltage, such as the LM35, TMP36 and pH modules, may read about 5 % low; check with [Sensor check] and do a 1-point calibration, or use DC jack power (7–12 V).
board.nano-r4.notes.1: The 3V3 pin supplies about 150 mA in total for all modules. Plug high-current modules such as CO₂ and particulate matter sensors into the 5V pin if they are marked 'VIN 3–5 V'.
board.mega-2560.notes.3: Plug the thermocouple (MAX6675) and PT100 (MAX31865) into D10, D11, D12 and D13 (not the SPI D50–D53 or ICSP printed on the board).
board.nano-esp32.notes.1: Power 5 V-only sensors from the VBUS pin (5 V only on USB power), and bring the signal down to 3.3 V or less with a voltage divider.
board.nano-esp32.notes.2: I2C is on A4/A5, UART sensors on D0/D1 (Serial0). Firmware support is not ready yet, so the UART, pulse and thermocouple pins are not yet verified.
board.giga-r1.notes.1: It has a 5V pin that can power 5 V-only sensors, but the signal must be brought down to 3.3 V or less.
board.uno-q.notes.1: Analog inputs are 0–3.3 V. Power sensors that run on 3.3 V from the [3.3V] pin, and sensors marked '5 V only' from the [5V] pin on the power header, but keep the signal at or below 3.3 V (5 V on A0–A5 or D3 will damage the board).
board.uno-q.notes.2: UART sensors (particulate matter, MH-Z19) have not yet been tested on the UNO Q (D0/D1 are 3.3 V).
board.uno-q.notes.3: This is a 3.3 V board. Do not connect the signal wire of 5 V modules (MQ gas, HC-SR04, 5 V-only pH modules, etc.) directly.
board.uno-q.notes.4: Turn the board on and wait about 1 minute; the Bluetooth name ChemDict-01 will appear (the Linux system on the board has to start first).
board.uno-q.notes.5: First time only: in the Arduino IDE, install 'Arduino UNO Q Boards' from the Boards Manager, and ArduinoBLE 2.1.0 or later, Arduino_RouterBridge, OneWire and DallasTemperature from the Library Manager → open chemdict_lab.ino and upload with the board set to 'Arduino UNO Q'.
board.uno-q.notes.6: Calibration values and the group number are saved in the board's flash memory and stay after power-off.
conn.analog-5v.name: Analog 3-wire (5 V only)
conn.analog-5v.steps.0: You can use A1–A3 instead of A0. Tap the same port in 'Port' and the app sets it up automatically.
conn.analog-5v.cautions.0: This module needs a 5 V supply. On 3.3 V boards (UNO Q, Nano ESP32, etc.) plug VCC into the board's 5V (VBUS) pin; for modules whose signal goes above 3.3 V, add a 2:1 divider (10 kΩ+10 kΩ) on the signal wire, then set the scale to 2× in [Calibrate sensor].
conn.qwiic.cautions.0: Qwiic is 3.3 V. The SDA/SCL pins of the UNO R3, Nano, Mega and Leonardo have internal pull-ups to 5 V, so connecting a 3.3 V-only module such as a Modulino directly puts 5 V on it. Always use an I2C level shifter (or a Qwiic shield). Only modules marked 'VIN 3–5 V' may be connected directly.
conn.qwiic.cautions.1: The 3.3V pin supplies about 150 mA in total for all modules. Plug high-current modules such as CO₂ (SCD4x) and particulate matter sensors into the 5V pin if they are marked 'VIN 3–5 V'; otherwise use only one.
conn.i2c.cautions.1: The 3.3V pin supplies about 150 mA in total for all modules. Plug high-current modules (CO₂, particulate matter) into the 5V pin if they are marked 'VIN 3–5 V'.
conn.i2c.cautions.2: If two sensors with the same address are on one bus, only one is detected. On the UNO R4 WiFi, Nano R4 and UNO Q the Qwiic connector and the SDA/SCL pins are separate buses, so put one on each and both will work.
conn.pulse.cautions.0: Works only on the UNO R4, Nano R4, Mega and UNO Q (the UNO R3 and Nano do not have enough memory).
conn.pulse.cautions.2: Never put 5 V into D3 on a 3.3 V board (UNO Q, etc.). Pulse sensors usually output pulses as high as their supply voltage, so add a 1 kΩ+2 kΩ divider on the signal wire or use only sensors that run on 3.3 V.
conn.spi-rtd.cautions.1: If the module is not marked 'VIN 3–5 V' (no regulator), plug VIN into the 3.3V pin, not 5V (the MAX31865 chip runs on 3.0–3.6 V).
conn.uart.cautions.2: Only one UART sensor works at a time (there is only one Serial1). It needs 5 V and 100–150 mA, so on USB power do not use it together with other high-current sensors.
conn.ultrasonic.name: Ultrasonic 4-wire (5 V only)
conn.ultrasonic.cautions.0: Needs a 5 V supply (it does not work on 3.3 V). On a 3.3 V board plug VCC into the 5V (VBUS) pin and bring the ECHO signal (5 V) down with a 1 kΩ+2 kΩ divider.

conn.i2c-5v.steps.0: If the module has a Qwiic or STEMMA QT connector, you can connect it with a Qwiic cable.
conn.i2c-5v.steps.1: Several modules can share the same I2C lines (if their addresses differ).
conn.i2c-5v.cautions.0: Connect VDD to the 5V pin to measure up to ±4 V. SDA/SCL run at the board voltage.
