trouble.i2c-missing.title: My I2C (Qwiic) sensor is not found
trouble.i2c-missing.steps.0: Check that the Qwiic cable is pushed in until it clicks (either way round works).
trouble.i2c-missing.steps.1: If two sensors with the same address (e.g. color TCS34725 and distance VL53L0X, both 0x29) are on one bus, only one shows up. On the UNO R4 WiFi, Nano R4 and UNO Q, put one on the Qwiic connector and the other on the SDA/SCL pins.
trouble.i2c-missing.steps.2: Plugging a 3.3 V-only module (Modulino, etc.) into the SDA/SCL of a UNO R3, Nano, Mega or Leonardo without a level shifter means it is not detected or gets damaged.
trouble.i2c-missing.steps.3: Check that the module's VCC is on 3.3V (or 5V only for 'VIN 3–5 V' modules), and that SDA and SCL are not swapped.
trouble.i2c-missing.steps.4: On boards where A4/A5 are I2C (UNO R3, Nano, Nano R4), you cannot also plug analog sensors into those pins.
trouble.temp-stuck.title: Temperature stuck at 85 °C or −127 °C (DS18B20)
trouble.temp-stuck.steps.0: −127 °C means 'no sensor'. Check the DATA, VCC and GND wires and the 4.7 kΩ pull-up resistor (DATA–VCC).
trouble.temp-stuck.steps.1: 85 °C is the initial value right after power-up. If it stays there, the power or pull-up is too weak — with long wires or several sensors, always connect VCC (2-wire parasite power will not work).
trouble.temp-stuck.steps.2: Unplug and replug the USB, then press [Rescan sensors].
trouble.dht-empty.title: Temperature/humidity (DHT) values are empty
trouble.dht-empty.steps.0: There are no values for the first 2–3 seconds. A DHT22 cannot be read more often than every 2 s, a DHT11 every 1 s (the app already handles this).
trouble.dht-empty.steps.1: A bare 4-pin sensor (not a module) needs a 10 kΩ pull-up between DATA and VCC. On 3-pin modules, check the S / + / − markings.
trouble.dht-empty.steps.2: Keep wires short (within 1 m). Long wires give empty or jumping values.
trouble.power-budget.title: With several sensors plugged in, the board restarts or the values fluctuate
trouble.power-budget.steps.0: USB power is limited to 500 mA. Use at most two of MQ gas (about 150 mA), particulate matter (100 mA) and MH-Z19 (150 mA) sensors together.
trouble.power-budget.steps.1: Plug a 7–12 V adapter into the DC jack or VIN to fix it.
trouble.power-budget.steps.2: The Nano R4's 3V3 pin supplies up to 150 mA. If you connect many I2C modules, move 'VIN 3–5 V' modules to the 5V pin.
bb.circuit.series-ref.caution: Use at most 3 cells (4.5 V) on 5 V boards and 2 cells (3 V) on 3.3 V boards (UNO Q, etc.). A0 and A1 must never receive more than the board voltage.
check.T.name: Temperature (DS18B20)
check.T.response: In water 10–30 s, in air 1–2 min
check.T.errorNote: Error = measured value − reference value. Within ±0.5 °C in ice water matches the spec; within ±1 °C is good enough for school experiments.
check.T.ref.0: Ice water — add a little water to crushed ice, stir for 1 minute, then put the sensor between the ice pieces
check.T.ref.0.note: The most reliable reference point. With too much water it reads 2–4 °C
check.T.ref.1: Boiling water (1 atm) — keep the sensor tip off the bottom and sides
check.T.ref.1.note: Boils about 0.3 °C lower for every 1 kPa of lower pressure (high altitude, low pressure)
check.T.ref.2.note: Leave it for 2 minutes or more, away from air-conditioner or heater drafts
check.T.ref.3.note: Contact sensors read slightly below skin temperature
check.T.test.0: If the value is stuck at −127, 85, −196 or 0, check the signal wire, pull-up resistor and power (these numbers mean 'no reading', not a measurement).
check.T.test.1: Indoors, fluctuation within ±0.3 °C over 1 minute is normal (sensor noise).
check.T.test.2: Hold it in your hand for 1 minute and check that it rises, then falls when you let go (response time: in water 10–30 s, in air 1–2 min).
check.T.test.3: Pass if within ±1 °C at 0 °C in ice water. If not, set zero in [Calibrate sensor] or replace the sensor.
check.T.fail.0: Stuck at −127 °C → sensor not found (DATA, GND, VCC, 4.7 kΩ pull-up)
check.T.fail.1: Stuck at 85 °C → value right after a power reset. Power or pull-up too weak
check.T.fail.2: Value jumps every few seconds → loose wire or long cable (5 m or more)
check.TL.name: Temperature (LM35)
check.TL.errorNote: Analog sensors add the board's reference-voltage error (1–2 %), so a 2-point calibration with ice water and boiling water gets you to ±0.5 °C.
check.TL.ref.0: Ice water — add a little water to crushed ice, stir for 1 minute, then put the sensor between the ice pieces
check.TL.ref.0.note: The most reliable reference point. With too much water it reads 2–4 °C
check.TL.ref.1: Boiling water (1 atm) — keep the sensor tip off the bottom and sides
check.TL.ref.1.note: Boils about 0.3 °C lower for every 1 kPa of lower pressure (high altitude, low pressure)
check.TL.ref.2.note: Leave it for 2 minutes or more, away from air-conditioner or heater drafts
check.TL.ref.3.note: Contact sensors read slightly below skin temperature
check.TL.test.0: If the value is stuck at −127, 85, −196 or 0, check the signal wire, pull-up resistor and power (these numbers mean 'no reading', not a measurement).
check.TL.test.1: Indoors, fluctuation within ±0.3 °C over 1 minute is normal (sensor noise).
check.TL.test.2: Hold it in your hand for 1 minute and check that it rises, then falls when you let go (response time: in water 10–30 s, in air 1–2 min).
check.TL.test.3: Pass if within ±1 °C at 0 °C in ice water. If not, set zero in [Calibrate sensor] or replace the sensor.
check.TL.fail.0: Stuck near 0 °C → output pin unconnected, or supply is 3.3 V (the LM35 needs 4 V or more)
check.TL.fail.1: Stuck at 150 °C → VCC and OUT swapped
check.TM36.name: Temperature (TMP36)
check.TM36.errorNote: 0.75 V at 25 °C, 10 mV/°C. The basic error is ±2 °C, so a 2-point calibration is needed.
check.TM36.ref.0: Ice water — add a little water to crushed ice, stir for 1 minute, then put the sensor between the ice pieces
check.TM36.ref.0.note: The most reliable reference point. With too much water it reads 2–4 °C
check.TM36.ref.1: Boiling water (1 atm) — keep the sensor tip off the bottom and sides
check.TM36.ref.1.note: Boils about 0.3 °C lower for every 1 kPa of lower pressure (high altitude, low pressure)
check.TM36.ref.2.note: Leave it for 2 minutes or more, away from air-conditioner or heater drafts
check.TM36.ref.3.note: Contact sensors read slightly below skin temperature
check.TM36.test.0: If the value is stuck at −127, 85, −196 or 0, check the signal wire, pull-up resistor and power (these numbers mean 'no reading', not a measurement).
check.TM36.test.1: Indoors, fluctuation within ±0.3 °C over 1 minute is normal (sensor noise).
check.TM36.test.2: Hold it in your hand for 1 minute and check that it rises, then falls when you let go (response time: in water 10–30 s, in air 1–2 min).
check.TM36.test.3: Pass if within ±1 °C at 0 °C in ice water. If not, set zero in [Calibrate sensor] or replace the sensor.
check.TM36.fail.1: Off by 10 °C or more → check the pin order (+V, OUT, GND with the flat side facing you)
check.TNTC.name: Temperature (NTC thermistor)
check.TNTC.accuracy: ±1 °C (with an accurate B value), ±2 °C at both ends
check.TNTC.errorNote: If the B value (3950 K, etc.) is off, the error grows the further you are from 25 °C. Do a 2-point calibration with ice water and boiling water.
check.TNTC.ref.0: Ice water — add a little water to crushed ice, stir for 1 minute, then put the sensor between the ice pieces
check.TNTC.ref.0.note: The most reliable reference point. With too much water it reads 2–4 °C
check.TNTC.ref.1: Boiling water (1 atm) — keep the sensor tip off the bottom and sides
check.TNTC.ref.1.note: Boils about 0.3 °C lower for every 1 kPa of lower pressure (high altitude, low pressure)
check.TNTC.ref.2.note: Leave it for 2 minutes or more, away from air-conditioner or heater drafts
check.TNTC.ref.3.note: Contact sensors read slightly below skin temperature
check.TNTC.test.0: If the value is stuck at −127, 85, −196 or 0, check the signal wire, pull-up resistor and power (these numbers mean 'no reading', not a measurement).
check.TNTC.test.1: Indoors, fluctuation within ±0.3 °C over 1 minute is normal (sensor noise).
check.TNTC.test.2: Hold it in your hand for 1 minute and check that it rises, then falls when you let go (response time: in water 10–30 s, in air 1–2 min).
check.TNTC.test.3: Pass if within ±1 °C at 0 °C in ice water. If not, set zero in [Calibrate sensor] or replace the sensor.
check.TNTC.fail.0: Stuck at an end value (−20 or 105) → divider resistor (10 kΩ) missing or broken wire
check.TK.name: Thermocouple temperature (K-type, MAX6675)
check.TK.errorNote: At low temperatures it is ±3 °C, so it is not suitable for freezing-point measurements. Use it for heating and combustion experiments above 100 °C.
check.TK.ref.0.note: Large error at low temperatures — for reference only
check.TK.ref.2.note: Compensation for the module's own temperature (cold junction) takes 1–2 minutes
check.TK.ref.3: Outer part of an alcohol-lamp flame
check.TK.ref.3.note: Varies a lot with position — just check that it changes
check.TK.test.0: If + and − are swapped, the temperature goes down when heated. Hold a lighter flame to it for 1 second and check that it rises.
check.TK.test.1: 97–103 °C in boiling water is normal. If the thermocouple junction is loose, the value jumps or drops to 0.
check.TK.test.2: Unplug the sensor at room temperature and you get 0 or 'NaN' → the open-circuit detection works.
check.TK.fail.0: Stuck at 0 °C → thermocouple wire disconnected (open-circuit detection)
check.TK.fail.1: Temperature moves the wrong way → + and − swapped
check.TK.fail.2: Value jumps in 1–2 °C steps → 0.25 °C resolution plus noise — normal
check.TIR.name: Non-contact infrared temperature (MLX90614)
check.TIR.errorNote: It outputs two values, object temperature and ambient temperature (the sensor itself); the app uses the object temperature.
check.TIR.ref.3.note: Steam gets in the way, so it reads low
check.TIR.test.0: Hold your palm 3 cm in front: it should read about 33 °C at once and return to room temperature as soon as you move it away.
check.TIR.test.1: At larger distances the background enters the field of view (90°) and the value drops → measure a 1 cm-wide object from within 1 cm.
check.TIR.test.2: Shiny metal has low emissivity and reads lower than it really is — stick on black tape and measure that.
check.TIR.fail.0: Value does not change → I2C (SDA/SCL) swapped or address 0x5A conflict
check.TA.name: Air temperature (DHT22 / BME280)
check.TA.errorNote: The DHT11 is ±2 °C, so use a DHT22 or BME280 for precise experiments.
check.TA.ref.1.note: Only the air temperature rises, so it changes just a little
check.TA.ref.2: Air 1 cm above ice water (covered with plastic wrap)
check.TA.ref.2.note: Do not put the sensor in the water
check.TA.test.0: A DHT gives no value if read more often than every 2 s (1 s for the DHT11). The app reads every 2 s.
check.TA.test.1: Breathe hard on it: temperature rises 1–3 °C and humidity jumps above 90 %, then both return over 2–3 minutes.
check.TA.test.2: Within ±1 °C of another thermometer in the same spot is normal.
check.TA.fail.0: No value (NaN) → DATA pin, pull-up (4.7–10 kΩ), read interval
check.TA.fail.1: Always the same value → sensor not responding, check power
check.RH.name: Humidity (DHT22 / BME280)
check.RH.errorNote: ±3 %RH is good for a humidity sensor. Relative humidity changes with temperature, so record temperature as well.
check.RH.ref.0: Above saturated salt water (NaCl) — sealed container, 25 °C, 1 hour or more
check.RH.ref.1: Breathe on the sensor for 3 s
check.RH.ref.3: Sealed container covered with a wet towel (30 min)
check.RH.test.0: Breathe on it: it should jump above 90 % at once and return to normal within 2–3 minutes.
check.RH.test.1: 71–79 % in the saturated-salt container is normal. If not, subtract the difference when you record (the app cannot calibrate this).
check.RH.test.2: Put two sensors side by side; if they differ by 5 % or more, one of them is wrong.
check.RH.fail.0: Stays at 100 % for a long time → condensation on the sensor. Dry it and try again
check.BP.name: Air pressure (BMP280 / BME280)
check.BP.errorNote: Absolute error ±0.1 kPa; changes are measured to ±0.01 kPa, which is very precise. You can see weather changes (0.5–1 kPa per day).
check.BP.ref.0: Classroom air (compare with the Korea Meteorological Administration station pressure)
check.BP.ref.0.note: Compare with 'station pressure', not sea-level pressure. About 1.2 kPa lower for every 100 m of height
check.BP.ref.1: Korea Meteorological Administration station pressure (nearest station)
check.BP.ref.1.note: Enter the weather-service value as the expected value and compare
check.BP.ref.2: Move from the 1st to the 3rd floor (about 8 m)
check.BP.ref.2.note: Change: −0.12 kPa per 10 m (the sensor is precise enough to see floor differences)
check.BP.test.0: Lift the sensor 1 m and it drops by about 0.012 kPa — normal if the third decimal place changes.
check.BP.test.1: Within ±0.3 kPa of the weather service's 'station pressure' is normal. Compared with sea-level pressure (usually 101–102) it reads lower by the altitude difference.
check.BP.test.2: Put it in a syringe and press the plunger: it should rise at once.
check.BP.fail.0: No value → I2C address (0x76/0x77) or 3.3 V supply
check.BP.fail.1: Stuck below 30 kPa or above 110 kPa → damaged sensor or read failure
check.P.name: Gas pressure (MPX5700, etc.)
check.P.errorNote: Absolute accuracy is low (±2.5 %), but linearity is good, so after a 1-point calibration it is good enough for Boyle's law and Charles's law comparisons.
check.P.ref.0: Open to the air (weather-service station pressure)
check.P.ref.0.note: Reference for zero calibration. Enter the weather-service value as the expected value
check.P.ref.1.note: Boyle's law: half the volume → twice the pressure
check.P.test.0: Open it to the air and compare with the weather-service station pressure → if they differ by more than 3 kPa, do a 1-point (zero) calibration in [Calibrate sensor].
check.P.test.1: Press the syringe plunger: it should rise at once and return to the original value when released (a leak makes it fall slowly).
check.P.test.2: Compare with the volume at which the pressure is halved; if P·V is constant within ±5 %, both the sensor and the seal are fine.
check.P.fail.0: Value does not change → hose disconnected or output pin unconnected
check.P.fail.1: Stuck at 0 or 700 → needs a 5 V supply (does not work on 3.3 V boards)
check.CO2.name: Carbon dioxide (SCD40/41, MH-Z19)
check.CO2.response: SCD4x every 5 s, settles in 1–2 min; MH-Z19 warm-up 1 min (fully 3 min)
check.CO2.errorNote: Error = 50 ppm + 5 % of the reading. Experiments that compare changes (how fast ppm rises and falls with fermentation, photosynthesis or respiration) are more accurate than absolute values.
check.CO2.ref.0: Outdoor air (outside the window, 3 min in a breezy spot)
check.CO2.ref.0.note: Global average about 425 ppm (2026). Do forced recalibration (FRC) here
check.CO2.ref.1.note: Ventilate above 1000 ppm (Korean school health law: 1000 ppm or less)
check.CO2.ref.2.note: Exhaled breath is about 40000 ppm → jumps to the sensor maximum and comes down over 2–5 minutes
check.CO2.test.0: 1–3 minutes after power-on, once the value is stable, 400–470 ppm in outdoor air is normal.
check.CO2.test.1: Breathe on it: it should jump above 2000 ppm at once. If not, check whether the sensor is somewhere air cannot reach it (inside a box).
check.CO2.test.2: The SCD4x has automatic self-calibration (ASC) on, so it must see outdoor-air levels (400s) about once a week. Leaving it in a closed classroom shifts its baseline.
check.CO2.fail.0: 0 ppm or no value → I2C address 0x62 (SCD4x) or UART crossover (MH-Z19 TX→RX)
check.CO2.fail.1: Stuck at 400 ppm → the MH-Z19's automatic zero set a closed room as 400 → leave it in outdoor air for 1 week, or turn ABC off
check.O2.name: Oxygen concentration (electrochemical)
check.O2.errorNote: Calibrated in air at 20.9 %, the 15–21 % range is reliable to ±0.5 %p. Photosynthesis, respiration and combustion experiments fall in this range.
check.O2.ref.1: Collect exhaled breath in a bag and put the sensor in it
check.O2.ref.2: Glass jar with a lit candle (after the flame goes out)
check.O2.ref.2.note: Combustion does not use up all the oxygen — the flame goes out at 15–17 %
check.O2.test.0: 20.9 ±1 % in air is normal. If not, do a 1-point calibration with air at 20.9 % in [Calibrate sensor].
check.O2.test.1: Put it in a bag of exhaled breath: it should fall to around 16 % within 1 minute.
check.O2.test.2: Electrochemical cells last 1–2 years — if the value in air keeps getting lower, it is time to replace it.
check.O2.fail.0: Stuck at 0 % → output pin unconnected or cell worn out
check.O2.fail.1: Stuck at 25 % → too much gain or a power problem
check.LUX.name: Illuminance (BH1750 / TSL2591 / VEML7700)
check.LUX.errorNote: Absolute illuminance is ±20 %, but relative measurements with the same sensor (distance, filter, change over time) are precise to ±2 %.
check.LUX.ref.0: On a classroom desk (fluorescent / LED lights on)
check.LUX.ref.3: By the window on a cloudy day
check.LUX.test.0: 0–2 lx when covered by your hand and 1000 lx or more with a flashlight at 10 cm is normal.
check.LUX.test.1: Doubling the distance from 10 cm to 20 cm should cut it to about 1/4 (inverse-square law, ±20 %).
check.LUX.test.2: Within ±30 % of a smartphone light-meter app in the same spot is normal (smartphones are ±20 % too).
check.LUX.fail.0: Stuck at 0 → I2C address (0x23/0x5C), ADDR pin
check.L.name: Brightness (photoresistor / photodiode, relative)
check.L.response: Photoresistor 0.1 s (slow when it gets darker)
check.L.errorNote: Read it as '% of the starting value', not absolute brightness. For the Beer–Lambert law, make a calculated column with log(starting value / measured value).
check.L.ref.1.note: Depends on the module and resistor value
check.L.test.0: Below 5 % when covered and above 85 % with a flashlight is normal. Values in between differ from module to module.
check.L.test.1: Photoresistors (CdS) lag 1–2 s when it gets darker — for flickering light use a photodiode or lux sensor.
check.L.test.2: For absorbance experiments, keep the same distance and light source inside a black container, set the 'blank (water)' to 100 and compare.
check.L.fail.0: Value does not change → plugged into DO instead of AO
check.COLR.name: Color / absorbance (TCS34725 / AS7341)
check.COLR.errorNote: Absolute color values depend on the lighting. Always read them 'relative to a reference' with the same LED, distance and shield.
check.COLR.ref.0.note: Color balance is fine if R, G and B are within ±10 % of each other
check.COLR.ref.2.note: Take this value as I₀ and A = log(I₀/I) = 0
check.COLR.test.0: R≈G≈B on white paper, and R more than 2× G and B on red paper, is normal.
check.COLR.test.1: Cover the cuvette holder with a black box to block outside light; if the blank cuvette stays within ±1 % for 1 minute, you are ready to measure absorbance.
check.COLR.test.2: Doubling the concentration should roughly double the absorbance A (±10 %) (Beer–Lambert law).
check.COLR.fail.0: All channels 0 → I2C address 0x29 conflict (same as VL53L0X, etc.) or LED pin
check.COLR.fail.1: All 100 % → saturated. Adjust integration time and distance
check.pH.errorNote: A pH difference of 0.1 is a 26 % difference in [H⁺]. Experiments that look at 'change', like the equivalence point, tolerate a slightly off calibration, but comparing absolute values requires a 2-point calibration. Far from 25 °C, add ±0.05 per 10 °C of error.
check.pH.ref.2.note: Reference for base experiments. Easily lowered by CO₂ from the air
check.pH.test.0: Rinse the electrode with distilled water, shake off the drops gently (do not wipe) and put it in pH 7 buffer for 1 minute → 6.85–7.15 is normal. If not, do a 2-point calibration in [Calibrate sensor].
check.pH.test.1: Move it to pH 4 buffer; if it reaches 3.85–4.15 within 1 minute, the electrode slope is fine. If it takes more than 1 minute or stays at 4.5 or above, the electrode is aging.
check.pH.test.2: Distilled water has few ions, so the value drifts between 5 and 8 — this is not an electrode fault.
check.pH.test.3: After measuring, keep it in 3 M KCl storage solution. Soak an electrode that has dried out in KCl for 24 hours before use.
check.pH.fail.0: Stuck near 7.0 → BNC disconnected or broken electrode (0 mV = pH 7)
check.pH.fail.1: Value keeps drifting → electrode dried out, reference electrolyte used up, or interference from an EC sensor in the same beaker
check.pH.fail.2: Calibration fails → contaminated buffer. Use fresh buffer
check.ORP.name: Redox potential (ORP)
check.ORP.errorNote: ORP changes with temperature and pH, so compare the change (before and after adding an oxidizer or reducer) at the same temperature.
check.ORP.ref.3: 1 g of vitamin C dissolved in water
check.ORP.test.0: With the BNC unplugged it drifts near 0 mV → with the electrode plugged in, 200–650 mV in tap water.
check.ORP.test.1: Adding vitamin C should drop it by 200 mV or more within 2 minutes; one drop of dilute bleach makes it rise.
check.ORP.test.2: Pass if within ±15 mV in the standard solution; otherwise do a 1-point calibration in [Calibrate sensor].
check.ORP.fail.0: Stuck at 0 mV → BNC or electrode disconnected
check.ORP.fail.1: Value keeps fluctuating by 10 mV or more → stirring, or a dirty electrode. Wipe the platinum tip with soft paper
check.EC.name: Electrical conductivity (EC)
check.EC.accuracy: ±5 % F.S. (after calibration); without temperature compensation, 2 %/°C more error
check.EC.errorNote: EC is nearly proportional to concentration (dilute solutions) but not perfectly linear. Make a calibration curve (3–4 standard solutions) to find the concentration.
check.EC.ref.2.note: Rises to 2–5 µS/cm from CO₂ in the air
check.EC.ref.4.note: Over range — needs a K=10 probe
check.EC.test.0: 0–5 µS/cm in air and 10 or less in distilled water means the zero is fine.
check.EC.test.1: Pass if 1340–1480 in the 1413 standard solution. Otherwise do a 2-point calibration in [Calibrate sensor].
check.EC.test.2: If a pH sensor is in the same beaker, the AC signal from the EC electrode makes the pH fluctuate → measure separately, or turn off the EC power while reading pH.
check.EC.test.3: Record the solution temperature. At 10 °C below 25 °C it reads about 20 % low.
check.EC.fail.1: Value jumps to double → K value (1/10) setting does not match the probe
check.TDS.name: Total dissolved solids (TDS)
check.TDS.errorNote: TDS = EC × 0.5 (conversion factor). 1 g/L of salt is about 1000 ppm. For precise comparisons, an EC sensor is better.
check.TDS.test.0: 5 ppm or less in distilled water and 50–300 ppm in tap water is normal.
check.TDS.test.1: Pass if within ±10 % in the standard solution; otherwise use [Calibrate sensor].
check.TDS.test.2: The TDS sensor has no temperature compensation and assumes 25 °C — record the solution temperature as well.
check.TDS.fail.0: Stuck at 0 → probe disconnected or power
check.TDS.fail.1: Stuck at 1000 → over range (seawater, strong salt water)
check.DOX.name: Dissolved oxygen (DO, galvanic)
check.DOX.errorNote: Photosynthesis and respiration experiments compare the 'change per unit time', so the conclusion is the same even if the absolute value is off by ±0.5. Saturation concentration changes with temperature and pressure.
check.DOX.ref.0: Air-saturated water (25 °C, air pump for 10 min)
check.DOX.ref.0.note: 9.1 at 20 °C, 8.3 at 25 °C, 7.6 mg/L at 30 °C — enter the value for your temperature
check.DOX.ref.1.note: Zero reference — prepared by the teacher
check.DOX.ref.3: Boiled and cooled water (right after cooling)
check.DOX.test.0: After filling the membrane cap with electrolyte, wait 10 minutes in air until the saturation voltage is stable.
check.DOX.test.1: Pass if within ±0.6 mg/L of the saturation concentration for that temperature, in water saturated with an air pump for 10 minutes.
check.DOX.test.2: If it falls below 0.3 mg/L in sodium sulfite solution, the zero is fine. Boiled water is not a good zero reference because oxygen dissolves back in.
check.DOX.fail.0: Value barely changes → no electrolyte in the membrane cap, or damaged membrane
check.DOX.fail.1: Stuck at 20 mg/L → over range or poor BNC contact
check.TURB.name: Turbidity (relative)
check.TURB.errorNote: Absolute NTU values need calibration standards, so at school compare settling and flocculation rates as '% relative to clear water'.
check.TURB.ref.0.note: Module output near 4.1 V → close to 0 % in the app
check.TURB.ref.1: Muddy water (one spoonful of soil / 200 mL, right after stirring)
check.TURB.test.0: Below 8 % in clear water and above 50 % in muddy water is normal.
check.TURB.test.1: If the top of the sensor gets wet, the values jump — immerse it only up to the cable joint and wipe off drops.
check.TURB.test.2: Record muddy water for 10 minutes: the value should fall slowly as the soil settles.
check.TURB.fail.0: Stuck at 100 % → sensor out of the water, or light blocked
check.TURB.fail.1: Stuck at 0 → check the 5 V supply
check.V.name: Voltage (analog divider)
check.V.errorNote: The board's reference voltage varies ±3 % with USB power. For precise measurements, do a 1-point calibration against the 3.3V pin, or use an INA219 (VDC).
check.V.test.0: A0 on GND reads 0.00–0.02 V and on the 3.3V pin 3.2–3.4 V → the board ADC is fine.
check.V.test.1: Pass if a new AA cell reads 1.55–1.65 V. Within ±0.05 V of a multimeter matches the spec.
check.V.test.2: Connect (−) to GND. Connected the other way round it reads 0 V (negative voltages cannot be read).
check.V.fail.0: Stuck at 0 V → (+) and (−) swapped, or divider resistor broken
check.V.fail.1: Stuck at 5 V (or 3.3 V) → input over range — risk of board damage, disconnect at once
check.VDC.name: Voltage (INA219)
check.VDC.errorNote: ±0.5 %, as good as a multimeter. Measure voltage and current together and get resistance and power (P = VI) with a calculated column.
check.VDC.test.0: 3.25–3.35 V on the 3.3V pin is normal — the INA219 is more precise than the board ADC.
check.VDC.test.1: Put VIN+ and VIN− in series in the circuit to read current as well (to read voltage only, connect VIN− to GND).
check.VDC.fail.0: Stuck at 0 V → I2C address 0x40, or VIN− not connected
check.IDC.name: Current (INA219)
check.IDC.errorNote: Suited to small circuits in the mA range. For 1 A or more, use the ACS712 (I5A).
check.IDC.test.0: 0 ±1 mA with the circuit open means the zero is fine.
check.IDC.test.1: Pass if 11–16 mA in an LED + 220 Ω circuit (within ±10 % of the value from Ohm's law).
check.IDC.test.2: If the current flows the other way, it reads negative — VIN+ goes on the supply side.
check.IDC.fail.0: Stuck at 0 → VIN+ or VIN− disconnected (current must flow through the shunt between them)
check.IDC.fail.1: Value jumps to ±3200 mA → over range or shorted shunt
check.I5A.name: Current (ACS712 Hall sensor, 5 A)
check.I5A.range: ±5 A (±20 / ±30 A for 20 A / 30 A modules)
check.I5A.errorNote: For cell, motor and bulb circuits of 1 A or more. The zero shifts slightly with temperature, so check 0 A just before measuring.
check.I5A.ref.0.note: Zero is a 2.5 V output → 0 A
check.I5A.test.0: 0 ±0.1 A with the circuit open means the zero is fine. Otherwise set zero in [Calibrate sensor].
check.I5A.test.1: The value should rise as soon as the bulb is switched on and return to 0 when it is switched off.
check.I5A.test.2: Noise is ±0.05 A, so measure currents below 0.1 A with an INA219 (IDC).
check.I5A.fail.0: Value stuck at ±5 A → output pin unconnected, or supply is not 5 V
check.I5A.fail.1: Jumps ±0.3 A around 0 → long wires or motor noise → add a capacitor on the supply, shorten the wires
check.M.name: Mass / force (HX711 + load cell)
check.M.range: Load cell rating (1 kg, 5 kg, 10 kg)
check.M.accuracy: ±0.05 % of rating (1 kg cell → ±0.5 g, after 2-point calibration) + creep and temperature drift
check.M.errorNote: In mass-change experiments (gas release, evaporation), looking at the difference from the starting value cancels the zero error. A 1 kg cell shows 0.1 g changes.
check.M.ref.3.note: Density 0.998 g/mL. Graduated cylinder error ±2.5 mL
check.M.test.0: After zeroing, it is stable if within ±0.3 g for 1 minute. If it drifts slowly (creep, temperature), zero it again after 5 minutes.
check.M.test.1: Put five 500-won coins (38.5 g) on it: pass if within ±1 g. If not, do a 2-point calibration in [Calibrate sensor] (zero + known mass).
check.M.test.2: If a coin reads within ±0.3 g both in the middle and at the edge of the pan, the load cell is mounted correctly (if it is tilted, the edge reading differs).
check.M.fail.0: Value jumps wildly → load cell's 4 wires (red, black, white, green) in the wrong order, or DT and SCK swapped
check.M.fail.1: Stuck at 0 → HX711 power, DT pin
check.M.fail.2: Grows negative → load cell mounted upside down (check the arrow)
check.DIST.name: Distance (HC-SR04 ultrasonic / VL53L0X laser)
check.DIST.errorNote: Velocity and acceleration are rates of change of distance, so noise grows. On the rate graph use a wide averaging window, and use a reflector (a rigid flat board).
check.DIST.ref.0: A book stood at 20.0 cm by a ruler
check.DIST.ref.3: Within 2 cm right in front of the sensor (minimum distance)
check.DIST.ref.3.note: Ultrasonic cannot measure below 2 cm → 0 or a large value
check.DIST.test.0: Stand a book at 20.0 cm by a ruler: 19.5–20.5 cm is normal. If all three distances match, a 'Linear' fit gives a slope of 1.00 ±0.02.
check.DIST.test.1: Move your hand slowly back and forth: the value should follow smoothly. Occasional jumps to 0 or 400 mean the reflecting surface is slanted, or is cloth or sponge (sound-absorbing).
check.DIST.test.2: The speed of sound changes with temperature (0.17 %/°C). It is based on 20 °C, so at 30 °C distances read 1.7 % short.
check.DIST.fail.0: Stuck at 0 → TRIG and ECHO swapped, or supply is not 5 V
check.DIST.fail.1: Value stuck at 400 → no echo (angle, sound-absorbing material)
check.FSR.name: Force / press / bend (FSR, flex, potentiometer; relative)
check.FSR.errorNote: For experiments that need force in N, use a load cell (M). An FSR is good for timing ('when did the press start').
check.FSR.test.0: Below 3 % when not pressed and above 60 % when pressed hard is normal.
check.FSR.test.1: An FSR is not proportional to force (closer to logarithmic) — make a calibration curve with 50, 100 and 200 g weights.
check.FSR.test.2: Within ±10 % when repeating the same force is good enough for experiments.
check.FSR.fail.0: Value does not change → divider resistor (10 kΩ) missing, or AO pin
check.FSR.fail.1: Always 100 % → resistor on the 5V side instead of GND
check.DBA.name: Sound level (dBA meter module)
check.DBA.errorNote: dB is a logarithmic scale: a 10 dB difference is 10× the intensity. Experiments that compare peak values and changes over time work better than averages.
check.DBA.ref.0: Quiet classroom (during a lesson, no talking)
check.DBA.ref.3: Smartphone alarm at full volume (10 cm)
check.DBA.test.0: 35–50 dBA in a quiet place and 55–65 dBA for conversation at 1 m is normal.
check.DBA.test.1: Pass if within ±3 dB of a smartphone sound-meter app (smartphone mics are ±2 dB too).
check.DBA.test.2: Doubling the sound intensity should give +3 dB, doubling the distance −6 dB.
check.DBA.fail.0: Stuck at 30 dBA → no microphone input, or power
check.DBA.fail.1: Stuck at 130 → input overload, or output pin unconnected
check.SND.name: Loudness (analog microphone, relative)
check.SND.errorNote: It reads instantaneous peaks, so a spiky graph is normal. Smooth it with a 10-point average calculated column.
check.SND.test.0: Below 10 % when quiet and jumping above 50 % on a hand clap is normal.
check.SND.test.1: If you need absolute dB, use the DBA meter module. This sensor is for 'was there a sound, and how much louder was it'.
check.SND.fail.0: Value does not change → plugged into DO instead of AO, or adjust the sensitivity screw
check.MAG.name: Magnetic field (magnetometer)
check.MAG.accuracy: ±2 % + zero error of a few µT
check.MAG.errorNote: Magnet distance vs. field experiments give a Power fit (≈ 1/r³). Subtract the Earth's field (background) as the starting value.
check.MAG.ref.0: Earth's magnetic field (away from electronics and iron, sum of three axes)
check.MAG.ref.2: No magnet, one axis only (depends on sensor orientation)
check.MAG.test.0: Turn the sensor slowly through one full turn: X and Y should change like sine curves, while the sum of the three axes (√(x²+y²+z²)) stays nearly constant at 45–55 µT.
check.MAG.test.1: It should increase at once when you bring a magnet close and return when you take it away. If it does not return, the sensor has been magnetized (avoid strong magnets).
check.MAG.test.2: Laptops, speakers and steel desks distort the Earth's field — use a wooden desk.
check.MAG.fail.0: Stuck at 0 → I2C address (0x0D / 0x1E) or power
check.MAG.fail.1: Value stuck at the end of the range → saturated (magnet too close)
check.AX.name: Acceleration (MPU6050 / ADXL345)
check.AX.range: ±2 g (±19.6 m/s²), up to ±16 g depending on the setting
check.AX.errorNote: Acceleration always includes gravity. Look at motion acceleration as 'the difference from the value at rest'; velocity is the area (integral), but errors accumulate, so use short intervals only.
check.AX.ref.0: Lying flat on a desk — Z axis
check.AX.ref.1: Lying flat on a desk — X/Y axes
check.AX.ref.3: Free fall (dropped from your hand, all axes)
check.AX.test.0: Lying flat, Z ≈ 9.8 and X, Y ≈ 0. Turn each face downward: if all six directions read ±9.8 ±0.4, it is normal.
check.AX.test.1: Tap the desk: there should be a sharp peak that dies away at once.
check.AX.test.2: When tilted, gravity is shared between the axes → it can also be used as tilt (ANG).
check.AX.fail.0: All 0 → I2C address 0x68 (AD0 pin) or power
check.AX.fail.1: Only one axis stuck at 0 → damaged sensor
check.ANG.name: Tilt angle
check.ANG.errorNote: In incline friction experiments, an angle error of ±1° gives a ±2 % error in the sine. Change the angle and measure several times.
check.ANG.test.0: 0 ±1.5° on the desk and 90 ±1.5° against a wall is normal.
check.ANG.test.1: Pass if within ±2° on a set square (30, 45, 60°). The desk itself may be tilted, so turn it 180° and take the average.
check.ANG.test.2: While moving, acceleration mixes in and the angle is wrong — stop, wait 1 second, then read.
check.ANG.fail.0: Value jumps → sensor shaking or power noise
check.PPG.name: Heart rate (MAX30102 and other optical sensors)
check.PPG.errorNote: Optical sensors are sensitive to movement. Keep your hand fixed on the desk while measuring, and look at the post-exercise 'recovery curve' with an Exponential approach fit.
check.PPG.ref.1: After 1 minute of running on the spot
check.PPG.test.0: Rest your finger lightly on it (pressing hard blocks the blood flow); 60–100 after 15 s is normal.
check.PPG.test.1: Pass if within ±5 of your wrist pulse counted for 15 s × 4.
check.PPG.test.2: When you lift your finger it should drop to 0 / no value. If numbers still appear, ambient light is getting in — shade the sensor.
check.PPG.fail.0: Stuck at 0 → sensor LED not lit (I2C 0x57, power)
check.PPG.fail.1: Reads double (150–200) → finger moving or pressing too hard
check.PM25.name: Particulate matter PM2.5 / PM10 (PMS7003 / SDS011)
check.PM25.errorNote: Low-cost light-scattering sensors read high above 80 % humidity. Compare 'before and after ventilation / change over time' rather than absolute values.
check.PM25.ref.0: Nearest AirKorea station value (outdoors, outside the window)
check.PM25.ref.0.note: Enter the station's PM2.5 value as the expected value; pass if within ±20 % + 10 µg/m³
check.PM25.ref.2: Burn one incense stick or match (1 m)
check.PM25.ref.2.note: Jumps at once and comes down over 10–30 minutes
check.PM25.ref.3.note: PM2.5 bands: Good 0–15, Moderate 16–35, Bad 36–75, Very bad 76+
check.PM25.test.0: 30 s after power-on, once the value is stable, compare with the AirKorea station → within ±20 % + 10 µg/m³ is normal.
check.PM25.test.1: Light and blow out a match: it should jump above 100 µg/m³ within 1 minute.
check.PM25.test.2: You should hear the fan. If the fan does not run, the 5 V supply or current (100 mA) is insufficient.
check.PM25.fail.0: Stuck at 0 → UART crossover (TX→RX) or fan stopped
check.PM25.fail.1: Value stays in the hundreds → inlet clogged with dust or fluff
check.UV.name: UV index (GUVA-S12SD / VEML6075)
check.UV.errorNote: Index 1 = 25 mW/m² (UV-B weighted). Sensor types differ (UV-A/UV-B sensitivity), so absolute values are for reference only; blocking comparisons (%) are reliable.
check.UV.ref.1: Korea Meteorological Administration UV index (noon, clear day)
check.UV.ref.1.note: Enter the KMA forecast as the expected value. Summer noon 7–10, winter 1–3
check.UV.test.0: 0–0.5 indoors; it should rise as soon as you go out into sunlight.
check.UV.test.1: Pass if within ±1.5 of the KMA UV index (varies with time of day and clouds).
check.UV.test.2: Covering it with clear film coated with sunscreen should cut it by 90 % or more (SPF experiment).
check.UV.fail.0: Stuck at 0 → output pin unconnected, or behind glass
check.UV.fail.1: Always high → right under a fluorescent lamp (which emits some UV)
check.SOIL.name: Soil moisture (relative)
check.SOIL.errorNote: The % value is only 'relative to saturation', not the actual water content (g/g). Compare drying curves with an Exponential approach fit.
check.SOIL.ref.3.note: Depends on soil type and compaction
check.SOIL.test.0: Below 5 % in air and above 90 % in water is normal (use these two for a 2-point [Calibrate sensor]).
check.SOIL.test.1: Push it into dry soil and water it: the value should rise within 1–2 minutes.
check.SOIL.test.2: Resistive sensors (two metal prongs) corrode, so power them only while measuring. Capacitive sensors (v1.2) can stay in.
check.SOIL.fail.0: Value does not change → AO pin or power
check.SOIL.fail.1: 60 % or less even in water → corroded electrodes, or poor soil contact for a capacitive sensor
check.GAS.name: Gas concentration (MQ series, relative)
check.GAS.accuracy: Relative value — not quantitative (±20 % or worse)
check.GAS.response: 10–30 s, recovery 1–3 min; burn in for 24–48 hours before first use
check.GAS.errorNote: Converting to ppm needs a calibration for each gas, so at school compare 'how many times the baseline'. The baseline shifts with temperature and humidity.
check.GAS.ref.0.note: Baseline — depends on module and temperature
check.GAS.ref.2: A little lighter gas (MQ-2, do not ignite)
check.GAS.test.0: Warm it up for 3 minutes after power-on; once the baseline is stable within ±2 %, you are ready (the heater has to be warm).
check.GAS.test.1: It should rise within 10–30 s when the target gas comes close and return to the baseline over 1–3 minutes when it is removed.
check.GAS.test.2: Leave a new sensor switched on for 24–48 hours before use so the baseline settles.
check.GAS.fail.0: Value does not change → heater supply not 5 V (does not work properly on 3.3 V boards) or AO pin
check.GAS.fail.1: Baseline keeps rising → not burned in enough, or humidity
check.FLOW.name: Flow rate (YF-S201 and other paddle-wheel sensors)
check.FLOW.errorNote: The area of flow rate (L/min) over time is the total volume (L). Slow flows (below 1 L/min) do not turn the paddle wheel and cannot be measured.
check.FLOW.ref.0: Fill a 1 L beaker from the tap (timed)
check.FLOW.ref.0.note: Find the total of 1 L as the area (integral) and compare
check.FLOW.test.0: It should rise as soon as water flows and be 0 when it stops.
check.FLOW.test.1: Pass if the area under the flow graph is 0.85–1.15 L while collecting 1 L.
check.FLOW.test.2: Water must flow in the direction of the arrow; air bubbles make the value jump.
check.FLOW.fail.0: Stuck at 0 → signal wire not on D3 (pulse port), or supply not 5 V
check.FLOW.fail.1: Value is half → the factor (7.5 Hz/L/min) setting does not match the sensor
check.CPM.name: Radiation (Geiger counter)
check.CPM.errorNote: The statistical error of N counts is √N. To get the error down to 10 % you need 100 counts; for 3 %, 1000 counts.
check.CPM.ref.1: Potassium fertilizer (KCl) or a bunch of bananas (1 cm)
check.CPM.ref.2: Uranium glass or a thorium lantern mantle (1 cm)
check.CPM.ref.2.note: Teaching sample kept by the teacher
check.CPM.test.0: With nothing nearby, a 1-minute average of 10–35 CPM is normal (0–2 'ticks' per second).
check.CPM.test.1: Hold a bag of KCl fertilizer to it: the 1-minute average should rise by 1.5× or more.
check.CPM.test.2: Radiation is random, so 1-minute values vary by ±30 % → compare 5–10 minute averages.
check.CPM.fail.0: Stuck at 0 → pulse wire not on D3, or high-voltage circuit off
check.CPM.fail.1: Stuck at thousands of CPM → noise or poor contact
check.WIND.name: Wind speed (anemometer)
check.WIND.errorNote: Wind speed around buildings varies a lot from place to place. Compare changes over time or with height at the same spot.
check.WIND.ref.1: Electric fan on high at 30 cm
check.WIND.ref.2: KMA current wind speed (rooftop, sports field)
check.WIND.ref.2.note: Enter the KMA value as the expected value, but around buildings a 1.5× difference is common
check.WIND.test.0: 0–0.3 indoors and 3 m/s or more in front of a fan is normal.
check.WIND.test.1: The value should step up with the fan on low, medium and high.
check.WIND.fail.0: Stuck at 0 → power (usually a separate 7–24 V) or the 0–5 V signal exceeds a 3.3 V board's range
sensor.DACC.name: Acceleration (magnitude)
sensor.DACC.note: Built-in accelerometer of this device. At rest it reads about 9.8 m/s² because of gravity.
sensor.DAX.name: Acceleration x
sensor.DAX.note: Built-in accelerometer, x axis (across the screen).
sensor.DAY.name: Acceleration y
sensor.DAY.note: Built-in accelerometer, y axis (up the screen).
sensor.DAZ.name: Acceleration z
sensor.DAZ.note: Built-in accelerometer, z axis (perpendicular to the screen).
sensor.DGYR.name: Rotation rate
sensor.DGYR.note: Built-in gyroscope. Magnitude of the rotation rate about all three axes.
sensor.DMAG.name: Magnetic field
sensor.DMAG.note: Built-in magnetometer. Earth's magnetic field is about 25–65 µT.
sensor.DBAR.name: Air pressure (device)
sensor.DSND.name: Loudness
sensor.DSND.note: Device microphone. Relative dB (approximate) — not as accurate as a sound level meter.
sensor.DFRQ.name: Sound frequency
sensor.DFRQ.note: Finds the strongest frequency with the device microphone. For tuning forks and musical pitch.
sensor.DCR.name: Camera red
sensor.DCR.note: Red brightness at the center of the device camera view (0–255).
sensor.DCG.name: Camera green
sensor.DCG.note: Green brightness at the center of the device camera view (0–255).
sensor.DCB.name: Camera blue
sensor.DCB.note: Blue brightness at the center of the device camera view (0–255).
sensor.DAR.name: Absorbance (red)
sensor.DAR.note: Absorbance from the camera's red light, A = −log(I/I₀). Set zero with water before measuring.
sensor.DAR.cal.hint: Point at water (blank) and set zero
sensor.DAG.name: Absorbance (green)
sensor.DAG.note: Absorbance from the camera's green light. Best for red and purple solutions.
sensor.DAG.cal.hint: Point at water (blank) and set zero
sensor.DAB.name: Absorbance (blue)
sensor.DAB.note: Absorbance from the camera's blue light. Best for yellow and orange solutions.
sensor.DAB.cal.hint: Point at water (blank) and set zero
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.title: Concentration and absorbance (camera colorimetry)
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.subject: Device sensor experiments
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.summary: Measure the absorbance of diluted solutions with the camera and check whether absorbance is proportional to concentration.
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.steps.0: Place a cuvette (clear test tube) in front of white paper and fix the device camera in place. Keep the lighting constant.
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.steps.1: Fill it with water, line it up with the square in the center of the screen, then press [Set zero].
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.steps.2: Swap in the 0 %, 20 %, 40 % … 100 % solutions one by one and press ‘Record value’ for each.
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.steps.3: Choose the absorbance for the complementary color of the solution (red light for a blue solution) and use ‘Curve fit → Linear’ to see the proportional relationship.
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.steps.4: Use the absorbance of a solution of unknown concentration to find its concentration.
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.materials.1: Copper(II) sulfate solution or food coloring
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.cautions.0: After setting zero, do not move the camera, the lighting or the cuvette.
exp.cur-d-beer-lambert.cautions.1: Keep the device off the tray so no solution spills on it.
exp.cur-d-bottle-pitch.title: Water level and bottle pitch
exp.cur-d-bottle-pitch.subject: Device sensor experiments
exp.cur-d-bottle-pitch.summary: See how the frequency of the sound made by blowing across a bottle changes as you fill it with water.
exp.cur-d-bottle-pitch.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-d-bottle-pitch.steps.0: Blow across the mouth of an empty glass bottle to make a sound and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-d-bottle-pitch.steps.1: Add water 2 cm at a time and record the same way.
exp.cur-d-bottle-pitch.steps.2: Use ‘Curve fit’ to find the relationship between the length of the remaining air column and the frequency.
exp.cur-d-building-height.title: Measuring building height with air pressure
exp.cur-d-building-height.subject: Device sensor experiments
exp.cur-d-building-height.summary: Climb the stairs and find the height from how much the air pressure drops (about 0.1 kPa per 8 m).
exp.cur-d-building-height.markers.label: Floor
exp.cur-d-building-height.steps.0: Start the run on the 1st floor.
exp.cur-d-building-height.steps.1: Each time you go up a floor, write the floor in ‘Add note’.
exp.cur-d-building-height.steps.2: Find the height as pressure difference (kPa) × about 80 m, and compare it with the real floor height.
exp.cur-d-building-height.materials.0: iPhone or iPad with a barometer
exp.cur-d-building-height.cautions.0: Do not look at the screen while walking on stairs.
exp.cur-d-elevator.title: Feeling heavier in an elevator
exp.cur-d-elevator.subject: Device sensor experiments
exp.cur-d-elevator.summary: See the floor-direction acceleration rise above and fall below 9.8 as the elevator starts and stops.
exp.cur-d-elevator.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-d-elevator.steps.0: Place the device screen-up on the floor of the elevator.
exp.cur-d-elevator.steps.1: Start the run and press the button for an upper floor.
exp.cur-d-elevator.steps.2: Check whether z rises above or falls below 9.8 when the elevator starts and stops.
exp.cur-d-elevator.steps.3: Use ‘Area’ to integrate (z − 9.8) and find the elevator's speed.
exp.cur-d-elevator.cautions.0: Do not get in the way of other people using the elevator.
exp.cur-d-fading-color.title: Rate of a fading-color reaction
exp.cur-d-fading-color.subject: Device sensor experiments
exp.cur-d-fading-color.summary: Use the graph of falling absorbance as a dye is bleached to study how reaction rate depends on concentration.
exp.cur-d-fading-color.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-d-fading-color.steps.0: Fill the cuvette with water and press [Set zero].
exp.cur-d-fading-color.steps.1: Add the (blue) food coloring solution and start the run the moment you add a few drops of bleach.
exp.cur-d-fading-color.steps.2: Fit the falling absorbance curve with ‘Curve fit → Exponential’ and find the half-life.
exp.cur-d-fading-color.steps.3: Change the amount of bleach, do a new run and compare the slopes (tangents).
exp.cur-d-fading-color.cautions.0: Wear safety glasses and gloves so bleach does not touch your eyes or skin.
exp.cur-d-fading-color.cautions.1: Do not mix with acidic solutions (chlorine gas).
exp.cur-d-iodine-clock.title: Iodine clock reaction (camera color)
exp.cur-d-iodine-clock.subject: Device sensor experiments
exp.cur-d-iodine-clock.summary: Time the moment the solution suddenly turns blue using camera color values, and compare concentration with reaction time.
exp.cur-d-iodine-clock.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-d-iodine-clock.steps.0: Place the beaker in front of white paper and fix the camera so the beaker fills the center square.
exp.cur-d-iodine-clock.steps.1: Start the run the moment you mix the two solutions.
exp.cur-d-iodine-clock.steps.2: Read the time when the red and green values drop sharply as the reaction time.
exp.cur-d-iodine-clock.steps.3: Change the concentration, do a new run and compare 1/time with concentration.
exp.cur-d-iodine-clock.cautions.0: Keep the device at a distance so reagents do not splash on it.
exp.cur-d-magnet-distance.title: Magnetic field strength and distance
exp.cur-d-magnet-distance.subject: Device sensor experiments
exp.cur-d-magnet-distance.summary: See how the magnetic field strength drops as you move a magnet away from the device.
exp.cur-d-magnet-distance.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-d-magnet-distance.steps.0: First write down the value with no magnet (Earth's magnetic field).
exp.cur-d-magnet-distance.steps.1: Starting 2 cm from the top of the device, move the magnet away 1 cm at a time and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-d-magnet-distance.steps.2: Subtract Earth's field and fit the values with ‘Curve fit → Power’.
exp.cur-d-magnet-distance.cautions.0: Do not put strong magnets against the device.
exp.cur-d-pendulum.title: Period of a pendulum (device acceleration)
exp.cur-d-pendulum.subject: Device sensor experiments
exp.cur-d-pendulum.summary: Use the device as the pendulum bob, measure the repeating period of the acceleration and study how period depends on string length.
exp.cur-d-pendulum.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-d-pendulum.steps.0: Put the device in a sturdy case and hang it from two strings in a V shape so it swings like a swing.
exp.cur-d-pendulum.steps.1: Pull it back about 10°, let go and start the run.
exp.cur-d-pendulum.steps.2: Read the time between the highest acceleration peaks (half a period) and find the period.
exp.cur-d-pendulum.steps.3: Change the string length, do a new run and compare period² with length.
exp.cur-d-pendulum.cautions.0: Check the knots twice and put a cushion underneath so the device cannot fall.
exp.cur-d-sound-distance.title: Loudness and distance
exp.cur-d-sound-distance.subject: Device sensor experiments
exp.cur-d-sound-distance.summary: See how loudness (dB) drops as you move away from a sound source.
exp.cur-d-sound-distance.markers.label: Add note
exp.cur-d-sound-distance.steps.0: Play a steady sound (e.g. 1000 Hz) from a speaker.
exp.cur-d-sound-distance.steps.1: Move the device 0.5 m at a time and press ‘Record value’.
exp.cur-d-sound-distance.steps.2: Use ‘Curve fit → Logarithmic’ to check that loudness drops about 6 dB each time the distance doubles.
device.dev-accel.name: Acceleration (magnitude)
device.dev-accel.how.0: Fix the device firmly to the setup (cart, pendulum bob, elevator floor).
device.dev-accel.how.1: Press [Start] and move it. If it reads about 9.8 m/s² (gravity) at rest, it is working.
device.dev-accel.how.2: For fast motion, shorten the sampling interval to 0.05 s.
device.dev-accel.cautions.0: Use a case and a strap so it does not fall.
device.dev-accel.cautions.1: Holding it in a shaky hand makes the values jump around.
device.dev-accel.ideas.0: Elevator speeding up and slowing down
device.dev-accel3.name: Acceleration, 3 axes (x, y, z)
device.dev-accel3.how.0: Lying flat, screen up: z ≈ 9.8, x and y ≈ 0.
device.dev-accel3.how.1: Tilting it changes how gravity is shared between the axes.
device.dev-accel3.how.2: Fix it in place, then press [Start].
device.dev-accel3.cautions.0: Axes: x across the screen, y up the screen, z perpendicular to the screen (+ towards the screen side).
device.dev-gyro.name: Rotation rate (gyro)
device.dev-gyro.how.0: Fix the device at the center of a turntable or swivel chair.
device.dev-gyro.how.1: Press [Start], then spin. 1 turn per second = about 6.28 rad/s.
device.dev-gyro.cautions.0: Near the edge of a turntable it can slide off.
device.dev-mag.name: Magnetic field
device.dev-mag.how.0: Slowly move a magnet or a wire near the top of the device.
device.dev-mag.how.1: With nothing nearby it shows Earth's magnetic field (about 25–65 µT).
device.dev-mag.cautions.0: Do not put strong magnets against the device (the compass and sensor can be thrown off).
device.dev-mag.ideas.1: Magnetic field of an electric current
device.dev-baro.name: Air pressure (built-in)
device.dev-baro.how.0: Carry the device up or down stairs, or take an elevator.
device.dev-baro.how.1: Going up about 8 m lowers the pressure by about 0.1 kPa.
device.dev-baro.cautions.0: On iPads without a barometer this card is not shown.
device.dev-sound.name: Loudness
device.dev-sound.how.0: Point the device microphone (hole at the bottom) towards the sound.
device.dev-sound.how.1: The first time, you are asked for microphone permission. Press [Allow].
device.dev-sound.cautions.0: Values are relative dB (approximate). They differ between devices, so compare using the same device.
device.dev-sound.cautions.1: No audio is recorded — only loudness is logged.
device.dev-pitch.name: Sound frequency (pitch)
device.dev-pitch.how.0: Sound a tuning fork, an instrument or a water-filled glass bottle close to the microphone.
device.dev-pitch.how.1: The strongest frequency is shown in Hz (middle C ≈ 262 Hz).
device.dev-pitch.cautions.0: In a noisy room other frequencies get picked up.
device.dev-color.name: Camera color (RGB)
device.dev-color.how.0: Place a clear test tube or cuvette in front of white paper and fix the camera in place.
device.dev-color.how.1: Line up the solution inside the square in the center of the screen.
device.dev-color.how.2: Keep the lighting constant and press [Start].
device.dev-color.cautions.0: If the brightness changes, the values change. Indoor lighting is steadier than sunlight from a window.
device.dev-absorb.name: Absorbance (camera colorimetry)
device.dev-absorb.how.0: Fix the cuvette as for the camera color card, with a white background and constant lighting.
device.dev-absorb.how.1: Fill it with water (blank) and press [Set zero].
device.dev-absorb.how.2: Record values while swapping in solutions of different concentration. Look at the absorbance for the opposite (complementary) color of the solution.
device.dev-absorb.cautions.0: After setting zero, do not move the camera, the lighting or the cuvette.
device.dev-absorb.cautions.1: These are classroom estimates, not precision spectrophotometer values.
